text: Achalasia — Distal esophageal spasm and other esophageal motility disorders Gastroesophageal reflux disease with peptic stricture Esophageal or gastric cardia malignancy causing pseudoachalasia Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi infection) Eosinophilic esophagitis Scleroderma-related esophageal dysmotility Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi) causing destruction of myenteric plexus with achalasia-like esophageal dysfunction Barium esophagram — shows esophageal dilation with distal 'bird's beak' tapering and poor emptying High-resolution esophageal manometry — confirms diagnosis via absent peristalsis and impaired LES relaxation, and subtypes achalasia (I–III) Upper endoscopy — mandatory to exclude a mechanical or malignant cause (pseudoachalasia) at or near the gastroesophageal junction Endoscopic ultrasound or CT chest/abdomen — used selectively when pseudoachalasia from tumor infiltration is suspected Serology for Trypanosoma cruzi — considered in patients from endemic regions to exclude Chagas disease Timed barium swallow — assesses esophageal emptying and is useful for monitoring treatment response Chest imaging — may incidentally reveal a dilated, air/fluid-filled esophagus or absent gastric air bubble Peptic or malignant esophageal stricture Esophageal or gastroesophageal junction carcinoma (pseudoachalasia) Diffuse esophageal spasm Scleroderma esophagus Eosinophilic esophagitis Achalasia results from degeneration of inhibitory neurons in the myenteric (Auerbach) plexus of the esophagus, leading to loss of coordinated peristalsis in the esophageal body and failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax appropriately with swallowing. The cause is usually idiopathic, though an autoimmune or postviral inflammatory process targeting these neurons is suspected in many

Acute Bronchitis — Community-acquired pneumonia (distinguished by a new infiltrate on chest radiography and focal exam findings) (p.1024). Acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis / COPD (p.1024). Heart failure (p.1024). Pulmonary embolism (p.1024). Influenza and nonspecific upper respiratory infection, which overlap clinically with lower-tract infection (p.252). Pneumonia (cough plus sputum, dyspnea, chest pain, fever, and a new infiltrate point to pneumonia rather than bronchitis) (p.1537, p.1024). Influenza (overlapping cough and systemic features; can be complicated by secondary bacterial infection) (p.1537). Pertussis / subacute postinfectious tracheobronchitis (a frequent cause of cough persisting 3-8 weeks) (p.272). Chest radiography should be obtained whenever pneumonia is suspected, to confirm the absence of an infiltrate that defines acute bronchitis (p.1537). Specific viral diagnosis is generally unnecessary but, when needed, RT-PCR/multiplex respiratory panels are the most sensitive tests; results must be interpreted cautiously because viral genome can persist for weeks after a resolved infection (p.1537). Acute coronary syndrome / myocardial infarction presenting as cough and dyspnea, illustrated by a fatal case in which exertional dyspnea and chest heaviness were prematurely labeled acute bronchitis (p.21). Cough-variant asthma (p.272). Gastroesophageal reflux (p.272). Rhinosinusitis with postnasal drainage (p.272).

Acute liver failure — Decompensated chronic liver disease (cirrhosis with acute-on-chronic liver failure) Severe acute hepatitis without encephalopathy (acute liver injury short of failure) Ischemic hepatitis (shock liver) Acute Budd-Chiari syndrome and other vascular liver outflow obstruction Acute fatty liver of pregnancy / HELLP syndrome Malignant infiltration of the liver causing acute hepatic dysfunction Viral hepatitis A, B, D (with B), and E Herpes simplex virus hepatitis Cytomegalovirus hepatitis Leptospirosis with hepatic involvement Severe sepsis with secondary hepatic dysfunction Prothrombin time/INR — core diagnostic criterion and key prognostic marker Arterial ammonia level — correlates with risk of cerebral edema and severe encephalopathy Acetaminophen level and detailed drug/toxin/supplement history — identifies the most common treatable etiology Viral hepatitis serologies (A, B, C, D, E) and, where relevant, HSV/CMV testing — identifies infectious causes Autoimmune markers (ANA, smooth muscle antibody, immunoglobulins) and ceruloplasmin/copper studies — screens for autoimmune hepatitis and Wilson disease Doppler ultrasound of hepatic and portal vasculature — evaluates for vascular outflow obstruction Arterial blood gas, lactate, and renal function — assess systemic perfusion and evolving multiorgan dysfunction Blood and other cultures with a low threshold for infection screening — ALF patients are prone to occult sepsis

Adult-onset Still disease — Systemic lupus erythematosus Lymphoma and other malignancy Viral or bacterial systemic infection Reactive arthritis Vasculitis (e.g., polyarteritis nodosa) Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms Viral exanthems (parvovirus B19, rubella, hepatitis) Infective endocarditis Occult bacterial sepsis Tuberculosis Serum ferritin and glycosylated ferritin fraction — marked elevation with low glycosylated fraction supports diagnosis Complete blood count with differential — neutrophilic leukocytosis typical; cytopenias raise concern for macrophage activation syndrome Liver function tests — transaminitis is common Blood cultures and viral serologies — to exclude infectious mimics before immunosuppression ANA and rheumatoid factor — expected negative, helps exclude other connective tissue disease Imaging or lymph node biopsy — to exclude lymphoma when lymphadenopathy is prominent Joint imaging — assess for erosive arthritis, notably of the wrist, in chronic disease Triglycerides, fibrinogen, soluble CD25/IL-2 receptor — screen for macrophage activation syndrome if clinical deterioration occurs Systemic lupus erythematosus Lymphoma Kikuchi disease Drug hypersensitivity reaction Familial Mediterranean fever and other periodic fever syndromes AOSD is an autoinflammatory disorder driven by innate immune activation rather than autoantibody-mediated disease, with overproduction of proinflammatory cytokines including interleukin-1, interleukin-6, interleukin-18, and tumor necrosis factor. This cytokine storm produces the systemic febrile illness, marked acute-phase response, and hyperferritinemia seen clinically. Amoebic Liver Abscess — Pyogenic liver abscess (the most important imaging-based distinction once a hepatic abscess is identified) (p.1801) Malaria (p.1801) Typhoid/enteric fever (p.1801) Pulmonary disease (p.1801) Gallbladder disease (p.1801) Any febrile illness with few localizing signs / fever of unknown origin, since 10-15% present with fever alone (p.1799, p.1801) Pyogenic liver abscess (p.1801) Malaria (p.1801) Typhoid (enteric) fever (p.1801) Serum alkaline phosphatase and aminotransferases (enzymes often normal/minimally elevated; raised aminotransferases suggest acute disease or complication) (p.1800) Full blood count for leukocytosis >10,000/uL, present in about three-quarters of patients, especially with acute or complicated disease (p.1800) Enzyme immunoassay for the Gal/GalNAc lectin antigen, usable on stool and on liver-abscess aspirates (p.1800) Multiplex PCR for E. histolytica DNA (near 100% sensitivity/specificity) (p.1800) Loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) on abscess pus as a low-cost molecular option (p.1800) Diagnostic aspirate sent for Gram stain and bacterial culture when distinguishing amebic from pyogenic abscess (p.1801) Gallbladder disease (p.1801) Pulmonary disease presenting with right-sided pleural/pleuritic findings (p.1801) Entamoeba histolytica trophozoites invade colonic mucosal venules and travel via the portal venous system to the liver; the organism is resistant to complement-mediated lysis, which is critical to its survival in the bloodstream. An early acute infiltrate (predominantly neutrophils) is followed by lysis of those neutrophils on contact with amebae, and the released neutrophil toxins are thought to contribute to hepatocyte necrosis. The liver parenchyma is progressively replaced by necrotic material surrounded

Aspiration Pneumonia — Foreign-body/food aspiration causing major-airway obstruction with atelectasis and nonspecific inflammation, managed by removal rather than antibiotics (p.1418) Chemical (acid) pneumonitis, e.g., Mendelson syndrome from regurgitated gastric contents (p.1418) Pneumococcal pneumonia, distinguished by its more acute presentation (p.1418) Lung abscess (subacute anaerobic infection) as a related/overlapping entity (p.1072, p.1418) Pneumococcal pneumonia presenting more acutely than indolent anaerobic aspiration infection (p.1418) Chest radiography looking for consolidation in dependent lung segments (basilar lower-lobe segments if aspiration occurred upright; posterior segment of the upper lobe or superior segment of the lower lobe if supine) (p.1418) Gram stain of sputum, which characteristically shows a mixed bacterial population with many polymorphonuclear leukocytes (p.1418) Bronchoscopic protected-brush specimens or bronchoalveolar lavage, which may recover anaerobes from the lower tract with less oropharyngeal contamination (role still being defined) (p.1418) Assessment of dentition/oral hygiene, given the association of severe dental disease with aspiration pneumonia (p.1418) Chemical pneumonitis (Mendelson syndrome) from aspiration of acidic gastric juices, with rapid alveolar injury and pulmonary edema, often without fever and frequently needing no antibiotics (p.1418) Foreign-body/food aspiration with airway obstruction and atelectasis (p.1418)

Autoimmune encephalitis — Herpes simplex virus encephalitis Other viral or infectious encephalitides Primary psychiatric disorder (new-onset psychosis, catatonia) Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease and other rapidly progressive dementias Toxic-metabolic encephalopathy Non-convulsive status epilepticus of other etiology Herpes simplex encephalitis Enteroviral or arboviral encephalitis Bacterial meningoencephalitis Neurosyphilis HIV-associated encephalopathy Serum and CSF autoimmune/paraneoplastic antibody panel (NMDAR, LGI1, CASPR2, GABA-B, AMPA, and onconeural antibodies) — confirms specific antibody-mediated syndrome MRI brain with contrast — assesses for mesial temporal/limbic T2-FLAIR signal change and excludes structural or infectious mimics CSF analysis (cell count, protein, oligoclonal bands, HSV PCR) — distinguishes autoimmune from infectious causes and supports diagnosis EEG — detects epileptiform activity, extreme delta brush pattern (suggestive of anti-NMDAR encephalitis), or non-convulsive status epilepticus Whole-body imaging (CT/MRI chest-abdomen-pelvis, pelvic ultrasound/MRI in women, testicular ultrasound in men) — screens for occult tumor, especially ovarian teratoma or thymoma FDG-PET brain — may show characteristic regional hyper- or hypometabolism when MRI is unrevealing Thyroid function and thyroid antibodies — evaluates for Hashimoto encephalopathy as a mimic Tumor markers/gynecologic evaluation as guided by antibody subtype — directs targeted tumor search

Autoimmune hepatitis — Drug-induced liver injury Viral hepatitis (acute or chronic hepatitis B or C) Wilson disease Primary biliary cholangitis Primary sclerosing cholangitis Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis Acute viral hepatitis A, B, C, or E Epstein-Barr virus or cytomegalovirus hepatitis ANA and anti-smooth-muscle antibody — supports type 1 AIH diagnosis Anti-LKM1 antibody — supports type 2 AIH, more typical in pediatric cases Serum IgG level — characteristic hypergammaglobulinemia aids diagnosis and monitoring Liver biopsy — confirms interface hepatitis and plasma cell infiltrate, stages fibrosis Viral hepatitis serologies (hepatitis B and C) — exclude viral etiology Ceruloplasmin and copper studies — exclude Wilson disease, especially in younger patients Alkaline phosphatase and antimitochondrial antibody — screen for overlap with primary biliary cholangitis Standardized AIH scoring system (simplified diagnostic criteria) — integrates autoantibodies, IgG, histology, and viral exclusion Drug-induced or toxin-induced hepatitis Wilson disease Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease/steatohepatitis Primary biliary cholangitis and primary sclerosing cholangitis overlap AIH results from a breakdown in immune self-tolerance leading to T-cell-mediated attack on hepatocytes in a genetically susceptible host, often triggered by an environmental factor such as a viral infection or drug exposure. Autoantibody production (ANA, anti-smooth-muscle antibody, or anti-LKM1) accompanies the T-cell-driven injury but is thought to be a marker rather than the primary mediator of hepatocyte damage. Chronic interface hepatitis with ongoing necroinflammation can progress to fibrosis and cirrhosis if untreated.

Brain Abscess — Subdural empyema Bacterial meningitis Viral meningoencephalitis Superior sagittal sinus thrombosis Acute disseminated encephalomyelitis Primary or metastatic brain tumor (the major consideration when fever is absent) Cerebral infarction or hematoma (can resemble abscess on CT/MRI) Neurocysticercosis Tuberculoma (a major cause of focal CNS mass lesions in India and East Asia) Subdural empyema Bacterial meningitis Viral meningoencephalitis Cerebral toxoplasmosis (reactivation, mainly in immunocompromised/HIV hosts) Neurocysticercosis Tuberculoma Nocardial, Aspergillus, Candida, or Cryptococcus CNS lesions in immunocompromised hosts MRI is preferred over CT, being superior for detecting early (cerebritis-stage) lesions and posterior fossa abscesses (p.1178). Diffusion-weighted imaging with apparent diffusion coefficient mapping to separate abscess (restricted diffusion) from tumor (p.1178). Gram stain plus aerobic, anaerobic, mycobacterial, and fungal cultures of abscess material obtained by CT-guided stereotactic needle aspiration (p.1179). Inflammatory markers: peripheral leukocytosis in about half, elevated ESR in about 60%, and elevated C-reactive protein in about 80% of patients (p.1179). Serum IgG antibody to Toxoplasma gondii when imaging suggests toxoplasmosis (p.1181). Enzyme-linked immunotransfer blot as a confirmatory test for neurocysticercosis, plus funduscopic examination in suspected cases (p.1181).

Bronchiectasis Exacerbation — COPD - airflow obstruction on pulmonary function testing overlaps with bronchiectasis at presentation (Harrison 22e p.2243) Asthma - may coexist; ABPA should be considered in refractory asthma (Harrison 22e p.2242-2243) Cystic fibrosis - should be excluded early in any diffuse bronchiectasis workup (Harrison 22e p.2243) Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis (central-airway-predominant) (Harrison 22e p.2242-2243) Nontuberculous mycobacterial (especially MAC) airway infection - organisms may be colonisers rather than true pathogens, complicating interpretation of positive cultures (Harrison 22e p.2243) Active or reactivated tuberculosis (in endemic areas, a cause and mimic of recurrent airway infection) (Harrison 22e p.2242) High-resolution chest CT - imaging modality of choice; more specific than chest radiograph; look for airway dilation as 'tram tracks' or the 'signet-ring sign' (airway diameter at least 1.5x the adjacent vessel), lack of bronchial tapering, bronchial wall thickening, and inspissated secretions in a 'tree-in-bud' pattern (Harrison 22e p.2243) Bronchoscopy - almost always required in focal bronchiectasis to exclude airway obstruction by mass or foreign body; consider with BAL in diffuse disease if no pathogen is identified (Harrison 22e p.2243) Pulmonary function testing - functional assessment, typically showing mild-to-moderate airflow obstruction (Harrison 22e p.2243)

Community Acquired Pneumonia (non-severe) — Acute bronchitis (Harrison 22e p.1068) Acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis/COPD (Harrison 22e p.1068) Tuberculosis (suggested by an upper-lobe cavitating lesion) (Harrison 22e p.1068) Sputum Gram stain and culture (recommended chiefly for hospitalized patients, particularly severe cases or those at risk for MRSA or P. aeruginosa; an adequate specimen needs >25 neutrophils and <10 squamous epithelial cells per low-power field) (Harrison 22e p.1068) Blood cultures (reserved for high-risk patients such as neutropenia, asplenia, complement deficiency, chronic liver disease, or severe CAP, and those at risk for MRSA/P. aeruginosa; yield only ~5-14% in hospitalized CAP) (Harrison 22e p.1068) Pneumococcal and Legionella urinary antigen tests (reserved for severe cases or relevant epidemiology; Legionella test detects only serogroup 1) (Harrison 22e p.1068) Multiplex respiratory PCR / nasopharyngeal swab PCR (standard for viral diagnosis including influenza and coronaviruses; can also detect Legionella, M. pneumoniae, C. pneumoniae, mycobacteria) (Harrison 22e p.1068) Procalcitonin and C-reactive protein (adjuncts for stewardship only; PCT is not accurate enough to diagnose bacterial CAP or to withhold initial antibiotics, and CRP is even less sensitive) (Harrison 22e p.1068-1069) CT chest (for suspected loculated effusion, cavitary disease, or postobstructive pneumonia from tumor or foreign body) (Harrison 22e p.1068)

Carcinoid syndrome — Systemic mastocytosis / mast cell activation syndrome Pheochromocytoma Menopausal flushing VIPoma or other functional pancreatic neuroendocrine tumors Medullary thyroid carcinoma with calcitonin/other peptide secretion Anaphylaxis or food/alcohol-induced flushing reactions 24-hour urinary 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (5-HIAA) — main biochemical marker of serotonin turnover, though affected by diet and certain drugs Plasma chromogranin A — general neuroendocrine tumor marker, useful for diagnosis and monitoring tumor burden Serum serotonin level — supportive but less specific/standardized than urinary 5-HIAA Somatostatin receptor imaging (e.g., 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT) — localizes primary tumor and metastases with high sensitivity Cross-sectional imaging (contrast CT or MRI abdomen) — assesses primary tumor site, liver metastases, and mesenteric fibrosis Echocardiography — screens for carcinoid heart disease (tricuspid/pulmonic valve involvement) Endoscopy/enteroscopy or capsule endoscopy — identifies small bowel primary when suspected Rosacea Idiopathic flushing syndrome Irritable bowel syndrome (for the diarrhea component) Alcohol-induced flushing (especially in those with aldehyde dehydrogenase variants) Carcinoid syndrome arises from a neuroendocrine tumor (most often midgut origin) that secretes serotonin and other vasoactive substances (histamine, tachykinins, prostaglandins, kallikrein) directly into the systemic circulation, bypassing hepatic inactivation once liver metastases develop or when the primary tumor drains outside the portal system. These circulating mediators produce the characteristic flushing, diarrhea, and bronchoconstriction, while chronic exposure to serotonin and related factors promotes fibrous plaque deposition on cardiac valve

Castleman disease — Lymphoma (Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin) Autoimmune/rheumatologic disease with lymphadenopathy (e.g., systemic lupus erythematosus, rheumatoid arthritis) IgG4-related disease Reactive lymphadenopathy from chronic infection POEMS syndrome Kaposi sarcoma / HHV-8-associated disease Tuberculous lymphadenitis HIV-associated persistent generalized lymphadenopathy Infectious mononucleosis (EBV) Cat-scratch disease Excisional lymph node biopsy — required for definitive histopathologic diagnosis and subtype classification HIV serology and HHV-8 testing (blood PCR or tissue staining) — identifies virus-associated multicentric disease Complete blood count — screens for anemia, thrombocytopenia, or thrombocytosis seen in multicentric/TAFRO variants Serum IL-6 and inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR) — supports the systemic inflammatory phenotype Serum protein electrophoresis and immunoglobulin levels — assesses hypergammaglobulinemia and screens for paraproteins/POEMS Cross-sectional imaging (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis) — defines extent of nodal disease and organomegaly, distinguishes unicentric from multicentric involvement Renal and liver function testing — evaluates end-organ involvement from systemic cytokine excess Bone marrow examination — helps exclude lymphoma or plasma cell dyscrasia when systemic disease is suspected Lymphoma Sarcoidosis IgG4-related disease Autoimmune lymphoproliferative conditions

Catastrophic antiphospholipid syndrome — Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura / atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome Disseminated intravascular coagulation (from sepsis or malignancy) Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia with thrombosis Systemic vasculitis (e.g., ANCA-associated vasculitis) Severe sepsis with multi-organ dysfunction Thrombotic microangiopathy secondary to malignancy or drugs Severe sepsis / septic shock with multi-organ failure and coagulopathy Disseminated intravascular coagulation triggered by systemic infection Antiphospholipid antibody panel (lupus anticoagulant, anticardiolipin, anti-beta2-glycoprotein I) — confirms underlying antibody-driven process Complete blood count with peripheral smear — detects thrombocytopenia and schistocytes suggesting microangiopathic hemolysis Coagulation studies (PT, aPTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer) — assesses for overlapping consumptive coagulopathy Renal and liver function panels — screens for organ involvement and severity ADAMTS13 activity — helps exclude thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura as an alternative or coexisting diagnosis Imaging (CT/MRI) of suspected organs — identifies infarcts in brain, lung, kidney, or bowel Tissue biopsy of an accessible affected organ (skin, kidney) — provides histologic confirmation of small-vessel thrombosis when feasible Blood and other relevant cultures — evaluates for an infectious trigger or mimicking sepsis Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura

Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infection — Asymptomatic bacteriuria / catheter-associated asymptomatic bacteriuria (positive culture without localizing or systemic symptoms attributable to UTI) Complicated UTI extending beyond the bladder (prostatitis, pyelonephritis, bacteremia) Candiduria representing colonization rather than true infection in a catheterized patient Other infectious or noninfectious source of fever or altered mentation in a catheterized patient, which must be systematically excluded before attributing symptoms to CAUTI Asymptomatic bacteriuria with incidental pyuria Candida colonization of the catheter/urine without invasive infection Another concurrent infection (e.g., respiratory, intra-abdominal, bloodstream) causing the fever or systemic findings Urine culture collected from a freshly placed catheter (after exchanging/removing the indwelling catheter) to reflect bladder rather than biofilm microbiology, with susceptibilities to guide therapy Urine dipstick (nitrite, leukocyte esterase) and microscopic urinalysis, interpreted with awareness that pyuria and bacteriuria are expected in catheterized patients Systematic workup to exclude alternative infectious and non-infectious causes of fever or altered mental status before settling on CAUTI Delirium from non-infectious causes (e.g., metabolic, medication-related) in an older patient, mistaken for UTI-related encephalopathy Pyuria due to urinary stasis from an obstructed catheter rather than active infection

Coeliac disease — Tropical sprue Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth Autoimmune enteropathy Common variable immunodeficiency with enteropathy Crohn disease of the small bowel Irritable bowel syndrome Giardiasis Tropical sprue (presumed infectious/environmental etiology) Whipple disease IgA tissue transglutaminase antibody — first-line serologic screen, high sensitivity and specificity Total serum IgA — excludes IgA deficiency causing false-negative serology IgA or IgG deamidated gliadin peptide antibody — useful adjunct, especially in young children or IgA-deficient patients Upper endoscopy with multiple duodenal biopsies — confirms diagnosis via villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and intraepithelial lymphocytosis HLA-DQ2/DQ8 genotyping — high negative predictive value, useful to exclude disease when serology/histology are equivocal Complete blood count and iron studies — screens for iron-deficiency anaemia from malabsorption Bone mineral density (DEXA) — assesses for osteopenia/osteoporosis from calcium/vitamin D malabsorption Fat-soluble vitamin levels (A, D, E, K) and folate/B12 — evaluates extent of malabsorption Non-coeliac gluten sensitivity Lactose intolerance Autoimmune enteropathy Collagenous sprue Eosinophilic gastroenteritis Olmesartan-induced enteropathy Coeliac disease is an immune-mediated enteropathy triggered by dietary gluten (from wheat, barley, and rye) in genetically susceptible individuals, most of whom carry HLA-DQ2 or HLA-DQ8. Deamidation of gluten peptides by tissue transglutaminase enhances their binding to these HLA molecules, driving an aberrant T-cell response that damages small intestinal enterocytes. Cellulitis — Erysipelas (S. pyogenes superficial dermal/lymphatic infection with sharply demarcated, raised, indurated borders and abrupt fiery-red swelling) (Harrison 22e p.1095) Necrotizing fasciitis / deeper necrotizing soft-tissue infection (Harrison 22e p.1095) Purulent cellulitis associated with a focal staphylococcal lesion such as a furuncle, carbuncle, or abscess (Harrison 22e p.1095) Herpes zoster (dermatomal vesicular eruption may be mistaken for cellulitis early) (Harrison 22e p.93) Gram stain and culture of drainage, open wound, or identifiable portal of entry when present, for definitive etiology (Harrison 22e p.1095) Needle aspiration of the leading edge or punch biopsy of involved skin in selected cases, recognizing low (~20%) culture yield (Harrison 22e p.1095) Stasis dermatitis, which when acutely inflamed with crusting and exudate is easily confused with cellulitis; symmetric bilateral leg involvement favors stasis dermatitis (Harrison 22e p.428, p.436) Eczema (Harrison 22e p.93) Lymphedema (Harrison 22e p.93) Contact dermatitis (Harrison 22e p.428) Bacteria reach the dermis and subcutaneous soft tissue after disruption of the epidermal barrier by cracks, abrasions, cuts, burns, insect bites, surgical incisions, IV catheters, trauma, tinea/fungal infection, or pressure and venous-stasis ulcers. Organisms already colonizing the skin (notably S. aureus and group A streptococci) most readily exploit such breaks, though many exogenous bacteria can be introduced. Streptococcal disease characteristically spreads diffusely via lymphatics, producing lymphangitis, whereas staphylococcal disease spreads from a central focus such as an abscess or infected foreign body. Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis — Arterial ischemic stroke Idiopathic intracranial hypertension Subarachnoid hemorrhage Meningitis or encephalitis Posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome Primary or metastatic brain tumor with mass effect Bacterial meningitis Cerebral abscess Septic (infective) intracranial venous sinus thrombosis from adjacent otitis, mastoiditis, or sinusitis MR venography or CT venography — confirms sinus/cortical vein occlusion and is the primary diagnostic study Non-contrast head CT — may show hyperdense sinus or hemorrhagic venous infarct but can be normal early on MRI brain with venous sequences — detects venous infarction, edema, and hemorrhage better than CT D-dimer — supportive if elevated but a normal level does not exclude the diagnosis, especially with isolated headache Coagulation and thrombophilia workup — evaluates for underlying prothrombotic states once acute treatment is underway Lumbar puncture with opening pressure — assesses for raised intracranial pressure and excludes infectious causes when imaging is inconclusive Ophthalmologic exam for papilledema — assesses risk of visual loss from raised intracranial pressure Screening for precipitating factors (pregnancy/postpartum status, oral contraceptive or hormonal therapy use, malignancy, recent infection or dehydration) Idiopathic intracranial hypertension (pseudotumor cerebri) Arterial ischemic stroke Subarachnoid or intraparenchymal hemorrhage from other causes

Chikungunya — Dengue (co-circulating Aedes-borne flavivirus; may coinfect) (Harrison 22e p.1712, p.1060) Zika virus infection (Aedes-borne; can also cause joint manifestations) (Harrison 22e p.1712, p.1060) Other arthritogenic alphaviruses with clinically similar presentations: Ross River virus, Barmah Forest virus, Sindbis virus, o'nyong-nyong virus, Mayaro virus (Harrison 22e p.1712) CHIKV is an arthropod-borne alphavirus (family Togaviridae) spread by Aedes mosquitoes. It produces an acute febrile illness with prominent joint involvement; rheumatic manifestations span arthralgia with or without inflammatory signs (periarticular redness, swelling, immobility). Adults experience more severe and articular-predominant disease than children. Chronic musculoskeletal sequelae are thought to relate to host factors, with increased risk in patients who have preexisting osteoarthritis, severe acute disease, or the HLA-B27 subtype, and may be associated with cryoglobulins (Harrison 22e p.1712). Chikungunya virus (CHIKV) is an arthritogenic alphavirus transmitted by Aedes (yellow-fever and Asian tiger) mosquitoes; after a 2-10 day incubation it causes abrupt high fever, sometimes with a saddleback pattern, plus severe arthralgia (Harrison 22e p.1712). Migratory polyarthritis predominantly involves the small joints of the hands, wrists, ankles, and feet, though larger joints may also be affected; periarticular swelling and immobility are common, while frank effusions are less frequent (Harrison 22e p.1712).

Acute Cholangitis — Biliary colic / choledocholithiasis without infection Acute cholecystitis Gallstone pancreatitis Obstructive jaundice from malignancy of the pancreatic head, bile ducts, or ampulla of Vater (often painless jaundice) Primary sclerosing cholangitis with superimposed bacterial cholangitis Acute cholecystitis Hepatic (pyogenic) abscess Septic shock from another occult source (e.g., pneumonia, pyelonephritis) presenting before the biliary source is evident Serum alkaline phosphatase (almost always elevated in biliary obstruction; rise may precede clinical jaundice) Serum aminotransferases (two- to tenfold elevation, especially with acute obstruction) ERCP with endoscopic sphincterotomy as the preferred initial procedure for both definitive diagnosis and therapeutic drainage EUS as a less invasive alternative for detecting duct stones when the pretest probability of a persistent stone is lower Biliary colic from choledocholithiasis (pain without fever or rigors) Painless obstructive jaundice from neoplastic biliary obstruction IgG4-associated (sclerosing) cholangitis, which causes biliary stricturing and is glucocorticoid-responsive Gallstone pancreatitis Acute cholangitis arises from infection within an obstructed biliary tree, most often due to choledocholithiasis (common duct stones complicate about 10-15% of cholelithiasis). At least partial obstruction to bile flow combined with bacterial colonization of bile produces inflammation; rising intrabiliary pressure in an obstructed system promotes translocation of organisms into the bloodstream, causing bacteremia and biliary sepsis. In suppurative cholangitis, pus accumulates under pressure within a completely obstructed duct, driving severe toxicity (Harrison 22e p.2489, p.2735).

Acute Cholecystitis — Choledocholithiasis / common bile duct stone (suggested by elevated bilirubin and/or alkaline phosphatase with biliary pain) (Harrison 22e p.2731) Peptic ulcer disease, especially perforated peptic ulcer (Harrison 22e p.113, p.155) Gastritis / GERD (Harrison 22e p.113) Hepatitis (Harrison 22e p.113) Right lower-lobe pneumonia / pleurisy / subdiaphragmatic abscess (Harrison 22e p.113) Mirizzi's syndrome (cystic-duct/gallbladder-neck stone compressing the CBD with obstruction and jaundice) (Harrison 22e p.2732) Acute cholangitis (overlapping fever, RUQ pain, leukocytosis; empyema of the gallbladder may clinically resemble cholangitis) (Harrison 22e p.2733) Hepatitis (Harrison 22e p.113) Right-sided pneumonia / empyema / subdiaphragmatic abscess presenting as RUQ pain (Harrison 22e p.113) Ultrasound demonstrates calculi in about 90-95% of cases and shows signs of inflammation: gallbladder wall thickening, pericholecystic fluid, and bile-duct dilatation (Harrison 22e p.2732). Radionuclide (HIDA/DISIDA) biliary scan can be confirmatory when bile-duct imaging is seen without gallbladder visualization, indicating cystic-duct obstruction; useful when ultrasound is equivocal (Harrison 22e p.2730, p.2732). WBC count typically shows leukocytosis around 10,000-15,000/uL with a left shift (Harrison 22e p.2732). Serum bilirubin is mildly elevated (<5 mg/dL [85.5 umol/L]) in fewer than half of patients; about one-fourth have modest aminotransferase elevations (usually <5-fold) (Harrison 22e p.2732).

Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy — Guillain-Barre syndrome (acute inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy) POEMS syndrome and other paraproteinemic neuropathies Hereditary demyelinating neuropathies (e.g., Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1) Diabetic or other metabolic polyneuropathy Multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block Neuropathy associated with lymphoma, amyloidosis, or vasculitis HIV-associated demyelinating polyneuropathy Hepatitis C-associated neuropathy Lyme disease-related polyradiculoneuropathy Nerve conduction studies/EMG — demonstrates demyelinating features such as conduction block and slowed velocities Lumbar puncture with CSF protein and cell count — supports diagnosis via albuminocytologic dissociation and helps exclude infection or malignancy Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation — screens for an associated monoclonal gammopathy Fasting glucose/HbA1c — evaluates for coexisting diabetic neuropathy that can confound the picture Nerve biopsy (selected cases) — shows demyelination and onion-bulb formation when diagnosis remains uncertain Anti-paranodal antibody testing (e.g., neurofascin-155, contactin-1) — identifies a nodopathy subgroup with distinct treatment response MRI of spinal nerve roots/plexus with contrast — may show root or plexus enhancement/hypertrophy supporting a proximal demyelinating process HIV and hepatitis serologies — excludes infectious associations Diabetic lumbosacral radiculoplexus neuropathy

CNS Tuberculosis (TB Meningitis) — Fungal (subacute/chronic) meningitis, e.g. Cryptococcus neoformans, Histoplasma capsulatum, Coccidioides immitis (p.1124, 1127) Listeria monocytogenes meningoencephalitis (p.1124) Syphilitic (Treponema pallidum) meningitis (p.1127) Neoplastic / carcinomatous meningitis (p.1124) Neurosarcoidosis (p.1124) Cryptococcal meningitis (lymphocytic CSF with low glucose) (p.1124, 1127) Histoplasma and Coccidioides meningitis (p.1127) Listeria meningoencephalitis (p.1124) Neurosyphilis (p.1127) Viral meningitis due to mumps, LCMV, HSV-2, VZV or enteroviruses, which can occasionally cause low CSF glucose and mimic the TB profile (p.1124) CSF AFB smear taken from the last LP tube, or from any pellicle/cobweb clot - but smears are positive in only ~10-40% of adult cases (p.1127). Mycobacterial CSF culture - gold standard, but takes 4-8 weeks and is positive in only ~50% to up to 80% of cases (p.1127, 1389). CSF nucleic acid amplification testing - Xpert MTB/RIF Ultra or Xpert MTB/RIF; in the TB chapter the Xpert MTB/RIF assay has sensitivity up to 80% and is the preferred initial diagnostic option, with treatment started immediately on a positive result; a negative result does not exclude TB (p.1127, 1389). CSF opening pressure measurement (characteristically elevated) (p.1127). Repeat lumbar puncture to increase diagnostic yield, since AFB are infrequently seen on a single direct smear (p.1389).

Complicated Urinary Tract Infection — Acute bacterial prostatitis (consider in men with UTI plus systemic symptoms and no other clear anatomic source) (p.1132) Chronic bacterial prostatitis (consider with recurrent UTI in men, especially outside catheterization) (p.1132) Pyelonephritis with or without urinary obstruction (p.1132-1133) Chronic pelvic pain syndrome in men (not associated with bacteriuria, not improved by antibiotics) (p.1132) Sexually transmitted infection / cervicitis (Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae) presenting with dysuria (p.1133) Vaginitis (Candida albicans, Trichomonas vaginalis) (p.1133) Herpetic urethritis (p.1133) Urethritis from STI pathogens (gonococcal, chlamydial, Mycoplasma genitalium); urethral pain, pruritus, or discharge should prompt STI evaluation (p.1130, p.1133) CT or ultrasound imaging in men with febrile UTI to evaluate for anatomic abnormality or obstruction (p.1132) Blood cultures when complicated UTI, pyelonephritis, or systemic features are present (p.1134 diagnostic algorithm) Urine dipstick (nitrite and leukocyte esterase) and microscopic urinalysis as point-of-care tools mainly useful for ruling out UTI when the clinical diagnosis is unclear (p.1133-1135) Imaging to identify renal calculi or other nidus, plus assessment for urinary retention, in recurrent UTI (p.1138) Serum creatinine monitoring (a rapid rise may be the first sign of bilateral papillary necrosis) (p.1133)

Acute COPD Exacerbation — Pneumonia - the most frequent abnormal finding on chest imaging in this setting; about 25% of x-rays obtained for moderate-to-severe exacerbations in severe COPD are abnormal (p.2301). Arterial blood gas in patients with advanced COPD, a history of hypercarbia, altered mental status (confusion, sleepiness), or significant distress; hypercarbia is defined as PCO2 >45 mmHg and carries treatment implications (p.2301). Chest x-ray or chest CT in patients with severe underlying COPD, moderate-to-severe distress, or focal examination findings (p.2301). C-reactive protein, as part of emerging expert-consensus objective criteria (combining dyspnea, vital signs, CRP, and arterial blood gases) to diagnose and stage exacerbation severity, mainly of use in the emergency department (p.2301-2302). Pulmonary embolism - should be actively considered because the incidence of PE is increased during COPD exacerbations (p.2301). Congestive heart failure - a common alternative or contributing finding on imaging in patients presenting as an exacerbation (p.2301). Pneumothorax - asymmetry on chest examination may indicate pneumothorax (or large-airway obstruction) mimicking an exacerbation (p.2301). A variety of stimuli converge on a final common pathway of airway inflammation with increased respiratory symptoms. Viral respiratory infection, once thought less common than bacterial infection, is detected by PCR-based studies in over half of exacerbations; acquisition of a new bacterial strain is associated with increased near-term exacerbation risk. Non-infective contributors include air pollution, allergens, and environmental/Aspergillus sensitization, and in a significant minority no specific precipitant is identified (p.1756, p.2301).

Acute Uncomplicated Cystitis — Cervicitis (Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae) presenting with dysuria (p.1090) Urethritis, including gonococcal/chlamydial and herpetic urethritis (p.1087, p.1090) Sexually transmitted infection mistaken for UTI, especially with multiple partners or inconsistent condom use; vaginal discharge should prompt STI consideration (p.1090-1091) Vaginitis due to Candida albicans or Trichomonas vaginalis causing dysuria (p.1090) Sexually transmitted urethritis/cervicitis (gonococcal, chlamydial, Mycoplasma genitalium) (p.1087, p.1090) Acute or chronic bacterial prostatitis in men presenting as cystitis-like symptoms (p.1089) Urine dipstick for nitrite and leukocyte esterase as point-of-care testing, used mainly to help rule out UTI when the clinical diagnosis is unclear (p.1091) Microscopic urinalysis (white and red cell counts); pyuria is present in nearly all cystitis and hematuria in about 30% (p.1092) Urine culture when a resistant organism is suspected, in recurrent UTI, after prior treatment failure, or in all male UTI; a colony count threshold of >10^2 bacteria/mL is more sensitive than 10^5/mL for diagnosing cystitis in symptomatic women (p.1089, p.1092) STI screening / pelvic examination in women with risk factors for STI or with vaginal discharge (p.1090-1091) Interstitial cystitis / bladder pain syndrome (p.1090) Noninfectious vaginal or vulvar irritation (p.1090) Chronic pelvic pain syndrome in men (not associated with bacteriuria, not improved by antibiotics) (p.1089)

Clostridioides difficile Infection — Only diarrhoeal (unformed) stool should be tested; testing of asymptomatic patients is not recommended except for epidemiologic study (Harrison 22e p.1084). NAAT/PCR for the toxin gene is rapid and sensitive but may detect mere colonisation in a patient whose diarrhoea is due to another cause; toxin EIA is specific but insensitive (Harrison 22e p.1084). Recommended multi-step algorithms: NAAT followed by toxin EIA on NAAT-positive results, or GDH (glutamate dehydrogenase common-antigen) plus toxin EIA with NAAT as arbiter when the two disagree; confirming actual toxin in stool is favoured to avoid over-diagnosing colonisation (Harrison 22e p.1084). Empirical treatment is appropriate if stool testing is delayed (Harrison 22e p.1084). Endoscopy (sigmoidoscopy/colonoscopy) is highly specific only if pseudomembranes are seen but is insensitive (pseudomembranes visible in only ~50% of culture/toxin-positive diarrhoea); a negative endoscopy does NOT exclude CDI. It is most useful as a rapid test in the seriously ill patient with an acute abdomen and no diarrhoea (Harrison 22e p.1084). Abdominal CT in colitis shows bowel-wall thickening (significantly more prominent than in other colitides), wall oedema, mesenteric stranding and ascites (Harrison 22e p.640, p.1085). Ingested spores of toxigenic C. difficile survive gastric acid, germinate in the small bowel, and colonise the lower gut once antibiotic exposure has disrupted the protective microbiota. There they elaborate two large clostridial toxins: toxin A (an enterotoxin and potent neutrophil chemoattractant) and toxin B (a cytotoxin). Both glucosylate Rho-family GTP-binding proteins that regulate the actin cytoskeleton, causing loss of cell shape, adherence and tight junctions, with epit

Dengue Fever — Zika virus disease (often misdiagnosed as dengue; low-grade fever, itchy maculopapular rash, arthralgia/myalgia, nonpurulent conjunctivitis) Influenza Other arboviral fevers presenting as fever-and-myalgia syndrome Chikungunya Zika virus infection Yellow fever Leptospirosis Other viral hemorrhagic fevers Antigen-detection ELISA or RT-PCR (nucleic acid amplification) during the acute phase, useful within roughly the first 5 days of illness (p.1714, 1721) Combination point-of-care testing pairing NS1 antigen with IgM antibody assay, increasingly used clinically (p.1721) Paired (acute and convalescent) serology during recovery (p.1714) Serum AST (often modestly elevated without true hepatic synthetic dysfunction) (p.1714) Tourniquet test as a bedside marker of microvascular fragility (p.1714) Dengue is caused by the four flavivirus (orthoflavivirus) serotypes DENV-1 to DENV-4, transmitted mainly by Aedes aegypti (and the secondary vector Aedes albopictus), which bite during the day. After infection of one serotype, the cross-protection against a different (heterotypic) serotype is only transient and wanes within weeks to a few weeks of convalescence; subsequent heterotypic infection can produce classic dengue or, less often, severe dengue. The progression to severe disease centers on immune-mediated enhancement, in which enhancing, non-neutralizing antibodies are implicated, whereas neutralizing antibodies are associated with lower viremia on reinfection. The hallmark of severe dengue is a vascular-leak syndrome producing increased capillary permeability, intravascular volume depletion, hypoalbuminemia, and serosal (pleural, ascitic) effusions; recent evidence assigns the DENV NS1 protein a key role in this vascular leak. Host/viral risk modifiers include ag

Device-Related Infection (CIED / Vascular Catheter) — Left-sided native-valve or prosthetic-valve endocarditis (may coexist with or be mistaken for CIED-IE) (Harrison 22e p.1078, p.1084) Bloodstream infection from an extracardiac focus (e.g., gram-negative, streptococcal, or enterococcal bacteremia) not arising from the device (Harrison 22e p.1084) Remote-site metastatic infection complicating bacteremic CIED infection, such as vertebral osteomyelitis (Harrison 22e p.1084) Non-device bloodstream infection from a separate source presenting with fever and sepsis in a CIED patient (Harrison 22e p.1084) Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE): detects vegetations in >90% of patients with definite IE; an initial study may be falsely negative in a minority, so a negative TEE when IE is likely should be repeated in 7-10 days rather than used to exclude the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1083). Three or more separate blood culture sets (two-bottle, ~10 mL per bottle) from different venipuncture sites; if negative at 48-72 h, obtain additional sets and consult the lab for optimal techniques (Harrison 22e p.1082-1083). FDG-PET/CT: less sensitive than TEE for intracardiac pathology in CIED-IE but useful for assessing CIED pocket and lead infection and extracardiac/remote complications (Harrison 22e p.1083). Aspiration of any pyogenic collection at the device/pocket site, combined with blood cultures, to establish the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1201).

Diabetic Foot Infection — Charcot neuroarthropathy (neuropathic joint disease) — can mimic or coexist with foot osteomyelitis (p.1111, 3272) Purely neuropathic ulcer without infection (p.3272) Cellulitis without underlying ulceration (p.3272) Probe-to-bone test with a blunt sterile instrument as a bedside clinical assessment (p.92, 1112, 3272) Bone biopsy with culture (preferred basis for diagnosing/treating osteomyelitis given poor swab-to-bone correlation) (p.1112) Cultures taken from the debrided ulcer base, purulent drainage, or wound aspiration rather than superficial swabs (p.3272) MRI when pretest probability is lower or imaging needed (sensitivity 80-100%, specificity 80-90%) (p.1112) Nuclear medicine studies (PET, CT/SPECT) or labeled white-cell scans as alternatives to MRI (p.3272) Ankle-brachial index screening for peripheral arterial disease in diabetics >50 years with risk factors (p.3272) Charcot (neuropathic) arthropathy with bony deformity, which can radiographically and clinically resemble osteomyelitis (p.1111, 3272) Callus or pressure changes from abnormal foot biomechanics (p.3271) Diabetic foot infection arises from the interaction of peripheral sensory, motor, and autonomic neuropathy with abnormal foot biomechanics, peripheral arterial disease, and impaired wound healing. Sensory neuropathy removes protective pain sensation, allowing unrecognized repetitive or major trauma; impaired proprioception causes abnormal weight-bearing and callus/ulcer formation. Motor and sensory neuropathy produce structural deformities (hammer/claw toe, prominent metatarsal heads, Charcot joint). Autonomic neuropathy causes anhidrosis with dry, fissured skin. Peripheral arterial disease and poor healing then allow minor skin breaks to enlarge and become infected. Foot

Disseminated (Miliary) Tuberculosis — Disseminated fungal infection (a differential when miliary or interstitial pulmonary infiltrates and multi-organ involvement are present) (Harrison 22e p.1390) Dilated fundoscopic eye examination for choroidal tubercles (pathognomonic, up to ~30% of cases) (Harrison 22e p.1390) Bronchoalveolar lavage and transbronchial biopsy for improved bacteriologic confirmation (Harrison 22e p.1390) Full blood count for hematologic clues (anemia with leukopenia, lymphopenia, neutrophilic leukocytosis/leukemoid reactions, polycythemia; pancytopenia in nonreactive form; DIC reported) (Harrison 22e p.1390) Liver function tests including alkaline phosphatase (elevated with hepatic involvement) (Harrison 22e p.1390) Tuberculin skin test (may be falsely negative in up to half of cases) (Harrison 22e p.1390) Xpert MTB/RIF as the initial test when TB meningitis is suspected; positive results prompt immediate treatment (Harrison 22e p.1393) Miliary/disseminated TB results from hematogenous spread of M. tuberculosis when an acquired immune response fails to contain infection. Bacilli carried to regional lymph nodes reach the central venous return and the systemic circulation, seeding multiple organs with innumerable small (1-2 mm) yellowish granulomas resembling millet seeds. Occult hematogenous dissemination commonly follows primary infection; in the very young and the immunocompromised (including people living with HIV), insufficient immunity allows progression to fatal miliary disease or tuberculous meningitis (Harrison 22e p.1386, 1390).

DRESS syndrome — Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis Viral exanthem (e.g., EBV, CMV, HHV-6 primary infection) Hypereosinophilic syndrome Serum sickness-like reaction Autoimmune connective tissue disease with rash and organ involvement Infectious mononucleosis (EBV) Primary CMV infection Acute HIV seroconversion Measles or other viral exanthems Complete blood count with differential — assesses eosinophilia and atypical lymphocytosis Liver function tests — screens for hepatitis, the most common visceral involvement Serum creatinine and urinalysis — evaluates renal involvement Chest imaging — assesses for pulmonary infiltrates or pneumonitis Skin biopsy — supports diagnosis and helps exclude other severe cutaneous adverse reactions HHV-6 (and other herpesvirus) serology/PCR — assesses viral reactivation contributing to disease course Cardiac enzymes/echocardiography if myocarditis suspected — detects cardiac involvement Thyroid function tests at follow-up — late autoimmune thyroiditis can occur after recovery Stevens-Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis Acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis Hypereosinophilic syndrome Lymphoma with paraneoplastic skin findings Autoimmune/connective tissue disease flare DRESS is a severe, delayed T-cell-mediated drug hypersensitivity reaction, thought to arise from impaired drug detoxification pathways or specific HLA associations that lead to a robust immune response against drug-modified proteins. The resulting systemic activation of eosinophils and lymphocytes drives multi-organ inflammation. Reactivation of latent herpesviruses, particularly HHV-6, is commonly observed and may amplify and prolong the immune response, contributing to the characteristic waxing-waning co

Dysentery (Invasive Bacterial Diarrhea) — Shigella species (bacillary dysentery; prototypic invasive cause) Klebsiella oxytoca (antibiotic-associated haemorrhagic colitis) Shiga toxin-producing / enterohaemorrhagic E. coli (STEC/EHEC, e.g. O157:H7) Enteroinvasive E. coli (EIEC; shigellosis-like dysentery, shares ancestry with Shigella) Campylobacter jejuni (inflammatory diarrhoea, ~10% grossly bloody in adults) Non-typhoidal Salmonella (inflammatory diarrhoea; full dysentery uncommon) Yersinia enterocolitica (terminal ileitis/right-sided pain mimicking appendicitis) Entamoeba histolytica (amoebic dysentery; subacute, travel/endemic exposure) Vibrio parahaemolyticus (can cause dysentery; shellfish exposure) Clostridioides difficile (cytotoxin-mediated colitis; antibiotic/healthcare exposure) Clostridioides difficile colitis (consider with recent or current antibiotic use, hospitalisation/long-term care; can also be community-acquired without prior antibiotics) Enteric fever (Salmonella Typhi, Yersinia enterocolitica) - penetrating organisms that can present with fever and abdominal pain; fecal mononuclear leukocytes rather than frank dysentery Schistosomiasis and other invasive parasitic colitides in endemic exposure Sexually transmitted proctocolitis (gonococcal, syphilitic, chlamydial/LGV) presenting with bloody mucoid rectal discharge and tenesmus Fecal leukocyte smear (methylene blue wet mount) - suggests inflammatory disease, though predictive value is debated (p.1078-1079)

Encephalitis — Rabies (encephalitic/furious form with hydrophobia and aerophobia, or paralytic form) - bat exposure is the key risk in the US and a bite history may be lacking Cytomegalovirus, EBV, HHV-6 encephalitis (notably in immunocompromised / allogeneic stem-cell transplant recipients) Enterovirus A71 / D68 with acute flaccid myelitis-like presentation Nipah virus encephalitis (Paramyxoviridae; Southeast Asian outbreaks) SARS-CoV-2 - true viral CNS encephalitis (rare) versus encephalopathy from systemic/hyperinflammatory illness Mycobacteria (tuberculous meningitis/meningoencephalitis) Baylisascaris procyonis (raccoon roundworm) encephalitis - usually children, dirt/raccoon-feces exposure, eosinophilia Leptospirosis Lyme disease and cat-scratch disease Fungi Rickettsiae Listeria monocytogenes (including rhombencephalitis) Mycoplasma Bartonella and other bacteria Neurosyphilis Naegleria fowleri primary amebic meningoencephalitis (neutrophilic CSF, low glucose, motile trophozoites in warm fresh CSF; warm freshwater exposure) Acanthamoeba / Balamuthia mandrillaris granulomatous amebic encephalitis (can mimic acute viral encephalitis; near-100% mortality) Diffusion-weighted and FLAIR MRI sequences in addition to standard MRI - increase sensitivity for HSV temporal-lobe lesions (detect ~90% when added) Repeat CSF HSV PCR if the initial test is obtained within the first ~72 h and clinical suspicion of HSV remains high (early PCR can be falsely negative)

Enteric Fever (Typhoid) — Malaria Viral hepatitis Bacterial enteritis Dengue fever Rickettsial infection Leptospirosis Amebic liver abscess Acute HIV infection Malaria Dengue fever Leptospirosis Rickettsial infection Viral hepatitis Acute (primary) HIV infection Amebic liver abscess Bacterial enteritis / other Salmonella gastroenteritis Buffy-coat (centrifuged blood) culture — speeds isolation because most S. Typhi reside in the mononuclear-cell/platelet fraction, though it does not raise overall sensitivity (p.1360). Bone marrow culture — about 80% sensitive and, unlike blood culture, its yield is not reduced by up to 5 days of prior antibiotics (p.1360). Culture of intestinal/duodenal secretions (noninvasive duodenal string test) — can be positive even when bone marrow culture is negative; combining blood, marrow and intestinal-secretion cultures gives a yield over 90% (p.1360). Stool culture — often negative in the first week (negative in 60-70%) but may turn positive by the third week in untreated patients (p.1360). Culture of rose-spot punch biopsies (p.1360). Rapid immunodiagnostic serologic tests (e.g., Tubex, Typhidot detecting IgM/IgG to O and H antigens) — point-of-care, low cost, but only ~70-80% sensitive and ~80-90% specific, so insufficient to replace blood culture (p.1360). Blood PCR for S. Typhi/S. Paratyphi — reported sensitivity ~40-100% depending on gene target (p.1360). After ingestion (infectious dose ~200 to 10^6 CFU; lower gastric acidity or impaired intestinal integrity raises susceptibility), S. Typhi and S. Paratyphi traverse the small-bowel mucosa via M cells overlying Peyer's patches, using a type III secretion system to induce membrane ruffling and bacterium-mediated endocytosis. Crossing the epithelium, they are phagocytosed by macrophages

Eosinophilic oesophagitis — Gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD) with secondary esophageal eosinophilia Achalasia and other esophageal motility disorders Eosinophilic gastroenteritis with esophageal involvement Infectious esophagitis (candidal, viral) Pill-induced esophagitis Esophageal webs, Schatzki ring, or peptic stricture from other causes Candida esophagitis Herpes simplex virus esophagitis Cytomegalovirus esophagitis Upper endoscopy with multiple esophageal biopsies (proximal and distal) — required to confirm eosinophil-predominant inflammation and exclude mimics Histology quantifying peak eosinophil count per high-power field — supports diagnostic threshold for EoE Trial of acid suppression before/around diagnostic biopsy — helps distinguish reflux-related eosinophilia from primary EoE Barium esophagram — useful to characterize strictures, rings, or narrow-caliber esophagus, particularly pre-dilation Allergy evaluation (skin prick/patch or specific IgE testing) — may help guide elimination diet strategy though imperfect at predicting food triggers Esophageal functional/impedance-pH testing — considered when reflux contribution is uncertain Peripheral eosinophil count and total IgE — sometimes elevated but neither sensitive nor specific Repeat endoscopy with biopsy after treatment — used to assess histologic response to dietary or pharmacologic therapy GERD-related reflux esophagitis Pill-induced esophageal injury

Erysipelas — Cellulitis (deeper dermal/subcutaneous involvement, with less sharply demarcated borders) (Harrison 22e p.1210) Staphylococcus aureus cellulitis, which can produce a similar appearance, especially when the lesion is atypical, less intensely red, fades into surrounding skin, or arises around a wound or ulcer (Harrison 22e p.1210-1211) Streptococcus pyogenes infecting the epidermis is translocated laterally to deeper structures via lymphatics, producing the characteristic rapid superficial spread of erysipelas. Subsequent engorgement or obstruction of lymphatics causes flaccid edema of the epidermis. The infection is confined to the superficial dermis and superficial lymphatics (in contrast to cellulitis, which involves deeper subcutaneous tissue), and extension to deeper soft tissues is rare (Harrison 22e p.1051-1052, p.1210). Abrupt onset of fiery-red swelling of the face or extremities, with well-defined indurated margins (notably along the nasolabial fold), rapid progression, and intense pain (Harrison 22e p.1052). The sharply demarcated, raised border distinguishes erysipelas from cellulitis and reflects involvement limited to the superficial (upper) dermis and superficial lymphatics rather than the deeper subcutaneous tissue (Harrison 22e p.1051, p.1210). A peau d'orange (orange-peel) texture of the skin is characteristic and is thought to reflect involvement of superficial lymphatics (Harrison 22e p.1210).

Erythema nodosum — Nodular vasculitis / erythema induratum (lobular panniculitis, often with ulceration, seen more on posterior calves) Superficial thrombophlebitis Cellulitis or erysipelas Polyarteritis nodosa with cutaneous nodules Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis) Insect bite reaction or panniculitis from trauma Streptococcal pharyngitis-associated panniculitis Tuberculosis-related erythema nodosum (erythema induratum can mimic classic EN) Deep fungal infection (coccidioidomycosis, histoplasmosis) presenting with tender nodules Yersinia enterocolitis-associated panniculitis Cat-scratch disease with nodular skin lesions Throat culture and antistreptolysin O titer — screen for antecedent streptococcal infection, the most common identifiable trigger Chest radiograph — evaluate for hilar lymphadenopathy suggesting sarcoidosis or for findings of tuberculosis Complete blood count and inflammatory markers (ESR/CRP) — assess systemic inflammatory activity, often markedly elevated Stool studies or IBD-directed workup if gastrointestinal symptoms present — assess for inflammatory bowel disease Tuberculin skin test or interferon-gamma release assay — evaluate for underlying tuberculosis, especially in endemic regions Medication history review — identify possible drug-induced etiology Skin biopsy (deep incisional, including subcutaneous fat) — confirms septal panniculitis when diagnosis is uncertain or lesions are atypical

Febrile Neutropenia — Neutropenic enterocolitis (typhlitis) presenting as abdominal pain and fever in chemotherapy-induced marrow suppression (Harrison 22e p.154) Serial absolute neutrophil count (band forms plus mature neutrophils) to track depth and duration of neutropenia (Harrison 22e p.499) Skin examination for ecthyma gangrenosum suggesting Pseudomonas bacteremia (Harrison 22e p.186) Cross-sectional abdominal imaging when neutropenic enterocolitis/typhlitis is suspected, with serial clinical examination for perforation (Harrison 22e p.154) Acute graft-versus-host disease, which should be considered when a marrow-suppressed/transplant patient develops abdominal pain and fever (Harrison 22e p.154) Drug fever and chemotherapy-related fever in the absence of demonstrable infection Most cytotoxic chemotherapeutic agents suppress bone marrow function, and polymorphonuclear neutrophils, with their very short circulating half-life of roughly 6-8 hours, are the cell line most rapidly and severely depleted. As the neutrophil count falls, the host loses the first-line cellular defense that normally contains commensal flora at mucosal surfaces; below an ANC of 500/uL control of endogenous mouth and gut organisms is impaired, and below 200/uL the local inflammatory response is essentially absent, so signs of infection are blunted. The combination of profound neutropenia and chemotherapy-induced mucosal barrier injury allows translocation and rapid dissemination of bacteria from the patient's own gut and oral flora. Neutropenia is most commonly iatrogenic, arising from cytotoxic or immunosuppressive therapy. (Harrison 22e p.499-500, p.617)

Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis — Minimal change disease Membranous nephropathy IgA nephropathy Diabetic nephropathy Amyloidosis / other glomerular deposition diseases Alport syndrome and other hereditary nephropathies HIV-associated nephropathy (collapsing FSGS variant) Parvovirus B19-associated collapsing glomerulopathy Urinalysis with microscopy — assess proteinuria magnitude and look for associated hematuria/casts 24-hour urine protein or spot protein-to-creatinine ratio — quantify and monitor proteinuria Serum albumin and lipid panel — assess for nephrotic syndrome physiology Kidney biopsy with light, immunofluorescence, and electron microscopy — required to confirm FSGS and identify the histologic variant HIV testing and other relevant viral serologies — evaluate for virus-associated collapsing variant Genetic testing for podocyte-associated gene mutations (including APOL1) — consider in familial, pediatric, or steroid-resistant cases Renal ultrasound — assess kidney size/echogenicity and screen for reduced nephron mass or reflux-related changes Estimated GFR trend over time — gauge rate of progression and guide need for renal replacement planning Obesity-related glomerulopathy Reflux nephropathy / oligomeganephronia with reduced nephron number Sickle cell nephropathy Heroin nephropathy and other drug-induced podocytopathies Interferon or calcineurin-inhibitor-associated glomerular injury FSGS results from podocyte injury and loss that a glomerulus cannot adequately repair, leading to segmental capillary collapse and scarring in a portion of glomeruli. In primary disease a circulating permeability factor is suspected to injure podocytes directly, whereas secondary forms arise from maladaptive hyperfiltration in remnant or overworked nephrons, viral cytopathic e

Acute Gastroenteritis — Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (O157:H7 / Shiga toxin-producing) - watery progressing to bloody, HUS risk Enteroaggregative E. coli (emerging traveler's-diarrhea pathogen) Cholera (Vibrio cholerae) - profuse rice-water secretory diarrhea Preformed-toxin food poisoning (Staphylococcus aureus, Bacillus cereus, Clostridium perfringens) Sapovirus, astrovirus, enteric adenovirus types 40/41 (viral, mainly young children) Cryptosporidium, Cyclospora, Giardia (esp. travelers, hikers, immunocompromised, persistent cases) Enteric fever / typhoid (penetrating pathogens Salmonella Typhi, Yersinia enterocolitica with fever, relative bradycardia, splenomegaly) Yersinia enterocolitica terminal ileitis mimicking acute appendicitis Clostridioides difficile colitis (recent or current antibiotics; predominant nosocomial cause) Acute viral hepatitis A and other systemic infections (legionellosis, listeriosis, toxic shock, malaria) in which diarrhea is one feature SARS-CoV-2 - diarrhea can be an early symptom Fecal leukocyte smear (methylene blue) or, more sensitively, fecal lactoferrin to distinguish inflammatory from noninflammatory disease Culture-independent multiplex nucleic-acid amplification (PCR) stool panels - now first-line for severe/domestically acquired disease; faster and more sensitive than culture Stool culture for Salmonella, Shigella, and Campylobacter in febrile inflammatory diarrhea acquired outside hospital

Anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture) — ANCA-associated vasculitis (granulomatosis with polyangiitis, microscopic polyangiitis) Lupus nephritis with diffuse alveolar hemorrhage IgA nephropathy / IgA vasculitis with pulmonary involvement Post-infectious or other immune-complex crescentic glomerulonephritis Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis with pulmonary-renal syndrome Thrombotic microangiopathy causing combined renal and pulmonary injury Severe pneumonia with concurrent acute kidney injury mimicking a pulmonary-renal syndrome Leptospirosis with pulmonary hemorrhage and renal failure Serum anti-GBM antibody titer (ELISA) — confirms circulating autoantibody, main serologic diagnostic test ANCA serology (MPO/PR3) — detects dual-positive cases which alter relapse risk and monitoring Renal biopsy with immunofluorescence — linear IgG (and often C3) along GBM confirms diagnosis and grades crescent burden for prognosis Urinalysis with microscopy — dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts confirm glomerular bleeding Chest imaging (chest x-ray or CT) — detects alveolar infiltrates from pulmonary hemorrhage Diffusing capacity for carbon monoxide (DLCO) — an elevated DLCO supports active alveolar hemorrhage Complete blood count — unexplained drop in hemoglobin can be an early clue to occult pulmonary hemorrhage Serum creatinine and renal function trend — guides urgency of treatment and predicts recovery potential ANCA-associated vasculitis

Hospital Acquired Pneumonia — Purulent tracheobronchitis (notably in chronic ventilator units, where it can impede weaning) (p.1073) Antibiotic-associated diarrhoea (as an alternative source of fever/leukocytosis) (p.1074) Central line-associated infection (p.1074) Sinusitis (p.1074) Urinary tract infection (p.1074) Fungal or viral pneumonia (mimics requiring different antimicrobials than VAP) (p.1074) Quantitative culture of deep respiratory tract samples to separate colonisation from true infection; the more distal the sample, the more specific the result and the lower the colony-count threshold (e.g., endotracheal aspirate threshold ~10^6 cfu/mL vs protected specimen brush ~10^3 cfu/mL), at the cost of falling sensitivity for blindly collected distal samples (p.1074) Gram stain of endotracheal aspirate (absence of bacteria argues against pneumonia) (p.1074) Differential cell counts and staining for intracellular organisms on respiratory samples (p.1074) Detection of local protein levels elevated in response to infection (p.1074) Serial / repeat quantitative cultures to track microbiologic response and clarify treatment failure (p.1075) Procalcitonin to help guide duration of therapy in conjunction with the initial clinical response (already curated; Harrison adds the duration-of-therapy context, p.1075) Atypical pulmonary oedema (p.1074) Pulmonary contusion (p.1074) Alveolar haemorrhage (p.1074) Hypersensitivity pneumonitis (p.1074)

Hepatorenal syndrome — Prerenal azotemia from volume depletion (vomiting, diarrhea, over-diuresis, GI bleeding) Acute tubular necrosis from ischemia, sepsis, or nephrotoxin exposure Drug-induced acute kidney injury (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, contrast, ACE inhibitors/ARBs) Glomerulonephritis associated with chronic liver disease (e.g., IgA nephropathy, membranoproliferative pattern in hepatitis C) Abdominal compartment syndrome from tense ascites Obstructive uropathy Sepsis-associated acute kidney injury Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis with secondary renal hypoperfusion Urinary tract infection with associated prerenal physiology Serum creatinine trend and estimated GFR — establishes rate and severity of renal decline defining HRS-AKI vs HRS-NAKI Urinalysis with microscopy — bland sediment supports HRS over intrinsic renal disease Urine sodium and fractional excretion of sodium — typically very low, reflecting avid sodium retention Renal ultrasound — excludes obstruction and assesses for underlying structural kidney disease Diagnostic paracentesis with ascitic fluid cell count and culture — excludes spontaneous bacterial peritonitis as a precipitant Blood and urine cultures — identify occult infection precipitating renal decline Response to albumin volume challenge with diuretic withdrawal — required to confirm the diagnosis Liver function panel and coagulation studies — assess severity of underlying hepatic decompensation and transplant urgency

Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) — Severe sepsis / septic shock — the principal mimic, with overlapping fever, cytopenias and organ dysfunction Disseminated infection (EBV, CMV and other viruses; tuberculosis; visceral leishmaniasis; severe rickettsial disease) Lymphoma and other haematological malignancies, which can both trigger and mimic HLH Adult-onset Still's disease and systemic juvenile idiopathic arthritis complicated by macrophage activation syndrome Thrombotic microangiopathy (TTP/HUS) and other causes of fever with cytopenias Drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) Severe sepsis / septic shock Disseminated viral infection (EBV, CMV) Visceral leishmaniasis Miliary / disseminated tuberculosis Severe rickettsial or scrub typhus infection Serum ferritin — very high values (often above 10,000 micrograms/L in adults) are highly suggestive Fasting triglycerides and fibrinogen (hypertriglyceridemia and/or hypofibrinogenemia) Full blood count with film (bi- or tri-lineage cytopenias) Soluble CD25 (soluble IL-2 receptor) and NK-cell activity where available Bone marrow aspirate / biopsy for hemophagocytosis (may be absent early — a normal marrow does NOT exclude HLH) Liver function tests and coagulation profile (transaminitis, coagulopathy / DIC) Trigger work-up: EBV / CMV and other viral PCR, blood cultures, and evaluation for lymphoma and autoimmune disease H-score calculation to estimate the probability of secondary HLH in adults

Infective Endocarditis — Marantic (nonbacterial thrombotic) endocarditis associated with malignancy and chronic wasting disease Atrial myxoma Antiphospholipid antibody syndrome with bland valvular vegetations Systemic lupus erythematosus with sterile (Libman-Sacks-type) vegetations Culture-negative IE due to fastidious organisms (Coxiella burnetii, Bartonella spp., Tropheryma whipplei, Brucella, nutritionally variant Granulicatella/Gemella/Abiotrophia, Corynebacterium/Cutibacterium acnes, Mycobacterium chimaera) Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) detects vegetations in over 90% of definite IE and is preferred over TTE, which misses vegetations under 2 mm and yields inadequate images in about 20% of patients; a negative TEE with high clinical suspicion should be repeated in 7-10 days. Three-dimensional TEE to better define vegetations and perivalvular extension. ECG-gated multislice cardiac CT angiography - superior to TEE for pseudoaneurysm/abscess and can assess coronary patency preoperatively; CTA findings count as a major imaging criterion. 18F-FDG-PET/CT - increases sensitivity in suspected prosthetic-valve IE (including TAVR-PVE), aortic graft, CIED pocket/lead and LVAD infection, and extracardiac foci; false positives within 3 months of valve surgery. Molecular testing of excised/embolized vegetation: organism-specific PCR (C. burnetii, Bartonella, T. whipplei, C. acnes, M. hominis) and broad-range 16S (or 28S for fungi) rRNA PCR with sequencing; only moderately sensitive, so a negative result does not exclude IE.

IgA nephropathy — Thin basement membrane nephropathy (benign familial hematuria) Alport syndrome (hereditary nephritis) Post-infectious (post-streptococcal) glomerulonephritis Lupus nephritis IgA vasculitis with nephritis Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis Infective endocarditis-associated glomerulonephritis Hepatitis-associated glomerulonephritis Urinalysis with microscopy — confirms dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts indicating glomerular bleeding Urine protein-to-creatinine ratio or 24-hour urine protein — quantifies proteinuria for staging and prognosis Serum creatinine and estimated GFR — establishes baseline kidney function and tracks progression Serum complement levels (C3, C4) — typically normal in IgA nephropathy, helping exclude complement-mediated GN Kidney biopsy with light microscopy, immunofluorescence, and electron microscopy — required for definitive diagnosis and Oxford classification grading Serum IgA level — often elevated but neither sensitive nor specific enough to confirm diagnosis alone ANA, ANCA, and hepatitis serologies — helps exclude secondary causes and mimicking systemic diseases Renal ultrasound — assesses kidney size and excludes obstructive or structural causes of hematuria Thin basement membrane nephropathy Alport syndrome Lupus nephritis ANCA-associated vasculitis with glomerulonephritis Disease arises from circulating poorly galactosylated IgA1 molecules that form immune complexes, which deposit in the glomerular mesangium and trigger mesangial cell proliferation and matrix expansion. This deposition activates complement and local inflammatory pathways, leading to variable degrees of mesangial hypercellularity, segmental sclerosis, endocapillary proliferation, and interstitial fibrosis d

This unregulated insulin release drives glucose into tissues and suppresses hepatic glucose output, producing hypoglycemia. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis — Connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease (e.g., rheumatoid arthritis, systemic sclerosis) Chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis Nonspecific interstitial pneumonia Drug-induced pulmonary toxicity Asbestosis or other pneumoconiosis Combined pulmonary fibrosis and emphysema High-resolution CT chest — identifies UIP pattern and excludes alternative diagnoses Pulmonary function tests with DLCO — documents restrictive pattern and gas-transfer impairment, tracks progression Serologic autoimmune panel (ANA, rheumatoid factor, myositis antibodies) — screens for occult connective tissue disease Six-minute walk test with oximetry — assesses functional capacity and exertional desaturation Surgical or transbronchial cryobiopsy — considered when HRCT is indeterminate and histopathology would change management Echocardiogram — evaluates for pulmonary hypertension as a complication Bronchoalveolar lavage — helps exclude infection or alternative diagnoses in select atypical presentations Detailed exposure and medication history — identifies occupational, environmental, or drug-related causes of fibrosis Congestive heart failure with pulmonary edema Sarcoidosis Chronic hypersensitivity pneumonitis Connective tissue disease-associated interstitial lung disease Pulmonary drug toxicity IPF is thought to result from repeated micro-injury to alveolar epithelium in a genetically susceptible, typically older individual, triggering an aberrant wound-healing response rather than a primarily inflammatory process. This dysregulated repair leads to fibroblast/myofibroblast proliferation and excessive extracellular matrix deposition, producing the patchy, temporally heterogeneous fibrosis and architectural distortion characteristic of the usual int

The resulting medium-vessel vasculitis targets the coronary arteries, causing panvasculitis with destruction of the internal elastic lamina and media, which weakens the vessel wall and predisposes to aneurysm formation and later stenosis or thrombosis.
