Leptospirosis — Influenza and SARS-CoV-2 / other respiratory viral infections (when fever, headache, myalgia predominate) Chikungunya Ehrlichiosis / rickettsial diseases Acute HIV infection Hantavirus infection (hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome or hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome) Yellow fever and other viral hemorrhagic fevers (Rift Valley fever, filovirus infections, Lassa fever) when bleeding is present Acute schistosomiasis Dengue (and dengue hemorrhagic fever when bleeding present) Malaria Typhoid fever Scrub typhus (rash may be misattributed) Viral hepatitis Acute HIV infection Hantavirus infection Yellow fever / viral hemorrhagic fevers PCR (notably real-time PCR) of blood/CSF/urine — confirms diagnosis with high accuracy during the first 5 days of illness, before serology becomes positive (p.1443) Bilirubin, aminotransferases, alkaline phosphatase (bilirubin may be high; transaminase rises typically only moderate) (p.1443) Chest radiograph / CT (patchy bilateral lower-lobe alveolar pattern from alveolar hemorrhage; pleura-based densities; ground-glass ARDS pattern) (p.1443) ECG (nonspecific ST/T changes; repolarization abnormalities and arrhythmias are poor prognostic signs) (p.1443) CSF examination when meningitis suspected (pleocytosis from a few to >1000 cells/uL, lymphocytic but may be PMN-predominant early; protein normal or slightly raised, glucose normal) (p.1443) Co-testing for rickettsiae, dengue, and hantavirus given overlap and reported dual infections (p.1443)

Liver Abscess — Splenic abscess (different clinical setting and organism profile, most often associated with bacterial endocarditis; high index of suspicion needed as it is frequently fatal if untreated) (p.1118) Hepatic actinomycosis (Actinomyces israelii can produce multiple hepatic abscesses, sometimes with a contiguous splenic lesion) (p.1290 region) Candidal (fungal) liver abscess in immunocompromised/post-chemotherapy patients (p.1117) Amebic liver abscess (Entamoeba histolytica) — a treatable alternative with overlapping right-upper-quadrant pain, fever, and point hepatic tenderness; jaundice is rare and fewer than one-third have active diarrhoea at presentation (p.1117, p.1756) Imaging is the most reliable diagnostic modality: ultrasonography, CT, MRI, and indium-labelled-WBC or gallium scintigraphy; more than one study may be needed (p.1117). Chest radiography may give a clue — a newly elevated right hemidiaphragm, right basilar infiltrate, or right pleural effusion (p.1117). Diagnostic aspiration of abscess contents (with Gram stain and culture), together with blood cultures, ideally obtained before starting empirical antibiotics (p.1118). Amebic serology is positive in >95% of amebic liver abscess cases and PCR can also be used; negative results help exclude amebiasis (p.1117). Note enzyme immunoassay for the Gal/GalNAc lectin and LAMP/PCR can also be applied directly to abscess aspirate/pus (p.1756-1757).

Lung Abscess — Pulmonary malignancy presenting as a cavitary lesion (p.1035) Pulmonary infarction (p.1035) Pulmonary sequestration (p.1035) Cryptogenic organizing pneumonia (p.1035) Sarcoidosis (p.1035) Vasculitis / autoimmune disease such as granulomatosis with polyangiitis (p.1035) Infected lung cysts or bullae (fluid-containing) (p.1035) Septic emboli, e.g., from tricuspid valve endocarditis (p.1035) Pulmonary manifestations of inflammatory bowel disease or pyoderma gangrenosum (p.1035) Mycobacterium tuberculosis (and M. avium, M. kansasii) cavitary disease (p.1034) Endemic fungi: Coccidioides, Histoplasma capsulatum, Blastomyces (p.1034) Parasitic causes of cavitation: Entamoeba histolytica, Paragonimus westermani, Strongyloides stercoralis (p.1034) Nocardia, Aspergillus, Mucorales, Cryptococcus, Rhodococcus equi, Pneumocystis jirovecii in immunocompromised hosts (p.1034) Empyema / pleural space infection (must be distinguished from a peripheral abscess as it may need urgent drainage) (p.1035) CT chest, which defines cavitation earlier than plain film, can reveal an underlying cause such as malignancy, and helps separate a peripheral abscess from a pleural infection (p.1035) Molecular methods such as 16S rRNA gene amplification for more specific pathogen identification (p.1035) Serologic studies for opportunistic pathogens (viral/fungal) when abscess is secondary or empirical therapy fails (p.1035)

Malaria — Acute viral illness / minor febrile viral syndrome (early nonspecific malaria mimics this) (Harrison 22e p.1763) Bacterial meningitis (severe headache in malaria, but neck stiffness and photophobia are absent in malaria) (Harrison 22e p.1763) Sepsis / bacteremia with incidental parasitemia, especially in high-transmission areas (Harrison 22e pp.1765, 1767) Dengue fever (myalgia is prominent but usually more severe in dengue) (Harrison 22e p.1763) Leptospirosis (muscle tenderness, which malaria lacks; petechial hemorrhages a feature) (Harrison 22e p.1763) Typhus/rickettsial illness (tender muscles, unlike malaria) (Harrison 22e p.1763) Viral hemorrhagic fevers (petechial hemorrhages, which are very rare in malaria) (Harrison 22e p.1763) Nontyphoidal Salmonella and other bacteremia complicating or coinciding with malaria (Harrison 22e p.1765) Thick blood film (concentrates parasites ~40-100x over thin film, increasing sensitivity; examine 100-200 fields before calling negative) (Harrison 22e pp.1766-1767) Thin blood film for species identification and parasite quantification (parasitized cells per 1000 RBCs) (Harrison 22e pp.1766-1767) Giemsa (pH 7.2) or other Romanowsky stain; acridine orange for rapid detection of low-level parasitemia (Harrison 22e p.1766) Rapid diagnostic tests detecting PfHRP2, parasite LDH, or aldolase (note PfHRP2/3 gene-deletion false negatives and that RDTs do not quantify parasitemia) (Harrison 22e p.1767)

Mixed connective tissue disease — Systemic lupus erythematosus Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma) Polymyositis/dermatomyositis Rheumatoid arthritis Undifferentiated connective tissue disease Sjögren syndrome ANA with reflex extractable nuclear antigen panel — screens for anti-U1-RNP, the defining autoantibody Anti-U1-RNP antibody titer — confirms diagnosis when present in high titer, typically without anti-Sm or anti-dsDNA Creatine kinase and aldolase — assess for accompanying myositis Pulmonary function tests with diffusion capacity (DLCO) — detect early interstitial lung disease or pulmonary vascular involvement Transthoracic echocardiogram — screen for pulmonary arterial hypertension, a major prognostic driver High-resolution chest CT — evaluate for interstitial lung disease Esophageal manometry or barium swallow — assess for dysmotility seen in sclerodermoid overlap Urinalysis and renal function panel — screen for renal involvement, which is less common but clinically important Systemic lupus erythematosus Limited or diffuse systemic sclerosis Idiopathic inflammatory myopathy Antisynthetase syndrome Primary Raynaud phenomenon with isolated ANA positivity MCTD is an overlap autoimmune connective tissue disorder characterized by immune-mediated vasculopathy and fibrosis affecting skin, synovium, muscle, esophagus, lungs, and vasculature. It is strongly associated with high titers of antibody against the U1-RNP component of the spliceosome, which is thought to contribute to immune complex formation and endothelial injury. The vascular pathology, particularly intimal proliferation in pulmonary and other vessels, resembles that seen in systemic sclerosis and underlies the propensity for pulmonary arterial hypertension.

Melioidosis — Pulmonary or disseminated tuberculosis Community-acquired or nosocomial gram-negative sepsis/pneumonia Staphylococcal bacteremia with metastatic abscesses Fungal infection (histoplasmosis, coccidioidomycosis) in returning travelers Enteric fever or other systemic febrile illness in returning travelers Actinomycosis or nocardiosis Pulmonary tuberculosis Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia with septic emboli Nocardiosis Actinomycosis Blood, sputum, urine, and wound/abscess cultures with explicit lab alert — definitive diagnosis rests on culture isolation of B. pseudomallei Contrast CT of chest/abdomen — to detect occult multifocal abscesses (splenic, hepatic, prostatic, renal) Chest radiography — may show cavitary upper-lobe infiltrates mimicking tuberculosis Serology (indirect hemagglutination) — supportive but limited by background seropositivity in endemic areas, so not diagnostic alone HbA1c/fasting glucose — screen for underlying diabetes mellitus, the principal risk factor Renal function tests — assess for chronic kidney disease as a predisposing condition and to guide drug dosing considerations Blood cultures for sepsis workup — essential given the high risk of bacteremic dissemination MRI or CT brain in patients with neurologic signs — to detect rare but described CNS melioidosis (brainstem encephalitis) Metastatic malignancy with multiple organ lesions Vasculitis with pulmonary cavitation

Acute Bacterial Meningitis — Herpes simplex virus encephalitis (headache, fever, altered consciousness, focal deficits, seizures; distinguished by CSF profile, MRI temporal-lobe changes and HSV CSF PCR) (p.1121) Subacute meningitis presenting acutely: M. tuberculosis, Cryptococcus neoformans, Histoplasma, Coccidioides, Treponema pallidum (p.1122) Mycoplasma pneumoniae CNS infection, which can mimic viral meningitis/encephalitis (p.1124) Viral (aseptic) meningoencephalitis, especially enteroviral and HSV (p.1121) Rocky Mountain spotted fever (Rickettsia rickettsii) with early maculopapular rash that can resemble meningococcemia (p.1121) Ehrlichiosis/anaplasmosis (tick-borne) with fever, headache, confusion and sometimes rash (p.1121) Focal suppurative CNS infections: subdural empyema, epidural empyema, brain abscess (consider when focal neurologic findings present) (p.1121) Fungal, tuberculous, Listeria, Brucella, Coxiella, Leptospira meningitis (lymphocytic pleocytosis, hypoglycorrhachia may be absent early) (p.1124) CSF opening pressure measurement: raised (>180 mmH2O) in over 90% of cases, >400 mmH2O in about 20% (p.1120) CSF cell count and differential: PMN pleocytosis, >100 cells/uL in ~90% (p.1120) CSF glucose and CSF/serum glucose ratio: low glucose (<40 mg/dL) and ratio <0.4 are highly suggestive (ratio also low in fungal/TB/carcinomatous meningitis) (p.1120) CSF protein: elevated (>45 mg/dL) in ~90% (p.1120)

Microscopic colitis — Bile acid diarrhea/malabsorption Celiac disease Irritable bowel syndrome (diarrhea-predominant) Inflammatory bowel disease (Crohn disease, ulcerative colitis) Drug-induced diarrhea (independent of microscopic colitis itself) Small intestinal bacterial overgrowth Chronic Clostridioides difficile infection Giardiasis Chronic bacterial or parasitic enterocolitis Colonoscopy with random biopsies from multiple colonic segments — required for histologic diagnosis since mucosa often appears normal Histopathology — distinguishes collagenous (thickened collagen band) from lymphocytic (intraepithelial lymphocytosis) subtype Celiac serology (tissue transglutaminase IgA) — screens for coexisting celiac disease Thyroid function tests — screens for associated autoimmune thyroid disease Stool studies (culture, C. difficile testing, ova and parasites) — excludes infectious causes of chronic diarrhea Medication review — identifies causative drugs such as NSAIDs, PPIs, SSRIs, and statins Fecal calprotectin — typically normal or only mildly elevated, helps differentiate from classic IBD SeHCAT or serum C4/FGF-19 testing where available — evaluates for concurrent bile acid diarrhea Diarrhea-predominant irritable bowel syndrome Bile acid malabsorption Celiac disease Endocrine causes of diarrhea (e.g., hyperthyroidism, neuroendocrine tumors) Microscopic colitis is thought to result from a dysregulated mucosal immune response to luminal antigens (including bile acids, bacterial products, and certain drugs) in a genetically or immunologically susceptible host, producing intraepithelial lymphocytic infiltration with or without subepithelial collagen deposition. This impairs colonic epithelial barrier function and fluid/electrolyte absorption, producing a secretory-type wat

Minimal change disease — Focal segmental glomerulosclerosis (FSGS) Membranous nephropathy Membranoproliferative glomerulonephritis Diabetic nephropathy IgA nephropathy with heavy proteinuria Amyloidosis or other infiltrative nephropathies Post-infectious glomerulonephritis Hepatitis B/C-associated glomerulonephritis HIV-associated nephropathy Urinalysis with microscopy — assess for selective proteinuria and absence of significant hematuria or cellular casts 24-hour urine protein or spot urine protein-to-creatinine ratio — quantify nephrotic-range proteinuria Serum albumin and lipid panel — confirm hypoalbuminemia and hyperlipidemia typical of nephrotic syndrome Renal function panel (creatinine, eGFR) — establish baseline and monitor for atypical renal impairment Renal biopsy with electron microscopy — required in adults or steroid-resistant cases to confirm diagnosis and exclude FSGS/other glomerulopathies Serum complement levels — typically normal in minimal change disease, helps exclude complement-mediated glomerulonephritides Age-appropriate malignancy screening in adults — evaluate for underlying lymphoproliferative disease, especially if steroid-resistant Coagulation studies/consideration of thromboembolic risk — nephrotic syndrome predisposes to venous thromboembolism NSAID-induced acute interstitial nephritis with nephrotic-range proteinuria Paraneoplastic nephrotic syndrome (Hodgkin lymphoma, other lymphoproliferative disorders)

Necrotizing Fasciitis — Clostridial myonecrosis / gas gangrene (distinguished from clostridial NF by muscle biopsy) Streptococcal necrotizing myositis (GAS infection extending into muscle) Pyomyositis (usually S. aureus; localized, shock uncommon unless toxin-producing) Synergistic nonclostridial anaerobic myonecrosis (necrotizing cutaneous myositis / synergistic necrotizing cellulitis) — a mixed aerobic-anaerobic variant Cellulitis / erysipelas (superficial; skin more abnormal but pain mild-moderate) Halophilic Vibrio vulnificus infection (can be as fulminant as NF; Gulf/Atlantic water exposure or raw seafood in cirrhosis) Aeromonas soft-tissue infection (freshwater laceration exposure) Aggressive cellulitis from Vibrio vulnificus or Aeromonas hydrophila Ecthyma gangrenosum (Pseudomonas, neutropenic hosts) Clostridial myonecrosis Soft-tissue plain radiography, CT, and MRI to assess depth of infection and detect tissue gas or a localized abscess — most useful when lesions progress rapidly or SIRS is present; note imaging may show only soft-tissue swelling and is NOT specific for fulminant GAS NF/myonecrosis, where gas is typically absent Gram stain and aerobic/anaerobic culture of surgically excised tissue to identify GAS vs mixed flora vs MRSA vs Clostridium Frozen-section histology of aspirate or punch biopsy (valuable in NF), though aspiration/biopsy is negative in ~80% of cases Serum CPK (markedly elevated when myonecrosis coexists)

Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria — Autoimmune hemolytic anemia (warm or cold antibody type) Aplastic anemia Myelodysplastic syndrome Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura / atypical hemolytic uremic syndrome Hereditary spherocytosis or other membrane defects G6PD deficiency and other hemolytic enzymopathies Flow cytometry for GPI-anchored proteins (FLAER, CD55, CD59) on granulocytes and erythrocytes — confirms and sizes the PNH clone Complete blood count with reticulocyte count — documents hemolysis and identifies coexisting cytopenias LDH, indirect bilirubin, haptoglobin — supports intravascular hemolysis Urinalysis for hemoglobinuria and urinary hemosiderin — evidence of chronic intravascular hemolysis Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test — should be negative, helping exclude autoimmune hemolysis Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy with cytogenetics — assesses for underlying aplastic anemia or MDS Iron studies — chronic hemoglobinuria can cause iron deficiency despite hemolysis Imaging (Doppler ultrasound, CT/MR venography) if thrombosis at an atypical site is suspected Autoimmune hemolytic anemia Microangiopathic hemolytic anemias (TTP/HUS, DIC) Aplastic anemia without a PNH clone Budd-Chiari syndrome from other hypercoagulable states Cold agglutinin disease PNH arises from an acquired somatic mutation in the X-linked PIGA gene within a hematopoietic stem cell, impairing synthesis of the glycosylphosphatidylinositol (GPI) anchor required to display several surface proteins. Loss of the complement regulators CD55 (decay-accelerating factor) and CD59 (membrane inhibitor of reactive lysis) leaves the abnormal red cell clone vulnerable to unchecked complement-mediated intravascular lysis. The clonal population expands, often in the setting of an immune-mediated marrow injury

Primary biliary cholangitis — Primary sclerosing cholangitis Drug-induced cholestatic liver injury Autoimmune hepatitis (including PBC-AIH overlap syndrome) Extrahepatic biliary obstruction (choledocholithiasis, stricture, malignancy) Sarcoidosis with hepatic involvement Idiopathic adulthood ductopenia Alkaline phosphatase and GGT — establish and quantify cholestatic pattern Antimitochondrial antibody (AMA) — key serologic marker, positive in most cases Antinuclear antibody (ANA), including PBC-specific patterns (anti-gp210, anti-sp100) — useful when AMA is negative Serum IgM — characteristically elevated in PBC Abdominal ultrasound or cross-sectional imaging — exclude extrahepatic biliary obstruction Liver biopsy — confirms diagnosis in AMA-negative cases and stages disease when diagnosis is uncertain Transient elastography (FibroScan) or other noninvasive fibrosis assessment — staging and monitoring Fat-soluble vitamin levels and bone density (DEXA) — assess complications of chronic cholestasis Drug-induced cholestasis Primary sclerosing cholangitis Autoimmune hepatitis Hepatic sarcoidosis Mechanical biliary obstruction PBC is an autoimmune, T-cell-mediated process that progressively destroys small and medium intrahepatic bile ducts, producing chronic cholestasis. Ongoing bile duct injury leads to periportal inflammation, fibrosis, and eventually biliary-type cirrhosis if untreated. Genetic susceptibility combined with environmental triggers is thought to break tolerance to mitochondrial autoantigens, driving the characteristic antimitochondrial antibody response.

Progressive fibro-obliteration produces multifocal strictures with intervening dilations, eventually causing biliary obstruction, secondary bacterial cholangitis, and biliary cirrhosis. Acute Bacterial Prostatitis — Chronic bacterial prostatitis (CBP) — presents insidiously as recurrent episodes of cystitis, sometimes with pelvic and perineal pain, usually without systemic signs of infection; should be suspected with recurrent UTI not in the context of catheterization (Harrison 22e p.1089, p.1136). Pyelonephritis — another febrile genitourinary infection that must be excluded as the anatomic source before attributing systemic symptoms to ABP (Harrison 22e p.1136). Acute cystitis in men — uncommon and warrants caution; urine culture should be obtained in all male UTI to help identify a prostatic focus (Harrison 22e p.1089). Pyelonephritis — overlapping febrile UTI presentation; distinguished by flank/costovertebral angle pain and an upper-tract source (Harrison 22e p.1089). Urethritis — urethral pain, pruritus, or discharge should prompt evaluation for sexually transmitted infections (Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Chlamydia trachomatis, Mycoplasma genitalium) rather than assuming prostatitis (Harrison 22e p.1087). Urine culture in all male UTI — documenting bacteriuria differentiates bacterial prostatitis from chronic pelvic pain syndrome; dipstick and/or microscopy alone are not sufficient (Harrison 22e p.1089). Cross-sectional imaging (CT or ultrasound) for men with febrile UTI, including the first episode, if not previously done, to evaluate for urinary tract abnormalities or obstruction (Harrison 22e p.1089).

Scrub Typhus — Other rickettsioses presenting with eschar, rash, fever and headache (e.g., Mediterranean spotted fever, African tick-bite fever, rickettsialpox, murine and epidemic typhus) (Harrison 22e p.1455-1456). Other undifferentiated tropical febrile illnesses with thrombocytopenia and transaminitis. Serology is the mainstay of laboratory diagnosis: indirect fluorescent antibody, indirect immunoperoxidase, enzyme immunoassays, and rapid lateral-flow chromatographic tests (Harrison 22e p.1460). PCR amplification of Orientia genes is effective when performed on eschar material, but is less sensitive on blood (Harrison 22e p.1460). Platelet count: thrombocytopenia is a characteristic laboratory finding in scrub typhus (as in other rickettsioses) (Harrison 22e p.1455). WBC count is typically normal or low (Harrison 22e p.1455). Serum sodium: hyponatremia is a recognized associated finding across the rickettsioses (Harrison 22e p.1455). Hepatic aminotransferases: mild to moderate elevation is commonly seen (Harrison 22e p.1455). Scrub typhus is caused by Orientia tsutsugamushi, an obligate intracellular organism placed in a separate genus within the family Rickettsiaceae. It differs substantially from Rickettsia species both genetically and in cell-wall composition, notably lacking lipopolysaccharide. Disease results from infection of vascular endothelial cells with increased vascular permeability (a mechanism shared across the rickettsioses). Upper Respiratory Tract Infection (common cold) — Influenza (more prominent myalgias and systemic symptoms) COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2 can cause virtually any upper respiratory symptom; new loss of taste or smell appears specific for COVID-19) Measles (cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis) Acute HIV infection (sore throat and rash often predominate) Allergic, inflammatory, autoimmune, or neoplastic causes of upper respiratory symptoms Influenza COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2) Acute HIV infection Measles Streptococcal pharyngitis Acute bacterial sinusitis Acute otitis media No specific viral testing is needed for diagnosis; multiplex RT-PCR panels exist but are often unnecessary and may be falsely positive due to recent prior infection (Harrison 22e p.296) Allergic rhinitis / allergic upper respiratory symptoms Other inflammatory upper respiratory conditions Autoimmune causes of upper respiratory symptoms Neoplastic causes of upper respiratory symptoms Nonspecific URI is an acute infection of the respiratory tract above the vocal cords, most commonly caused by respiratory viruses acquired through direct contact with infected people, contaminated surfaces, and large and small respiratory droplets. Susceptibility depends on prior exposure and immunity, general health, genetics, microbiome factors, and psychosocial factors including stress. Because immunity is serotype-specific (rhinovirus, adenovirus) or weak/short-lived (coronaviruses, parainfluenza, RSV, metapneumovirus), reinfection is frequent (Harrison 22e pp.295-296).

Waldenström macroglobulinaemia — Multiple myeloma (IgM myeloma is rare but distinguishable by lytic bone lesions and different marrow morphology) IgM monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) Chronic lymphocytic leukemia / small lymphocytic lymphoma Marginal zone lymphoma with plasmacytic differentiation Other B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphomas with paraproteinemia Amyloidosis (AL) presenting with neuropathy and paraproteinemia Serum protein electrophoresis and immunofixation — identifies and characterizes the monoclonal IgM spike Serum viscosity — quantifies hyperviscosity risk when symptomatic Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy with immunophenotyping — confirms lymphoplasmacytic infiltration MYD88 L265P mutation testing (allele-specific PCR) — supports diagnosis and distinguishes from other lymphomas CXCR4 mutation testing — informs prognosis and response to certain targeted therapies Complete blood count — assesses cytopenias from marrow infiltration Anti-MAG antibody testing — when peripheral neuropathy is present CT imaging of chest/abdomen/pelvis — evaluates lymphadenopathy and organomegaly IgM MGUS Multiple myeloma Chronic lymphocytic leukemia Marginal zone lymphoma Cryoglobulinemic vasculitis from other causes Chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy (CIDP) unrelated to paraproteinemia Waldenström macroglobulinaemia is a lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma in which clonal B-lymphoplasmacytic cells infiltrate the bone marrow (and sometimes lymph nodes and spleen) and secrete large quantities of monoclonal IgM. The pentameric structure of IgM raises serum viscosity disproportionately to its molar concentration, producing the hyperviscosity syndrome, and the paraprotein may also deposit in nerves, precipitate in the cold (cryoglobulinemia), or bind red cells

Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma) — Helicobacter pylori-associated peptic ulcer disease NSAID-induced peptic ulcer disease Idiopathic gastric acid hypersecretion Antral G-cell hyperplasia Other causes of chronic secretory diarrhea (VIPoma, carcinoid syndrome) Retained gastric antrum syndrome after prior gastric surgery Helicobacter pylori peptic ulcer disease Fasting serum gastrin — markedly elevated levels raise suspicion for gastrinoma Gastric pH measurement — low pH with high gastrin confirms inappropriate acid-driven hypergastrinemia Secretin stimulation test — paradoxical rise in gastrin supports the diagnosis when basal levels are equivocal Upper endoscopy — assesses ulcer burden, location, and mucosal complications Somatostatin-receptor imaging (e.g., DOTATATE PET/CT) — preferred for primary tumor and metastasis localization Cross-sectional imaging (CT or MRI abdomen) — evaluates tumor size, local invasion, and hepatic metastases Endoscopic ultrasound — useful for detecting small pancreatic/duodenal lesions Serum calcium and parathyroid hormone, prolactin — screen for coexisting MEN1 NSAID-induced ulcer disease Idiopathic gastric acid hypersecretion VIPoma (pancreatic cholera) Carcinoid syndrome Antral G-cell hyperplasia Zollinger-Ellison syndrome results from a gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumor (gastrinoma), most often located in the duodenum or pancreas, that drives unregulated gastric acid hypersecretion. The resulting profound acid load overwhelms mucosal defenses and inactivates pancreatic enzymes, producing severe/recurrent peptic ulceration and secretory diarrhea with malabsorption. A substantial minority of cases occur in association with MEN1, reflecting a hereditary predisposition to multiple endocrine tumors.

Ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm — Acute mesenteric ischemia (SMA embolism/thrombosis) — also causes severe diffuse abdominal pain, classically pain out of proportion to exam findings (p.154). Thoracic / thoracoabdominal aortic aneurysm, which is often contiguous with infradiaphragmatic disease (p.2208). Mycotic (infective) aortic aneurysm from staphylococcal, streptococcal, Salmonella, or fungal seeding — typically saccular and often with positive blood cultures (p.2209). Syphilitic aortitis — uncommon cause, predominantly involves the ascending aorta/arch rather than the abdominal aorta (p.2209). Tuberculous aneurysm — typically affects the thoracic aorta via contiguous spread from hilar nodes or abscess (p.2209). Abdominal ultrasound — delineates transverse and longitudinal dimensions, can detect mural thrombus, and is the tool for serial size surveillance and screening (p.2211). Plain abdominal radiograph — may show a calcified aneurysm outline, but ~25% are non-calcified and not visualized (p.2211). Contrast-enhanced CT or MRI — accurate for location and size and for planning open or endovascular repair (p.2211). Contrast aortography may underestimate true diameter when mural thrombus reduces luminal size, and carries risks of bleeding, allergy, and atheroembolism (p.2211). Renal/ureteric colic — rupturing AAA pain radiating to flank or genitalia can mimic urolithiasis (p.154). Rectus sheath hematoma — abdominal wall mass and pain, especially on anticoagulants (p.154).

Acute coronary syndrome — Stable angina (chronic, exertional) Esophageal spasm (can closely mimic angina and may respond to nitroglycerin) Gastroesophageal reflux / peptic ulcer disease Costochondritis / chest wall (musculoskeletal) syndromes Cervical radiculitis / disk disease Panic disorder and related psychiatric conditions (up to ~10% of ED chest pain) High-sensitivity cardiac troponin at presentation, repeated at 1-3 h (1-2 h rapid rule-out possible with hs-assays); conventional troponin repeated at 3-6 h Right-sided ECG leads when ischemia is suspected but standard 12-lead is nondiagnostic Chest radiograph (often normal in ACS; may show pulmonary edema; helps exclude pneumothorax, wide mediastinum) Echocardiography for regional wall-motion abnormality, mechanical complications, or tamponade when diagnosis is uncertain or there is hemodynamic instability Coronary CT angiography for low-intermediate probability (high negative predictive value; also excludes dissection, effusion, PE) Stress nuclear perfusion imaging or stress echocardiography for intermediate-risk patients eligible for further testing Cardiac MRI to characterize troponin elevation without definite CAD and to discriminate ischemic from non-ischemic injury B-type natriuretic peptide and D-dimer as adjuncts (for heart failure and PE exclusion respectively) Acute pericarditis (pleuritic pain, relieved by sitting forward, friction rub, diffuse ST elevation with PR depression)

Acute Limb Ischaemia — Handheld Doppler of distal pulses + ankle pressures Urgent CT/MR/catheter angiography to localise occlusion ECG (atrial fibrillation), FBC, coagulation, group-and-save Acute Limb Ischaemia (non-infective) — Vascular Sudden severe limb pain in a patient with an embolic source (atrial fibrillation) or peripheral arterial disease indicates acute limb ischaemia — a time-critical vascular emergency (the 6 Ps). Red flags: Time-critical — irreversible tissue loss within ~6 h; pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis, poikilothermia; Paralysis/anaesthesia (Rutherford IIb→III) → immediate revascularisation or the limb is lost; Systemic anticoagulate immediately unless contraindicated; urgent vascular referral

Progressive marrow infiltration crowds out normal hematopoiesis, yielding anemia, neutropenia, and thrombocytopenia. Blasts may also infiltrate lymph nodes, liver, spleen, mediastinum, and the central nervous system (a pharmacologic sanctuary site). Subtypes correspond to arrest at defined stages of B-cell or T-cell

Acute Myeloid Leukemia (AML) — Acute lymphoblastic leukemia (ALL) - distinguished by flow cytometry/immunophenotype; presence of Auer rods confirms AML and excludes ALL Myelodysplastic syndrome (MDS) - may precede/evolve into AML; AML-MR is defined by antecedent MDS or MDS/MPN and/or specific cytogenetic/molecular features Myeloproliferative neoplasm (including chronic myeloid leukemia) - antecedent hematologic disorder that can transform to AML Therapy-related (post-chemotherapy) AML - after alkylating agents (4-6 yr latency) or topoisomerase II inhibitors (1-3 yr latency) CBC with manual differential (anemia normocytic normochromic; median presenting WBC ~15,000/uL; platelets <100,000/uL in ~75%) Measurable residual disease (MRD) assessment by flow cytometry or quantitative RT-PCR (e.g., NPM1, RUNX1-RUNX1T1, CBFB-MYH11, PML-RARA transcripts) Bone marrow aspirate and biopsy with morphology, cytogenetics, flow cytometry, and molecular studies (cornerstone of diagnosis and classification) Cytogenetics and molecular testing at diagnosis (NPM1, FLT3-ITD/TKD, CEBPA bZIP, TP53, IDH1/IDH2, RUNX1, ASXL1 and others) for ELN risk stratification Peripheral blood smear for blasts and Auer rods; peroxidase staining Chemistry including uric acid, LDH, phosphorus, calcium, creatinine/BUN (tumor lysis screen); ~50% have mild-moderate uric acid elevation Coagulation studies - PT, PTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer (screen for DIC, especially APL)

Acute Rheumatic Fever — Always request: electrocardiogram (ECG), echocardiogram, complete blood count (CBC), C-reactive protein (CRP), and streptococcal serology (antistreptolysin O [ASO] and anti-DNase B [ADB]) (Harrison 22e p.2857). Echocardiography should be performed on all possible cases to aid diagnosis (including detection of subclinical carditis/valvulitis) and to establish baseline carditis severity; auscultation is poorly sensitive and specific for RHD in asymptomatic patients (Harrison 22e p.2855, p.2857). Because most cases lack a positive throat swab culture or rapid antigen test, serologic evidence of preceding group A strep infection is usually needed (ASO and anti-DNase B titers), ideally with locally derived age-specific reference ranges (Harrison 22e p.2856). In relevant situations: throat swab, skin sore swab, blood cultures, synovial fluid aspirate (cell count, microscopy, culture, gonococcal PCR), pregnancy test, and creatinine/UEC (since NSAIDs can affect renal function) (Harrison 22e p.2857). Tests to exclude alternative diagnoses (per clinical presentation/local endemic infections): autoantibodies, double-stranded DNA, anti-CCP antibodies; urine molecular testing for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis; serology for viral hepatitis, Yersinia, CMV, parvovirus B19, respiratory viruses, Ross River virus, Barmah Forest virus (Harrison 22e p.2857). Inflammatory markers should be monitored every 1-2 weeks until normalized (usually within 4-6 weeks), and a repeat echocardiogram performed after 1 month to assess for progression of carditis (Harrison 22e p.2858).

Glucocorticoid deficiency impairs vascular tone, gluconeogenesis and loss of feedback inhibition of AVP release (contributing to hyponatraemia and hypoglycaemia), while mineralocorticoid deficiency causes renal salt wasting with volume depletion, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and rising creatinine. The result is hypotension that may decomp

Adrenal Cortical Disorders — Cushing's disease (ACTH-producing pituitary corticotrope adenoma) vs ectopic ACTH syndrome (bronchial/pancreatic carcinoid, small-cell lung cancer, medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma) ACTH-independent adrenal Cushing's: cortisol-producing adenoma, adrenocortical carcinoma, primary bilateral macronodular adrenal hyperplasia, primary pigmented nodular adrenal disease (Carney complex), McCune-Albright syndrome Mineralocorticoid excess differential: bilateral micronodular hyperplasia vs unilateral aldosterone-producing adenoma (Conn's); glucocorticoid-remediable aldosteronism (GRA/FH-I) and other familial primary aldosteronism; apparent mineralocorticoid excess (HSD11B2 deficiency); Liddle's syndrome (ENaC mutations); deoxycorticosterone excess from CAH (CYP11B1 or CYP17A1 deficiency) Primary vs secondary (central) adrenal insufficiency, distinguished by plasma ACTH and renin Pseudo-Cushing states: alcohol-related hypercortisolism, major depression, morbid obesity, and cyclic Cushing's Tuberculous adrenalitis (still a frequent cause of primary adrenal insufficiency in developing countries) HIV-associated adrenal involvement (usually subclinical adrenal insufficiency) Sepsis-associated bilateral adrenal hemorrhage (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome) causing acute primary adrenal insufficiency Adrenal crisis presenting like an acute abdomen with fever, abdominal tenderness, nausea and vomiting

Acute kidney injury — Prerenal azotaemia from true volume loss (GI haemorrhage, burns, diarrhoea, diuretics) (p.340) Postrenal obstructive uropathy (urethral/bladder-outlet, bilateral ureteric, or solitary-kidney obstruction) (p.340) Cast nephropathy in multiple myeloma (a cause of anuria) (p.341) Prerenal from volume sequestration (pancreatitis, peritonitis, rhabdomyolysis) (p.340) Prerenal from reduced effective arterial volume (cardiogenic shock, sepsis, severe heart failure, hepatorenal syndrome) (p.340) Ischaemic ATN (major surgery, trauma, severe hypovolaemia, overwhelming sepsis, extensive burns) (p.340) Nephrotoxic ATN (drug/toxin-induced) (p.340) Acute (allergic) interstitial nephritis from drugs (antibiotics, NSAIDs, proton pump inhibitors) (p.340) Acute glomerulonephritis / vasculitis (acute nephritic syndrome) (p.341) Renal microvascular disease (haemolytic-uraemic syndrome, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, malignant hypertension) (p.341) Large-vessel occlusion: atheroemboli, thromboemboli, in-situ thrombosis, aortic dissection, vasculitis, renal vein thrombosis (p.341) Severe systemic infection (bacterial or viral) causing tubulointerstitial AKI (p.341) Sepsis producing prerenal hypoperfusion and/or ischaemic ATN (p.340) Urine sediment microscopy for casts (muddy-brown granular and tubular epithelial casts in ATN; hyaline/granular or normal in prerenal; RBC casts in glomerulonephritis; WBC casts in interstitial nephritis) (p.340-341)

Alcohol and Alcohol Use Disorders — Alcohol ketoacidosis versus diabetic ketoacidosis (alcohol-related shows raised ketones, only mild glucose elevation, large anion gap, mild-moderate lactate rise, beta-hydroxybutyrate/lactate ratio between 2:1 and 9:1) (Harrison 22e p.3675) Substance-induced mood, anxiety or psychotic disorder versus an independent primary psychiatric disorder; about 40% of those with AUD meet criteria for a major depressive episode but roughly half are substance-induced and resolve within a month of abstinence (Harrison 22e p.3676-3677) Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome and alcohol-related cognitive impairment versus other dementias; there is no single 'alcoholic dementia' entity (Harrison 22e p.3676) Peripheral neuropathy of alcohol versus diabetic neuropathy (both bilateral, distal, with numbness, tingling, paresthesias) (Harrison 22e p.3676) Gamma-glutamyl transferase (GGT >35 U) - marker of heavy consumption (Harrison 22e p.3678) Carbohydrate-deficient transferrin (CDT >20 U/L or >2.6%); combined with GGT for higher accuracy (Harrison 22e p.3679) Mean corpuscular volume (high-normal >=91) and serum uric acid (>7 mg/dL) (Harrison 22e p.3679) Blood ethanol level (e.g., 100 mg/dL = 0.10 g/dL) (Harrison 22e p.3675) Toxicology screen for other CNS depressants (benzodiazepines) and opioids in severe intoxication (Harrison 22e p.3679) AUDIT 10-item screening questionnaire (score >=8 may indicate harmful use) - screening only, not diagnostic (Harrison 22e p.3679-3680)

Alcohol-Associated Liver Disease — Viral hepatitis (e.g., hepatitis B or C) Wilson's disease Severe autoimmune liver disease Drug-induced liver injury (DILI), including amiodarone-related pseudoalcoholic injury Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD/NAFLD) and MetALD Hemochromatosis Ischemic hepatitis Biliary obstruction Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) Viral hepatitis (hepatitis B or C) producing aminotransferase elevation that can be confused with ALD Liver function tests with AST, ALT (AST/ALT ratio), GGT, bilirubin, INR, albumin, platelet count AUDIT (Alcohol Use Disorders Inventory Test) to identify alcohol use disorder Abdominal ultrasound, MRI, or CT to detect steatosis, nodularity, and signs of portal hypertension Controlled attenuation parameter (CAP) or MR proton density fat fraction (MR-PDFF) for noninvasive hepatic fat quantification Transient elastography / liver stiffness measurement (e.g., FibroScan) for fibrosis staging Fib-4 score (age, AST, ALT, platelets) to exclude advanced fibrosis/cirrhosis (threshold <3.25) Transjugular liver biopsy when confounding factors are present (to confirm alcohol-associated hepatitis) Imaging to exclude biliary obstruction and HCC; AFP and ultrasonography for HCC surveillance in cirrhosis Infection workup: chest x-ray plus blood, urine, and ascites cultures in alcohol-associated hepatitis MASLD/NAFLD (key distinction: ALD typically shows AST/ALT >2:1, whereas NAFLD usually has ALT >= AST)

Altitude Illness — Exhaustion Pulmonary embolism (for HAPE) Dehydration Hypothermia Alcoholic hangover Hyponatremia Migraine Anxiety attack (for HAPE) Pneumonia (for HAPE) Pneumothorax (for HAPE) Respiratory tract infection / viral illness (HAPE historically misdiagnosed as viral pneumonia or as a viral illness in reentry HAPE) Pneumonia (HAPE radiographic opacities simulating pneumonic consolidation) Bacterial or Giardia enteric infection (high-altitude GI bloating/distension must be distinguished from infectious diarrhea) Clinical assessment with Lake Louise Scoring System (used chiefly for research uniformity) Pulse oximetry (oxygen saturation; arterial blood gas usually not necessary for HAPE) Chest radiography (patchy/localized opacities or streaky interstitial edema in HAPE; Kerley B lines and bat-wing pattern are NOT seen) Electrocardiography (may show right ventricular strain or hypertrophy in HAPE) Brain MRI (T2 signal change in white matter and splenium of corpus callosum confirmatory of HACE; hemosiderin deposits as footprints) Echocardiography (recommended when HAPE occurs below 3000 m or when predisposing cardiopulmonary abnormality is suspected) Lung ultrasound comet-tail/B-line scoring (sensitive but not specific for HAPE) Cardiogenic pulmonary edema / heart failure (HAPE was historically mistaken for heart failure) Acute respiratory distress syndrome (another noncardiogenic edema, but lung architecture is preserved in HAPE)

Alzheimer's Disease — Vascular dementia (early prominent gait disturbance with only mild memory loss) (Harrison 22e p.3476) Dementia with Lewy bodies (early parkinsonism with fluctuating alertness, visual hallucinations, delusional misidentification) (Harrison 22e p.3476) Parkinson's disease / Parkinson's disease dementia (resting tremor, stooped posture, bradykinesia, masked facies) (Harrison 22e p.3476) Frontotemporal dementia (prominent behavioral changes with intact navigation and focal anterior-predominant atrophy) (Harrison 22e p.3476) Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease / prion disease (rapid progression over weeks-months with rigidity and myoclonus) (Harrison 22e p.3476, p.3482) Limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy (LATE) and primary age-related tauopathy (PART) - can mimic AD clinically, especially in biomarker-negative older patients with progressive amnestic dementia (Harrison 22e p.3476, p.3477) Huntington's disease and rare hereditary ataxias when family history of dementia is present (Harrison 22e p.3476) Primary or metastatic brain neoplasm (early focal seizure) (Harrison 22e p.3476) Viral or bacterial encephalitides (listed as causes of rapidly progressive dementia in the CJD differential) (Harrison 22e p.3483) MRI/CT structural imaging - mainly to exclude other disorders; AD shows posterior-predominant cortical and medial temporal (hippocampal) atrophy and may be normal early (Harrison 22e p.3476)

Amoebiasis (Intestinal) — Bacterial dysentery / inflammatory diarrhea (Campylobacter, enteroinvasive E. coli, Shigella, Salmonella, Vibrio) Inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis, Crohn disease) Carcinoma of the colon (especially when an ameboma mass is present) Acute appendicitis (with cecal involvement) Shigellosis (bacillary dysentery) Campylobacter colitis Enteroinvasive Escherichia coli infection Salmonella enterocolitis Vibrio enteritis Examination of at least three fresh stool specimens (wet mount, iodine-stained concentrate, trichrome-stained preparation) for cysts/trophozoites Stool test for occult blood (heme) and microscopy for neutrophils Stool antigen detection assay (monoclonal anti-Gal/GalNAc lectin enzyme immunoassay) Stool multiplex PCR / nucleic acid amplification for GI protozoa Serology (ELISA / indirect hemagglutination) for invasive amebiasis Sigmoidoscopy with biopsy of the edge of ulcers if stool studies negative (avoid in fulminant colitis) Biopsy of a colonic mass to confirm ameboma and exclude carcinoma Stool culture for bacterial pathogens to exclude bacterial dysentery Inflammatory bowel disease (ulcerative colitis / Crohn disease) Colonic carcinoma (mimicked by ameboma on barium studies) Acute appendicitis E. histolytica is acquired by ingesting viable cysts from fecally contaminated water, food, or hands (food-borne exposure being most common). Motile trophozoites excyst in the small intestine; in most patients they remain as harmless commensals in the large bowel and re-encyst, shedding infectious cysts in stool. In some patients trophozoites invade the colonic mucosa (causing colitis) or enter the portal bloodstream (causing distant abscesses, most often hepatic). Trophozoites attach to colonic mucus and epithelium via the Gal/Ga

Amyloidosis — Multiple myeloma and other plasma cell dyscrasias (AL arises from the same clonal disorder) Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) and smoldering myeloma Hypertensive or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (vs amyloid cardiomyopathy) Other causes of nephrotic syndrome / proteinuric renal disease Other causes of length-dependent peripheral and autonomic neuropathy AA amyloidosis is driven by chronic infections such as tuberculosis, osteomyelitis, or subacute bacterial endocarditis, which may be the presenting or underlying illness Congo red staining of aspirated abdominal subcutaneous fat (positive in >80%); if negative, biopsy of involved organ (kidney, heart, liver, tongue, GI tract) Amyloid typing: laser-capture microdissection with tandem mass spectrometry is the diagnostic standard (sensitivity ~88%, specificity ~96%); immunoelectron microscopy more reliable than immunohistochemistry Serum/urine immunofixation electrophoresis (SIFE/UIFE) and nephelometric serum free light chain assay with kappa/lambda ratio (>90% of AL patients have a detectable monoclonal light chain) Bone marrow examination for clonal plasma cells (kappa/lambda clonality by flow cytometry, immunohistochemistry, or in situ hybridization) Cardiac biomarkers NT-proBNP/BNP and troponin for staging, prognosis, and disease monitoring; ECG (low voltage, pseudo-infarct pattern) and echocardiography (concentric thickening, diastolic dysfunction, abnormal global longitudinal strain)

Amyloidosis and Other Restrictive Cardiomyopathies — Constrictive pericardial disease (the classic and most important differential, sharing dominant right-sided failure, edema, ascites, elevated JVP and Kussmaul sign; echocardiography readily distinguishes the two today) (Harrison 22e p.2020-2022) Hypertensive heart disease (usually shows LVH on ECG and requires years of severe uncontrolled hypertension to reach amyloid-degree wall thickening) (Harrison 22e p.2021) Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (rarely presents with peripheral edema and usually has LVH on ECG; distinction from amyloidosis is usually fairly clear) (Harrison 22e p.2021) Fabry disease and other infiltrative cardiomyopathies (may have typical skin manifestations and usually LVH on ECG) (Harrison 22e p.2021-2022) Mitochondrial cardiomyopathy (echocardiographic appearance can mimic amyloidosis but with distinct noncardiac features such as maternally inherited diabetes, deafness, and recurrent strokes) (Harrison 22e p.2022) Advanced diabetic heart disease with heavy proteinuria (obvious diabetes history and echocardiogram lacking amyloid features) (Harrison 22e p.2022) Echocardiography showing increased LV wall thickness without dilation, frequent biatrial enlargement, increased RV free-wall thickness, restrictive diastolic filling pattern, and a small transmitral A wave (the latter associated with increased thromboembolic risk) (Harrison 22e p.2022-2023) Longitudinal strain imaging demonstrating apical-sparing 'bull's-eye' pattern (Harrison 22e p.2022-2023)

Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) — Cervical spondylosis / compression of the cervical spinal cord or cervicomedullary junction (tumors, foramen magnum lesions, osteophytes) Multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block (MMCB) Diffuse lower motor axonal neuropathy associated with hematopoietic disorders (lymphoma, multiple myeloma) with serum M-component X-linked spinobulbar muscular atrophy (Kennedy's disease) Adult Tay-Sachs disease (hexosaminidase A deficiency) Spinal muscular atrophy Primary lateral sclerosis (upper motor neuron only) Progressive muscular atrophy (lower motor neuron only) Poliomyelitis Herpes zoster Coxsackie virus West Nile virus Retroviral myelopathy (HTLV-1) Lyme disease Tetanus MRI of head including foramen magnum and cervical spine to exclude compressive structural lesions Electrophysiologic testing (EMG/nerve conduction) to demonstrate denervation and to detect motor conduction block (suggests MMCB rather than ALS) CSF examination and culture Serum/CSF neurofilament light chains (Nfl) - prognostic marker of disease aggressiveness Complete blood count, sedimentation rate, total protein, anti-GM1 antibodies (should be obtained in all cases) Anti-Hu antibody (paraneoplastic), serum protein for M-component, bone marrow biopsy if indicated Fasting blood sugar, calcium, thyroid function, vitamin B12/E/folate, serum zinc and copper WBC DNA for mutational analysis (C9orf72, SOD1, TDP43, FUS/TLS) in suspected familial cases

Anaphylaxis — Systemic mastocytosis (elevated baseline tryptase; spindle-shaped mast cells on bone marrow) (p. 2813) Pheochromocytoma (elevated urine metanephrines) (p. 2813) Carcinoid syndrome (elevated urine 5-HIAA) (p. 2813) Hereditary angioedema (decreased C4 during attacks) (p. 2813) Acquired angioedema (decreased C1q) (p. 2813) Systemic capillary leak syndrome (severe hypotension with poor response to first-line agents) (p. 2813) Serum tryptase peaks 60-90 min after onset and remains measurable for up to about 5 h; apply the '20% + 2' rule (an acute level >20% above the patient's baseline plus 2 ng/mL is diagnostic of clinically significant mast-cell activation) (p. 2813) Repeat tryptase once the patient is stable to establish the individual baseline, since baseline serum tryptase varies widely and can be raised by hereditary alpha-tryptasemia or high environmental allergen exposure (p. 2813) Serum histamine is of limited use acutely - its measurable window expires within about 1 h of onset (p. 2813) Allergen-specific skin testing or serum-specific IgE to confirm a suspected drug or food trigger (p. 2813) Baseline tryptase in sting-induced anaphylaxis to screen for underlying systemic mastocytosis (p. 2813) Scombroid poisoning (ingested histamine from improperly stored histidine-rich fish such as tuna, mackerel, mahi-mahi); clinically mimics anaphylaxis but tryptase is NOT elevated because histamine is exogenous, and skin test/oral challenge to fish are negative (p. 2813)

Anemia Due to Acute Blood Loss — Hemolytic anemia (the other major cause of anemia with reticulocytosis) (p.807) Iron-deficiency anemia from chronic/protracted blood loss (p.807) Other hypoproliferative or production-failure anemias when reticulocyte count is not elevated (p.807) Serial hemoglobin/hematocrit measurements — recognizing that early values are misleadingly normal and fall over hours as volume is restored (p.807) Reticulocyte count and erythropoietin level — rise during the marrow recovery phase (p.807) Imaging or endoscopy (e.g., sonogram, endoscopy) to localize occult internal bleeding (p.807) Targeted physical examination for signs of concealed hemorrhage (Grey Turner sign, Cullen sign, chest dullness) (p.807) Hemolysis — also presents as anemia with an elevated reticulocyte count and a brisk marrow response, mimicking the recovery phase of acute blood loss (p.807) Hypovolemic shock from non-hemorrhagic causes (dehydration, fluid sequestration) can reproduce the early hypovolemic picture before any fall in hemoglobin (p.807) Blood loss produces anemia by two mechanisms: direct loss of red cells, and — if the bleeding is protracted — gradual depletion of iron stores leading to iron-deficiency anemia (the latter covered separately). Acute posthemorrhagic anemia follows the former. Hemorrhage may be external (trauma, obstetric) or internal (gastrointestinal tract, splenic rupture, ruptured ectopic pregnancy, subarachnoid hemorrhage, leaking aneurysm). After a sudden large loss there are three sequential clinical/pathophysiologic stages: (1) hypovolemia dominates and threatens high-flow organs (brain, kidneys), so impaired consciousness and acute renal failure are early dangers, while the blood count still appears normal because hemoglobin concentration is un

Symptomatic anaemia — Anemia of inflammation/chronic disease (diagnosis of exclusion; MCV often normal; hepcidin-mediated block of iron reutilization) (p.448-450) Acute/chronic leukaemia and other primary marrow neoplasms (p.450) Copper deficiency (with neutropenia and neurologic disease) and vitamin C deficiency/scurvy (p.450) Drug-induced macrocytosis (chemotherapy, some antiseizure drugs) (p.449) Alcohol use, liver disease, hypothyroidism (round macrocytosis) (p.449) Thalassaemia (microcytic, low/normal RDW, defective globin synthesis) (p.448-449) Sideroblastic anemia (defective heme synthesis; microcytic) (p.448-449) Megaloblastic anemia from B12 or folate deficiency (oval macrocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils) (p.449) Myelodysplastic syndrome (macrocytic anemia or pancytopenia; stem-cell defect) (p.449-450) Anemia of chronic kidney disease (EPO lack; usually present once GFR <30) (p.450) Anemia of aging/older adults (low EPO for degree of anemia; 11% community-dwelling, up to 40% nursing-home over 65) (p.450) Aplastic anemia (hypocellular marrow, pancytopenia) (p.450) Pure red cell aplasia (isolated very low reticulocytes; autoimmune or parvovirus B19) (p.450) Marrow-replacing infections such as histoplasmosis or tuberculosis causing a myelophthisic anemia (p.450) Parvovirus B19 causing pure red cell aplasia (p.450) Corrected (or absolute) reticulocyte count as the first mechanistic discriminator (p.447-448)

ACE-inhibitor / hereditary angioedema — Allergic (histaminergic, IgE/mast-cell-mediated) angioedema, typically with concurrent urticaria/pruritus and a more rapid onset and resolution (pp. 2807-2808). Hereditary angioedema (HAE) due to C1-inhibitor deficiency (type 1) or dysfunctional C1INH (type 2), suggested by childhood/adolescent onset, family history, recurrent attacks, and failure to respond to H1 antihistamines (p. 2808). Type 3 (normal-C1INH) HAE, sometimes associated with a mutant factor XII and normal complement protein levels (p. 2808). Acquired C1-inhibitor deficiency from excessive C1INH consumption or an anti-C1INH autoantibody in the setting of lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disease, lacking a family history (p. 2808). Idiopathic angioedema without an identifiable trigger (p. 2807). Urticarial vasculitis when lesions are painful rather than pruritic, last >36 h, or scar (p. 2809). Angioedema from other bradykinin-affecting or culprit drugs listed alongside ACE inhibitors: NSAIDs/aspirin, dipeptidyl peptidase-4 (DPP-4) inhibitors, radiocontrast media, opioids, antimicrobials, and angiotensin receptor-neprilysin inhibitor (ARNI/sacubitril-valsartan) (Table 363-1, p. 2807; Ch. 265, p. 1995). Diagnosis of bradykinin-mediated angioedema is largely clinical; the lack of pruritus/urticaria and failure to respond to H1 antihistamines point away from histaminergic causes (p. 2808). For isolated angioedema without urticaria: basic chemistries with liver function tests and complement levels (p. 2809).

Antiphospholipid Syndrome — Inherited or acquired thrombophilias including factor V Leiden and other causes Hypercholesterolemia For catastrophic APS: thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, hemolytic-uremic syndrome, disseminated intravascular coagulation, and heparin-induced thrombocytopenia Coombs-positive hemolytic anemia Thrombocytopenia of other cause Atherosclerosis Polyarteritis nodosa SLE Cryoglobulinemia Lymphomas Myeloproliferative disorders Lupus anticoagulant testing as a three-step procedure: screening with activated partial thromboplastin time (aPTT) and dilute Russell viper venom test (DRVVT), mixing study, and confirmation Anticardiolipin and anti-beta2GPI IgG/IgM antibodies by standardized ELISA Antiphosphatidylserine/prothrombin antibodies when APS features are present without classical aPL Repeat aPL testing 12 weeks apart to confirm persistence Assessment per 2023 ACR/EULAR classification criteria (>=3 points from clinical domains and >=3 points from laboratory domains) Renal biopsy for suspected aPL-nephropathy (thrombotic microangiopathy in acute phase; fibrous intima hyperplasia, fibrous/fibrocellular arteriolar occlusions, focal cortical atrophy in chronic phase) Cardiac MRI or histology for suspected myocardial disease; imaging for adrenal hemorrhage; BAL or pathology for pulmonary hemorrhage Other inherited or acquired thrombophilias (e.g., factor V Leiden) Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura

Aortic dissection — Acute myocardial infarction / acute coronary syndrome (chest pain, and dissection can occlude a coronary ostium) (Harrison 22e p.2169) Pulmonary embolism (Harrison 22e p.108) Pericarditis (Harrison 22e p.106) Esophageal pain / spasm, which can mimic angina (Harrison 22e p.106) CT (with contrast) — most commonly used given proximity of scanners to emergency rooms and rapidity; sensitivity and specificity >90% for the intimal flap and extent (Harrison 22e p.2169) MRI — highly accurate for intimal flap, extent, intramural hemorrhage and penetrating ulcers; sensitivity and specificity >90% (Harrison 22e p.2169) Transesophageal echocardiography — ~98% sensitivity and ~90% specificity for ascending and descending dissection (but not the arch); also assesses aortic regurgitation and pericardial effusion (Harrison 22e p.2169) Transthoracic echocardiography — rapid bedside test, overall sensitivity 60-85% (>80% for proximal ascending dissection), less useful for arch and descending aorta (Harrison 22e p.2169) Chest x-ray — may show widened superior mediastinum and/or pleural effusion (Harrison 22e p.2169) ECG — to look for ischemia and help differentiate from MI (Harrison 22e p.2169) Penetrating atherosclerotic ulcer of the aorta (Harrison 22e p.2168) Acute intramural hematoma of the aorta (Harrison 22e p.2168) Aortic rupture (Harrison 22e p.2168) Dissection begins with a tear of the intima, most often along the high-shear right lateral wall of the ascending aorta or in the descending thoracic aorta just below the ligamentum arteriosum. Pulsatile flow dissects along the elastic lamellar plates of the media to create a false lumen; the initiating event may be a primary intimal tear with secondary dissection into the media, or a medial hemorrhage that secondari

Aortic Regurgitation — Aortic stenosis (a mid-systolic ejection murmur and systolic thrill are frequently audible in isolated AR and do not necessarily signify coexisting AS) Combined aortic stenosis and aortic regurgitation (coexistence of hemodynamically significant AS with AR occurs almost exclusively in rheumatic or congenital disease) Mitral regurgitation (contrasted hemodynamically; severe AR can also coexist with MR) ECG: LV hypertrophy signs in chronic severe AR, with ST-segment depression and T-wave inversion in leads I, aVL, V5, V6 ('LV strain'); left axis deviation and/or QRS prolongation may be present (p.2044) Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE): cornerstone of longitudinal follow-up; assesses LV size/function and cause/severity of AR; LV global longitudinal strain (GLS) by speckle tracking may detect systolic dysfunction before EF falls (p.2044) Color flow Doppler: with severe AR the central jet width exceeds 65% of the LV outflow tract, regurgitant volume >=60 mL/beat, regurgitant fraction >=50%, and there is diastolic flow reversal in the proximal descending thoracic aorta; continuous-wave Doppler shows rapid deceleration time in acute severe AR (p.2044) Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE): detailed anatomic assessment of valve, root, and portions of the aorta (p.2044) Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR): accurate LV volumes and aortic size/contour when TTE is limited; can screen for increased LV interstitial (extracellular volume fraction) and replacement fibrosis (late gadolinium enhancement) (p.2044)

Aortic stenosis (syncope) — Aortic sclerosis (focal leaflet thickening/calcification without obstruction; Doppler jet velocity 2.5 m/s or less) can produce a grade 2-3 midsystolic murmur acoustically identical to AS (Harrison 22e p.1908). Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (subvalvular dynamic outflow obstruction) (Harrison 22e p.328, 1934). Subaortic membrane (fixed subvalvular obstruction that can mimic valvular AS) (Harrison 22e p.1934). Supravalvular aortic stenosis (exceedingly rare) (Harrison 22e p.1934). Pulmonic stenosis (midsystolic murmur, second left interspace) (Harrison 22e p.329). Atrial septal defect with increased pulmonic flow producing a midsystolic murmur with fixed splitting of S2 (Harrison 22e p.329). Mitral regurgitation, given the apical Gallavardin transmission of the AS murmur (Harrison 22e p.328). Transthoracic echocardiography to assess valve anatomy (tricuspid/bicuspid, leaflet calcification, excursion), stenosis severity, LV size/wall thickness/function, and aortic root and proximal ascending aorta (Harrison 22e p.329, 1933). Doppler estimation of transvalvular peak velocity and pressure gradient (Harrison 22e p.1933). Continuity-equation estimation of aortic valve area, the most accurate echo technique, especially when gradients are underestimated by LV dysfunction (Harrison 22e p.1933-1934). Dobutamine stress echocardiography to evaluate low-flow/low-gradient AS and determine whether the valve can open further (Harrison 22e p.1934).

Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS) — Cardiogenic (hydrostatic) pulmonary edema Bilateral pneumonia Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage Acute interstitial lung disease (e.g., acute interstitial pneumonitis) Acute immunologic injury (e.g., hypersensitivity pneumonitis) Toxin injury (e.g., radiation pneumonitis) Neurogenic pulmonary edema Bilateral pneumonia (may also coexist with ARDS) Arterial blood gas to determine PaO2/FiO2 ratio for Berlin severity grading Chest radiograph (bilateral opacities consistent with pulmonary edema, often involving >=three-quarters of lung fields) Echocardiography to exclude hydrostatic/cardiac etiology when no ARDS risk factor is present Chest CT (shows bilateral infiltrates with heterogeneous, often dependent lung involvement) Lung ultrasound permitted as an alternative imaging modality under proposed 2023 Berlin updates, especially in resource-limited settings Cardiogenic pulmonary edema Diffuse alveolar hemorrhage Acute interstitial pneumonitis Hypersensitivity pneumonitis Radiation pneumonitis Neurogenic pulmonary edema ARDS results from diffuse lung injury, either direct (e.g., pneumonia, aspiration, toxic inhalation, pulmonary contusion) or indirect (e.g., sepsis, severe trauma, multiple transfusions, pancreatitis). It evolves through three phases. In the EXUDATIVE phase (first ~7 days), alveolar capillary endothelial cells and type I pneumocytes are injured, the tight alveolar barrier is lost, and protein-rich edema fluid accumulates in the interstitial and alveolar spaces. Proinflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, TNF-alpha) and lipid mediators recruit neutrophils, and condensed plasma proteins plus cellular debris and dysfunctional surfactant form hyaline membranes (diffuse alveolar damage). Arterial and Venous Thrombosis — Atherosclerotic plaque rupture causing acute coronary syndrome Embolism (cardiac source) versus in-situ thrombosis Aortic or arterial dissection Vasculitis causing arterial occlusion Postthrombotic syndrome as sequela of DVT Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension after PE Thrombophilia evaluation (factor V Leiden, prothrombin G20210A, antithrombin, protein C, protein S deficiencies) in selected patients, recognizing many older genetic associations are being questioned in larger contemporary studies Antiphospholipid antibody testing when autoimmune prothrombotic state suspected Plasma homocysteine and MTHFR considerations as historically reported independent risk factors Assessment of acquired risk factors: malignancy screening, recent surgery/trauma, pregnancy status, hormonal therapy use Markers reflecting inflammation-thrombosis crosstalk (e.g., soluble CD40 ligand) noted as research-relevant Acute limb ischemia from arterial embolism rather than local thrombosis Superficial venous thrombophlebitis Lymphedema or cellulitis mimicking DVT-related limb swelling Extrinsic venous compression mimicking thrombotic obstruction Thrombus formation reflects dysregulated hemostasis involving the vessel wall, coagulation and fibrinolytic proteins, and platelets. Atrial fibrillation / arrhythmia — Multifocal atrial tachycardia (>=3 distinct P-wave morphologies with clear isoelectric intervals and a slower atrial rate than AF; typically in chronic pulmonary disease and acute illness) (p.1989). Other supraventricular tachycardias including atrial flutter, focal atrial tachycardia, AV nodal reentry, and AV reciprocating tachycardia, distinguished by 12-lead ECG appearance and response to AV nodal blockade (p.1976-1977). Preexcited (accessory-pathway) AF, presenting as an irregular wide-complex tachycardia with bizarre, beat-to-beat-variable QRS morphology (p.1985-1986). Transesophageal echocardiography to exclude left atrial appendage thrombus before cardioversion when AF duration is >48 h or unknown (p.1992). Cardiac CT angiography with delayed-acquisition imaging as an alternative to TEE for left atrial appendage thrombus detection, with high sensitivity and specificity (p.1992). Ambulatory ECG monitoring, implantable loop recorders, or wearable/home ECG devices to capture intermittent or subclinical episodes (p.1991, 1993). AF is characterized by disorganized, rapid, irregular atrial electrical activation with loss of organized atrial mechanical contraction; the AV node filters these impulses to produce an irregular ventricular rate. The pathophysiology is multifactorial and incompletely understood, with a proposed 'final common pathway' in which risk factors (age, cardiovascular disease, hypertension, diabetes, obesity, alcohol, sleep-disordered breathing) drive electrophysiologic changes in atrial tissue. Altered membrane channel regulation produces abnormal excitability; pulmonary vein musculature (and other foci such as the posterior left atrial wall, superior vena cava, coronary sinus, vein of Marshall) shows enhanced autom

Basic Biology of the Cardiovascular System — Flow-mediated dilatation of the brachial artery by ultrasound (cuff occlusion/release) to assess endothelial vasodilator function in vivo The cardiovascular system develops from cardiac progenitors in lateral splanchnic mesoderm that fuse into a linear heart tube of endocardium and spontaneously beating cardiomyocytes, then undergo asymmetric looping and chamber specification with continued addition of second-heart-field cells (Islet-1 positive). Septation separates the cardiac chambers and divides the truncus arteriosus into aorta and pulmonary artery; endocardial cushions, rich in hyaluronic-acid 'cardiac jelly', undergo epithelial-mesenchymal transformation to form valves. Neural crest cells direct aortic arch remodeling and supply smooth muscle to the great vessels, while proepicardial cells form coronary vasculature. Blood vessels share a trilaminar architecture (intimal endothelium, smooth-muscle media, fibroblast-rich adventitia), with capillaries reduced to an endothelial tube and pericytes and large vessels nourished by vasa vasorum. The endothelium maintains vascular homeostasis through balanced production of vasodilators (NO, prostacyclin) and vasoconstrictors (endothelin), regulation of leukocyte adhesion, and modulation of coagulation; loss of these functions underlies atherosclerosis, hypertension, capillary-leak states, and immune-mediated vascular injury. Vascular smooth-muscle tone is set by intracellular calcium and myosin light chain phosphorylation, integrated through sympathetic, parasympathetic, and nonadrenergic/noncholinergic (nitrergic, peptidergic) autonomic signaling. Bladder & Urinary Tract Cancer — Hematuria from malignancy in females is frequently mistaken for a urinary tract infection (Harrison 22e p.691). Urine cytology (detects cancer in only about 50% of high-grade bladder cancers) (Harrison 22e p.691). Cystoscopy for direct bladder visualization; blue light or narrow-band imaging cystoscopy improves detection of small or flat noninvasive tumors and is used routinely in monitoring (Harrison 22e p.691). CT urogram (or MR urogram if renal function is impaired) for the kidneys and upper tract (Harrison 22e p.691). Adjunct urine molecular tests (FISH for chromosomal changes, nuclear mitotic proteins, bladder tumor-associated antigens) used mainly for detecting recurrence, as they can be falsely positive (Harrison 22e p.691). Ureteroscopy or retrograde pyelography when upper-tract tumors are suspected with a normal bladder (Harrison 22e p.691). Transurethral resection of bladder tumor (TURBT) or endoscopic resection of upper tract tumors for histologic diagnosis and staging (Harrison 22e p.691). Genomic sequencing of tumor tissue and/or circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) recommended in all metastatic patients (Harrison 22e p.690). In females, malignant hematuria may be misattributed to menstrual bleeding (Harrison 22e p.691). Intravesical BCG side effects (dysuria, urinary frequency, bladder spasms, hematuria) overlap with infection/cystitis, and in <5% a systemic inflammatory response can mimic disseminated BCG infection (Harrison 22e p.692).

Bowel obstruction — Adynamic / paralytic ileus (loss of peristalsis with absent bowel sounds) rather than mechanical obstruction Colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie's syndrome) — colonic dilatation without a mechanical lesion Severe constipation / fecal impaction causing abdominal distension and discomfort Sigmoid or cecal volvulus as a cause of colonic obstruction Gastric outlet obstruction (malignancy or chronic peptic stenosis of the pylorus) presenting with vomiting of partially digested food hours after eating Esophageal obstruction by impacted food bolus / foreign body (proximal obstruction mimic) Low-dose CT is preferred over plain abdominal radiography when the indication for surgical/medical intervention is unclear in nontraumatic acute abdominal pain Plain upright/lateral-decubitus abdominal radiographs can show dilated bowel loops suggesting obstruction or ileus, but have limited utility and may be unnecessary when the cause (e.g., strangulated external hernia) is already evident Water-soluble contrast enema can be diagnostic in suspected colonic obstruction without perforation; oral barium sulfate should be avoided if colonic obstruction is suspected Serum amylase may be raised by strangulating intestinal obstruction (also by perforated ulcer, cholecystitis), so an elevation neither confirms nor excludes the need for operation Leukocytosis is non-specific (a WBC >20,000/uL may follow perforation but also pancreatitis, cholecystitis, infarction) and should never be the sole determinant of operative need; a normal count does not exclude perforation
