Brain tumour / mass lesion — Metastatic brain tumour - three times more common than all primary brain tumours combined in adults; commonest sources lung and breast, with melanoma having the greatest propensity to metastasize to brain (p.716, p.723) Diffuse glioma - the most common malignant PRIMARY brain tumour; subdivided into IDH-mutant astrocytoma, IDH-mutant 1p/19q-codeleted oligodendroglioma, and IDH wild-type glioblastoma (p.717-718) Meningioma - now the most common primary brain tumour overall (~35%); extra-axial dural-based lesion, WHO grades I-III (p.720-721) Vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma) - ~9% of primary brain tumours, presents with progressive unilateral hearing loss/tinnitus/dizziness (p.721) Primary CNS lymphoma - densely enhancing, often periventricular/basal ganglia/corpus callosum; associated with immunosuppression and EBV in HIV (p.720) Pituitary adenoma - amenorrhoea/galactorrhoea with headache suggests a prolactinoma (p.157, p.721) Pineal-region tumour presenting with Parinaud's syndrome and hydrocephalus (p.720) Colloid cyst of the third ventricle - intermittent hydrocephalus, rarely sudden death (p.722) Brain abscess - shares a ring-enhancing radiographic appearance with metastasis and high-grade glioma (p.723) Cerebral toxoplasmosis - in immunocompromised patients, multiple ring-enhancing lesions can be hard to distinguish from PCNSL or metastases (p.721) MRI with gadolinium is the preferred test; CT only if MRI cannot be done (p.716)

Breast Cancer — Inflammatory breast cancer is sometimes confused with mastitis or other breast infection (Harrison 22e p.638). Benign breast pathology such as atypical ductal or lobular hyperplasia (raises risk about four- to fivefold) and lobular carcinoma in situ (LCIS, raises risk 7- to 12-fold) (Harrison 22e p.633). Mastitis or other breast infection can be mimicked by inflammatory breast cancer, which presents with rapid onset of erythema, swelling, and tenderness of the breast; breast or skin biopsy is critical when breast inflammation fails to resolve after antibiotics (Harrison 22e p.638). Image-guided core biopsy for pathologic confirmation, tumor grade/morphology, and biomarker testing (ER, PR, HER2 protein, and potentially HER2 gene amplification) (Harrison 22e p.634). Diagnostic breast imaging: mammography, ultrasonography, and MRI if indicated; bilateral breast imaging because up to 3% have unsuspected contralateral disease (Harrison 22e p.634). Germline panel testing for breast cancer susceptibility mutations on DNA from peripheral blood or saliva after appropriate counseling (not recommended for the general population) (Harrison 22e p.633). For symptoms or findings of advanced disease (large tumor, skin changes, extensive adenopathy): CT and radionuclide bone scanning to look for overt metastatic disease, with biopsy of suspicious lesions to confirm metastatic disease (Harrison 22e p.635).

Brucellosis — Tuberculosis is the most important differential for vertebral osteomyelitis or septic arthritis; vertebral destruction or spinal cord impingement is rare in brucellosis and usually suggests tuberculosis (p.1333). Typhoid fever and malaria as causes of fever in endemic areas (p.1333). Glandular fever-like illness (EBV, Toxoplasma, cytomegalovirus, HIV, or Mycobacterium tuberculosis) when hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy is present (p.1333). Mumps and surgical conditions such as testicular torsion when epididymo-orchitis occurs (p.1333). Neurotuberculosis, atypical leptospirosis, and noninfectious conditions when lymphocytic meningoencephalitis develops (p.1333). Tuberculosis Typhoid fever Malaria Leptospirosis Epstein-Barr virus infection Cytomegalovirus infection Toxoplasmosis HIV infection Mumps Blood, CSF, bone marrow, joint fluid, or tissue aspirate/biopsy culture under containment conditions for dangerous pathogens; alert the laboratory when brucellosis is suspected (p.1333). Standard tube/plate/microagglutination serology as the mainstay, with complement fixation, Coombs antiglobulin, and ELISA tests; repeat after 2-4 weeks to detect a rising titer (p.1334). Peripheral blood PCR / nucleic acid amplification (e.g., targeting rrs-rrl spacer, outer-membrane protein genes, IS711, BCSP31) which is more sensitive and quicker than culture and avoids biohazard risk (p.1334). MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry for identification in well-resourced laboratories, with the caveat that earlier implementations often failed to identify Brucella correctly (p.1333).

Candidiasis — Dermatophytosis (tinea) on glabrous skin (Chap. 60, p.432) Tinea (pityriasis) versicolor due to Malassezia furfur (Chap. 60, p.432) Lichen planus / oral leukoplakia for oral white lesions Other invasive fungal infections in neutropenia: invasive aspergillosis and other molds (Chap. 79, p.578) Invasive aspergillosis and other molds (necrotic nodules) in immunocompromised hosts (Chap. 79, p.578; rash chapter) Disseminated cryptococcosis (molluscum-like nodular lesions) (rash chapter) Mucormycosis (rash chapter) Bacterial/septic endophthalmitis, including from endocarditis (Roth's spots also in leukemia, diabetes) (Chap. 34, p.269) KOH preparation of skin/mucosal scrapings demonstrating yeast and pseudohyphae for mucocutaneous candidiasis (Chap. 60, p.433) Culture of lesional material (Chap. 60, p.433) Blood cultures for candidemia (note insensitivity; see pitfalls) (Chap. 34, p.269; Chap. 79) Dilated funduscopic examination to detect candidal endophthalmitis in candidemia (Chap. 34, p.269) Erythema nodosum (tender lower-extremity nodules) for nodular eruptions (rash chapter) Sweet syndrome (acute febrile neutrophilic dermatosis) (rash chapter) Psoriasis / eczema in intertriginous areas Candida species (most often C. albicans) are normal saprophytic commensals of the gastrointestinal tract and skin. They overgrow and become pathogenic when local or systemic host defenses are disrupted, e.g., by broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy, diabetes mellitus, or immunosuppression. Mucocutaneous disease results from overgrowth at moist, macerated surfaces; invasive disease arises when the organism gains bloodstream access, frequently via intravascular catheters or the gut in neutropenic hosts (endogenous flora), producing candidemia and hematogenous (disseminated) seeding

Cannabis and Cannabis Use Disorder — Primary psychotic disorder (schizophrenia) versus cannabis-induced psychosis Other substance use disorders (alcohol, nicotine, opioids, stimulants) often co-occurring Primary anxiety, depressive, or panic disorder versus cannabis-induced symptoms Cyclic vomiting syndrome versus cannabis hyperemesis syndrome Other causes of impaired cognition, low IQ, or poor school performance in adolescents Urine immunoassay/confirmatory testing for 11-nor-carboxy-THC (11-COOH-THC), the inactive long-lived metabolite DSM-5 criteria-based clinical assessment for cannabis use disorder severity Screening for comorbid substance use (alcohol, nicotine, opioids, stimulants) and for psychiatric comorbidity (psychosis, depression, suicidality) In pregnancy: assessment of fetal growth given association with lower birth weight and preterm delivery Cyclic vomiting syndrome (mimics cannabis hyperemesis syndrome) Primary schizophrenia or other psychotic disorder (mimics cannabis-induced psychosis) Primary anxiety/panic disorder (mimics acute high-dose cannabis intoxication) EVALI (e-cigarette/vaping product use-associated lung injury) linked to vitamin E acetate diluent in black-market THC e-liquids Delta-9-THC is mainly a partial agonist at G protein-coupled cannabinoid receptors CB1R and CB2R, with euphorigenic effects mediated through CB1Rs on excitatory glutamatergic and inhibitory GABAergic interneurons and glial cells in brain regions processing stress, mood, and reward. These receptors are effectors of the endocannabinoid system (ECS), physiologically driven by endogenous ligands 2-arachidonoylglycerol (2-AG, a full agonist) and anandamide (a partial agonist) that are synthesized and degraded on demand to give temporally and regionally precise modulation.

Carcinoma of Unknown Primary — Intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma (commonly misdiagnosed as liver-presenting CUP) (Harrison 22e p.731) Extragonadal germ cell tumor in men with poorly/undifferentiated midline adenopathy (Harrison 22e pp.732, 735) Occult breast carcinoma in women with isolated axillary adenopathy (Harrison 22e pp.732, 735) Primary peritoneal papillary serous carcinoma versus colon or pancreaticobiliary cancer in women with peritoneal carcinomatosis (Harrison 22e p.735) Prostate carcinoma in men with blastic bone-only metastases and elevated PSA (Harrison 22e p.735) Lung or head-and-neck primary in older smokers presenting with mediastinal adenopathy (Harrison 22e p.735) Contrast CT of chest, abdomen, and pelvis is the standard baseline workup in all CUP patients absent contraindication (Harrison 22e p.732) Thorough history (risk factors, prior surgeries, family history) and physical exam including digital rectal exam in men and breast/pelvic exam in women (Harrison 22e p.731) Mammography (and breast MRI if mammogram/ultrasound negative) in women with metastatic adenocarcinoma, especially isolated axillary adenopathy (Harrison 22e p.732) For cervical squamous CUP: CT/MRI plus laryngoscopy, bronchoscopy, upper endoscopy, and consideration of staging tonsillectomy (Harrison 22e p.732) 18-FDG-PET, most useful in squamous cervical CUP (identifies a head/neck primary in about 21-30%) and in solitary metastasis or bone-metastasis candidates for aggressive multimodality therapy (Harrison 22e p.732)

Cardiac Transplantation and Prolonged Assisted Circulation — Other causes of advanced/refractory heart failure warranting evaluation: restrictive and infiltrative cardiomyopathy (e.g., amyloidosis), congenital heart disease, and chronic-infection-associated cardiomyopathy (Chagas disease, viral hepatitis-related, tuberculosis) Allograft dysfunction differential after transplant: acute cellular rejection vs antibody-mediated rejection vs cardiac allograft vasculopathy vs primary graft dysfunction Surveillance endomyocardial biopsy to grade and monitor rejection Immunofluorescence for immunoglobulin deposition and complement fixation, plus circulating donor-specific antibody testing, when AMR is suspected Cardiopulmonary exercise testing for peak VO2 to assess transplant/LVAS candidacy Invasive hemodynamic assessment of pulmonary vascular resistance and transpulmonary gradient (PVR >3 Wood units or transpulmonary gradient >15 are relative transplant contraindications unless reactive) Intravascular ultrasound or optical coherence tomography (more sensitive than angiography) and noninvasive coronary flow reserve for CAV detection and prognosis Prospective or virtual cross-match in allosensitized recipients with preformed antibodies Doppler-derived mean arterial pressure measurement in continuous-flow LVAS patients Lactate dehydrogenase as a hemolysis biomarker to screen for pump thrombosis In advanced (stage D) heart failure the myocardium can no longer maintain adequate output despite maximal medical therapy, producing a low cardiac output state with elevated filling and pulmonary pressures, intolerance of neurohormonal antagonists, and progressive cardiorenal dysfunction. Cardiac transplantation replaces the failing heart with an allograft that is surgically denervated, s

Cardiac Trauma — Acute coronary syndrome / myocardial infarction (traumatic coronary dissection or thrombosis can produce STEMI) Aortic dissection (traumatic aortic rupture can mimic its presentation) Acute pericarditis Cardiac tamponade from other causes Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy following emotional or physical trauma Musculoskeletal chest wall pain from rib or sternal injury 12-lead ECG in all patients with chest trauma (repeat as needed for evolving conduction disturbance/arrhythmia) Serial cardiac troponin (I or T); normal serial levels make cardiac injury very unlikely Transthoracic echocardiography in all suspected BCI and all penetrating chest injuries to assess wall motion, effusion, valves, and shunts Transesophageal echocardiography when adequate TTE images cannot be obtained Chest x-ray (mediastinal widening suggests aortic injury) Cardiac catheterization to confirm a suspected mechanical complication (shunt/valvular lesion) Non-traumatic acute myocardial infarction Non-traumatic aortic dissection Idiopathic or other-cause acute pericarditis Takotsubo cardiomyopathy Blunt forces (rapid deceleration, direct chest impact, crush, or blast) and penetrating objects damage the myocardium, valves, coronary arteries, pericardium, and great vessels. Myocardial contusion produces injury pathologically similar to infarction, with necrosis arising either directly or from traumatic coronary laceration, dissection, or thrombosis, predisposing to arrhythmias and conduction block. More severe injury causes free wall rupture (hemopericardium and tamponade) or ventricular septal rupture (intracardiac shunting). Valvular apparatus rupture (most often tricuspid or aortic) causes acute incompetence. Aortic rupture or transection, typically just above the aortic valve or a

Cardiogenic shock — Acute fulminant myocarditis End-stage / decompensated cardiomyopathy Takotsubo (apical ballooning) syndrome as a transient cause Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy with severe LV outflow obstruction Critical valvular disease (critical aortic/mitral stenosis; acute severe aortic or mitral regurgitation) Aortic dissection with aortic insufficiency or tamponade Refractory sustained tachyarrhythmia or bradyarrhythmia Right-ventricular failure from acute MI or acute/decompensated cor pulmonale Post-cardiac-arrest myocardial stunning; postcardiotomy shock Septic shock with myocardial depression (sepsis-induced cardiomyopathy), which can also coexist as a mixed shock state (p.2311, p.2326) Arterial blood gas (typically hypoxaemia with anion-gap metabolic acidosis) and serial arterial lactate (p.2326) Chest radiograph (pulmonary vascular congestion/oedema; normal in up to a third; enlarged heart suggests prior MI) (p.2326) ECG looking for multilead Q waves/ST elevation, LBBB; ST elevation in aVR with diffuse ST depression suggests left main / global ischaemia (p.2326) Echocardiography to define mechanism (LV/RV/biventricular, VSR, acute MR, tamponade, LVOT obstruction, valve lesions, aortic dissection) (p.2326) Right-sided ECG leads (e.g. V4R) for suspected RV infarction (p.2123) Pulmonary artery catheterisation in diagnostic/management uncertainty or severe unresponsive shock; equalised diastolic pressures suggest tamponade (p.2326)

Cardiovascular Collapse, Cardiac Arrest, and Sudden Cardiac Death — Vasovagal/neurocardiogenic syncope (transient, self-limited circulatory loss rather than true arrest) Primary respiratory arrest with secondary circulatory collapse Massive pulmonary embolism Acute aortic dissection Hypovolemic shock / exsanguination Cardiac tamponade Tension pneumothorax Profound metabolic derangement (severe hyperkalemia, severe acidosis, severe hypokalemia) Drug overdose (including opioid and QT-prolonging agents) Hypothermia Myocarditis presenting with malignant ventricular arrhythmia Sepsis-associated cardiovascular collapse/pulseless electrical activity Continuous ECG/rhythm monitoring and retrieval of AED rhythm strips to determine the initiating rhythm Arterial blood gas to assess hypoxia and metabolic acidosis during and after resuscitation Serum electrolytes (potassium, magnesium) and assessment for reversible causes Post-ROSC 12-lead ECG to detect ST-elevation MI and consideration of coronary angiography Echocardiography to assess LVEF, prior infarction, valvular and structural disease Cardiac MRI to characterize scar burden/heterogeneity and nonischemic cardiomyopathy Cardiac PET and/or endomyocardial biopsy when inflammatory cardiomyopathy (sarcoidosis, myocarditis) is suspected Electrophysiology study and provocative testing (epinephrine challenge for LQTS, sodium-channel-blocker challenge for Brugada) and genetic evaluation when a heritable arrhythmia syndrome is suspected

Bartonellosis (incl. Cat-Scratch Disease) — Pyogenic (bacterial) lymphadenitis Mycobacterial infection (incl. tuberculous lymphadenitis) Brucellosis Syphilis Tularemia Plague Toxoplasmosis Sporotrichosis Histoplasmosis Serology (immunofluorescence or enzyme immunoassay) is the most commonly used diagnostic, but has variable sensitivity/specificity; CSD serodiagnosis is often based on IgG alone (in the absence of IgM) and seroconversion may take a few weeks, complicating interpretation (p.1352). PCR of pus aspirated from a lymph node or the primary inoculation lesion is highly sensitive and specific and is particularly useful for definitive, rapid diagnosis in seronegative patients; PCR of a lymph node biopsy specimen may be less sensitive (possibly due to sampling error) (p.1352). Histopathology shows early lymphoid hyperplasia, later stellate granulomata with necrosis, coalescing microabscesses and occasional multinucleated giant cells (nonspecific but may narrow the differential) (p.1352). For endocarditis: blood cultures (even with lysis-centrifugation or EDTA tubes) are positive in only ~25% of cases (mostly B. quintana, rarely B. henselae) and require prolonged incubation up to 6 weeks; high-titer (>=1:800) IgG serology supports the diagnosis but cross-reacts between B. quintana and B. henselae and with C. burnetii and Chlamydia; species-level identification usually requires PCR and DNA sequencing of valve tissue (p.1353).

Cestode (Tapeworm) Infections — Intestinal taeniasis presenting only with passage of proglottids or vague abdominal symptoms (T. saginata, T. asiatica, T. solium, D. latus, D. caninum) Megaloblastic / pernicious-type anemia from vitamin B12 deficiency in D. latus fish tapeworm infection Seizure disorder / epilepsy of other cause in regions where neurocysticercosis is endemic Obstructive or communicating hydrocephalus from ventricular or subarachnoid cysticerci Sparganosis presenting as a migrating subcutaneous, periorbital or CNS mass (Spirometra plerocercoid) Coenurosis presenting as a CNS or subcutaneous space-occupying cystic lesion (T. multiceps, T. serialis) Tuberculoma / CNS tuberculosis (major cause of focal CNS mass lesions in India and East Asia) Toxoplasma encephalitis (ring-enhancing CNS lesions, especially in immunocompromised/HIV) Pyogenic brain abscess Other tissue helminths producing CNS or hepatic cysts (e.g., schistosomiasis, sparganosis) Stool microscopy for eggs/proglottids; perianal cellophane-tape swab when taeniasis suspected (eggs of the three Taenia species are morphologically indistinguishable) Examination of mature proglottids or scolex, or molecular testing, to distinguish T. solium from T. saginata/T. asiatica Neuroimaging (MRI and CT) for neurocysticercosis, including FIESTA/3D-CISS for ventricular/subarachnoid cysts and susceptibility-weighted imaging for calcifications Enzyme-linked immunoelectrotransfer blot (EITB) on serum for cysticercosis antibody

Trypanosomiasis (Chagas & Sleeping Sickness) — Chagas chronic cardiomyopathy: other dilated cardiomyopathies including ischemic heart disease (advanced Chagas carries a worse prognosis) (p.1790) Chagas megaesophagus: achalasia and other causes of dysphagia (p.1789) Chagas megacolon: Hirschsprung's disease and other causes of severe chronic constipation (p.1789) T. b. gambiense HAT systemic features: hypothyroidism and adrenal insufficiency (but thyroid/adrenal function tests are normal) (p.1794) HAT neuropsychiatric presentation: primary psychiatric illness (mental disorder is a key HAT feature easily misdiagnosed) (p.1794) T. b. rhodesiense acute febrile illness: malaria (suspect HAT especially if malaria tests are negative) (p.1794) Malaria (acute febrile illness overlapping T. b. rhodesiense HAT; HAT suspected when malaria tests are negative) (p.1794) Other febrile/systemic infections in returned travelers from endemic areas (p.1794) Chagas acute/reactivation: blood microscopy after concentration (Strout method, microhematocrit) or PCR of peripheral blood, CSF, or other body fluids (p.1790) Supportive HAT labs (nonspecific): anemia, thrombocytopenia, elevated C-reactive protein and IgM (p.1794) Chagas chronic: serology for anti-T. cruzi IgG - conventional/recombinant ELISA and immunofluorescence; two positive tests with different techniques/antigens to confirm (third test if discordant); immunochromatographic rapid tests for first-line screening where labs are limited (p.1790)

Chlamydial Infections — Neisseria gonorrhoeae urethritis/cervicitis/proctitis (clinically indistinguishable; frequent co-infection) Mycoplasma genitalium (now a leading cause of Chlamydia-negative and persistent NGU) Trichomonas vaginalis and herpes simplex virus as causes of NGU Mycoplasma pneumoniae and other atypical pneumonia pathogens (for C. pneumoniae) Crohn's disease of the rectum (mimicked by LGV proctocolitis on sigmoidoscopy and histology) Adenovirus or HSV follicular conjunctivitis (mimics adult inclusion/oculogenital conjunctivitis) Neisseria gonorrhoeae (urethritis, cervicitis, PID, proctitis, ophthalmia neonatorum) Mycoplasma genitalium urethritis/cervicitis Trichomonas vaginalis urethritis Herpes simplex virus (urethritis, proctitis, ulcerative conjunctivitis) Haemophilus influenzae or Streptococcus pneumoniae neonatal conjunctivitis Mycoplasma pneumoniae and other atypical CAP agents (for C. pneumoniae pneumonia) Adenovirus follicular conjunctivitis Haemophilus ducreyi and other genital-ulcer pathogens (for LGV primary lesion) NAAT (nucleic acid amplification test) on urine, vaginal/cervical, urethral, rectal, pharyngeal or conjunctival specimens - diagnostic assay of choice Laparoscopy / endometrial biopsy (plasma-cell endometritis) in suspected salpingitis/PID and perihepatitis Serovar/molecular genotyping when LGV is suspected (longer treatment duration required) First-void urine or vaginal swab self-collection for screening programs and outreach

Cholera — Other secretory/toxigenic watery diarrhoeas: enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (produces a heat-labile toxin like cholera toxin), and other dehydrating secretory diarrhoeal illnesses to which the term cholera has historically and loosely been applied (p.1325) Diarrhoea due to non-O1/O139 (noncholera) V. cholerae, which generally do not produce cholera toxin and do not cause large epidemics (p.1330) Enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (heat-labile enterotoxin resembling cholera toxin causing secretory diarrhoea) (p.1325-1326) Other Vibrio gastroenteritis, e.g. Vibrio parahaemolyticus and non-O1/O139 V. cholerae (p.1330) Stool culture on a selective medium such as taurocholate-tellurite-gelatin (TTG) agar or thiosulfate-citrate-bile salts-sucrose (TCBS) agar; the organism must be specifically sought (p.1328) Direct dark-field microscopy of a wet mount of fresh stool, with serotype discernible by immobilisation with specific antisera (p.1328) Point-of-care antigen-detection cholera dipstick (rapid diagnostic test) for field use or where laboratory facilities are lacking (p.1328) Cary-Blair transport medium and/or alkaline-peptone water-enrichment medium if sample processing will be delayed (p.1328) Vibrios are oxidase-positive; standard Enterobacteriaceae biochemical testing suffices for identification (p.1328) Supportive labs in dehydrated patients: elevated haematocrit (haemoconcentration) in non-anaemic patients, mild neutrophilic leukocytosis, raised blood urea nitrogen and creatinine (prerenal azotaemia), normal sodium/potassium/chloride, markedly reduced bicarbonate (<15 mmol/L), elevated anion gap and low arterial pH (~7.2) (p.1328)

Chronic and Recurrent Meningitis — Infectious: M. tuberculosis, Cryptococcus neoformans/gattii, syphilis, Lyme disease (Bannwarth's syndrome), Brucella, Nocardia, Actinomyces, Whipple's disease, partially treated bacterial meningitis, parameningeal infection Fungal: Coccidioides, Histoplasma, Blastomyces, Candida, Aspergillus, Sporothrix Parasitic/helminthic: cysticercosis (Taenia solium), Gnathostoma, Angiostrongylus, Baylisascaris, Toxoplasma, trypanosomiasis, Acanthamoeba/Balamuthia Viral: HSV-2 (Mollaret's, recurrent), mumps, lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus, enteroviruses (in agammaglobulinemia/B-cell depletion), HIV acute retroviral syndrome Malignancy: carcinomatous/lymphomatous meningitis (breast, lung, stomach, pancreas, melanoma, leukemia, gliomatosis) Inflammatory/autoimmune: neurosarcoidosis, Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada syndrome, Behcet's, SLE, granulomatosis with polyangiitis, IgG4-related hypertrophic pachymeningitis, primary CNS vasculitis, Sjogren's Monogenic autoinflammatory: TRAPS, CAPS, NOMID, complement factor I deficiency Chemical: leakage from epidermoid/dermoid tumor, craniopharyngioma, cholesteatoma; drug hypersensitivity (NSAIDs, sulfonamides, IVIG, others) Carcinomatous or lymphomatous meningitis (CSF seeding by malignant cells) Neurosarcoidosis (low CSF glucose can mimic tuberculous/fungal meningitis) Chemical meningitis from leaking epidermoid/dermoid cyst or craniopharyngioma Drug-induced aseptic meningitis

Chronic Hepatitis — Wilson disease (especially in adolescents, before neurologic signs/Kayser-Fleischer rings) Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency Primary biliary cholangitis Cryptogenic cirrhosis Celiac disease Ischemic liver disease Budd-Chiari syndrome (hepatic venous outflow obstruction) Immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) hepatitis Chronic hepatitis B Chronic hepatitis C Chronic hepatitis D (delta) superimposed on hepatitis B Hepatitis E (chronic in immunosuppressed/post-transplant hosts) Liver biochemical tests (AST, ALT, alkaline phosphatase, bilirubin, albumin, prothrombin time) HBV markers: HBsAg, IgG anti-HBc, HBeAg/anti-HBe, HBV DNA HCV markers: anti-HCV, HCV RNA HDV markers: anti-HDV, HDV RNA Autoantibodies: ANA (homogeneous), anti-smooth-muscle antibody (anti-actin), anti-LKM1, anti-SLA, anti-LC1, F-actin, atypical pANCA Serum immunoglobulins/globulins (hypergammaglobulinemia >2.5 g/dL in AIH; IgG level) Liver biopsy for grading (HAI/METAVIR) and staging of fibrosis Noninvasive fibrosis assessment: FIB-4, Enhanced Liver Fibrosis (ELF) score, liver elastography/stiffness imaging Ceruloplasmin, serum/urinary copper and liver copper (to exclude Wilson disease) Autoimmune hepatitis Drug- or toxin-induced liver injury (including minocycline) Alcohol-associated hepatitis Metabolic dysfunction-associated steatohepatitis (MASH/NASH) Wilson disease Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency Primary biliary cholangitis

Chronic Lymphocytic Leukemia (CLL) — Mantle cell lymphoma (CD5+, but CD23-negative, cyclin D1+, moderate/bright CD20 and surface Ig) — distinguished by immunophenotype (p.852) Marginal zone lymphoma (CD5 -/+, CD23 -/+, bright surface Ig) (p.852) Follicular lymphoma (CD5-negative, CD10-positive, CD23-positive) (p.852) Monoclonal B-cell lymphocytosis (clonal B cells below the CLL threshold without organ involvement or cytopenias) (p.852) Small lymphocytic lymphoma (tissue-based counterpart with identical molecular features) (p.852) B-cell prolymphocytic leukemia arising from CLL (clinically and therapeutically distinct, though classified under Richter's transformation) (p.853-854) Reactive lymphocytosis from viral infection — viral infections produce larger reactive lymphocytes with abundant cytoplasm, in contrast to the increased small lymphocytes and smudge cells of CLL (p.443) Flow cytometry of peripheral blood for the characteristic immunophenotype (CD19, CD20, CD22, CD23, CD200, CD5, dim surface Ig) — diagnostic test of choice (p.852) FISH for recurrent abnormalities del(13)(q14.3), trisomy 12, del(11)(q22.3), del(17)(p13.1); repeated before each line of therapy to detect acquired del(17p) (p.851) Stimulated metaphase karyotype, including assessment for complex karyotype (≥3 abnormalities) (p.851) Sequencing for TP53 and IGHV mutational status for prognostication (p.854) β2-microglobulin and LDH (prognostic; component of CLL International Prognostic Index) (p.853-854)

Chronic Myeloid Leukemia (CML) — Leukemoid reaction (reactive leukocytosis) - distinguished from CML by a high/normal leukocyte alkaline phosphatase score (CML has a LOW LAP) and absence of BCR::ABL1 (Harrison 22e p.837) Atypical CML (BCR::ABL1-negative) - lacks the Ph chromosome/BCR::ABL1, does not respond to TKI therapy, associated with SETBP1 (about 25%) and some CSF3R mutations, poor prognosis with median survival ~2-3 years (Harrison 22e p.835) Chronic neutrophilic leukemia - frequently CSF3R-mutated (about 80%); may respond to ruxolitinib (Harrison 22e p.835) Chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (Harrison 22e p.835) Myelodysplastic syndrome/myeloproliferative neoplasms, including MDS/MPN-RS-T (SF3B1-mutated) (Harrison 22e p.835) Essential thrombocythemia and other Ph-negative MPNs presenting with thrombocytosis - when JAK2 V617F is absent, cytogenetics/FISH for BCR::ABL1 are required to exclude CML (Harrison 22e p.832-833) Bone marrow aspiration with routine G-banding cytogenetics - required to confirm the Ph chromosome, detect additional chromosomal abnormalities (which FISH will not detect), and quantify marrow blasts and basophils; a diagnosis of CML must always rely on marrow analysis with cytogenetics (Harrison 22e p.837) FISH analysis for BCR::ABL1 on peripheral blood - quantifies percentage of Ph-positive cells; preferred when a Ph cytogenetic study is negative or for monitoring (Harrison 22e p.837) Quantitative RT-PCR for BCR::ABL1 transcripts on the International Scale - baseline transcript typing at diagnosis (to avoid spurious 'undetectable' results on follow-up with atypical transcripts) and serial molecular monitoring of response (Harrison 22e p.837-838)

Cocaine, Other Psychostimulants, and Hallucinogens — Sympathomimetic toxidrome from other agents (e.g., synthetic cathinones/bath salts, prescription stimulant misuse) Anticholinergic toxidrome Serotonin syndrome Neuroleptic malignant syndrome / malignant hyperthermia (hyperthermia, rigidity) Thyroid storm Pheochromocytoma / catecholamine excess Primary psychiatric psychosis or mania Alcohol or sedative withdrawal Sepsis with hyperthermia and tachycardia CNS infection (meningitis/encephalitis) presenting with agitation, fever, altered mental status Electrocardiogram for chest pain or arrhythmia evaluation Chest radiograph in cocaine-associated chest pain Cardiac biomarkers to exclude myocardial infarction Core body temperature monitoring (hyperthermia) Note that emerging substances/NPS are often NOT detected on standard ED drug screens or postmortem toxicology Hyperthyroidism / thyroid storm Pheochromocytoma Serotonin syndrome Neuroleptic malignant syndrome Primary psychotic or manic episode Hypoglycemia or hypoxemia (must be excluded before treating agitation) Psychostimulants increase synaptic monoamines. Cocaine binds the dopamine transporter and blocks reuptake of dopamine, norepinephrine, and serotonin, raising their levels centrally and peripherally; repeated exposure induces long-term neuronal changes including adaptations in glutamate-releasing neurons. Methamphetamine, a cationic lipophilic molecule structurally similar to monoamine transporters, reverses transporter function to dump newly synthesized catecholamines from storage vesicles into the synapse and also inhibits monoamine oxidase, attenuating monoamine metabolism; it is more potent than amphetamine with greater nerve-terminal toxicity. Colorectal Cancer — Hemorrhoids or benign anorectal disease as a cause of rectal bleeding (rectal bleeding and altered bowel habits still demand DRE and sigmoidoscopy) (Harrison 22e p.656) Other causes of iron-deficiency anemia from chronic occult GI blood loss (Harrison 22e p.656) Inflammatory bowel disease (both a risk factor and a differential for altered bowel habit and bleeding) (Harrison 22e p.655) Colonoscopy of the entire large bowel (gold standard for detecting cancer and synchronous neoplasms/polyps) (Harrison 22e p.656) Flexible sigmoidoscopy as a screening modality (Harrison 22e p.655-656) Stool-based tests: fecal occult blood test, fecal immunochemical test (FIT), and fecal DNA testing (Harrison 22e p.655-656) Serum carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) (Harrison 22e p.656) Complete blood count and comprehensive metabolic panel (Harrison 22e p.656) Chest, abdomen, and pelvic CT scan; MRI and PET as dictated by CT findings (Harrison 22e p.656) Pelvic MRI for rectal cancer to assess mesorectal margin and nodal status (Harrison 22e p.658) Tumor MMR/microsatellite instability testing (IHC or MSI) and germline genetic testing where indicated (Harrison 22e p.654, 656) Investigational: plasma circulating tumor DNA as a biomarker for residual/recurrent disease (Harrison 22e p.658) The majority of colorectal cancers develop through the adenoma-to-carcinoma sequence, in which adenomatous polyps accumulate sequential genetic and epigenetic events involving tumor suppressor genes and oncogenes. Common Atrial Flutter and Macroreentrant and Multifocal Atrial Tachycardias — Atrial fibrillation Focal atrial tachycardia Atypical (non-CTI-dependent) atrial flutter vs typical flutter Left atrial / perimitral flutter Sinus tachycardia 12-lead ECG to identify sawtooth flutter waves and conduction ratio Vagal/AV-nodal-blocking maneuvers to unmask flutter waves at higher conduction ratios Electrophysiology study with electroanatomic mapping to define circuit and confirm mechanism in atypical flutter or to distinguish from focal AT CHA2DS2-VASc scoring for thromboembolic risk and bleeding-risk assessment Atrial fibrillation (irregular, no isoelectric baseline between atrial activations) versus MAT (isoelectric intervals present, slower atrial rate) Focal atrial tachycardia versus left atrial/atypical flutter (distinguished by P-wave morphology and often only by electrophysiology study) Macroreentrant atrial tachycardia depends on a large anatomic reentry circuit, frequently involving areas of atrial scar with slow conduction. In common (typical) flutter, the wavefront encircles the tricuspid valve annulus, bounded anteriorly by the annulus and posteriorly by the inferior vena cava and Eustachian ridge, passing through the cavotricuspid isthmus between the IVC and tricuspid annulus. The circuit usually rotates counterclockwise as viewed from the ventricular apex; reversed (clockwise) rotation gives reverse typical flutter. AF and typical flutter are mechanistically interrelated: a line of functional block or coalescence of fibrillatory wavelets around barriers such as the crista terminalis and Eustachian valve may convert AF into organized flutter, and conduction-slowing antiarrhythmics promote this reentry. Purely respiratory viruses (e.g. rhinoviruses) replicate only in respiratory epithelium, whereas systemic viruses (e.g. measles, SARS-CoV) disseminate via the bloodstream and may also injure the airway. Concussion and Other Traumatic Brain Injuries — Postconcussion symptom overlap with preinjury mood or anxiety disorders (e.g., depression, PTSD) Transient ischemic attack (chronic subdural hematoma may mimic with brief hemiparesis or aphasia) Intracranial neoplasm or abscess (evolving contusion with surrounding enhancement and edema can be mistaken for these) Carotid or vertebral artery dissection presenting as focal deficit after trauma Vasovagal syncope after injury Drug or alcohol intoxication confounding the neurologic exam Cervical spine injury (may be clinically inapparent) Noncontrast CT - first-line for skull fracture, extra-axial hematoma, contusion, traumatic SAH, and large TAI lesions with blood MRI (including gradient-echo/susceptibility-weighted and diffusion sequences) - more sensitive than CT for microhemorrhage and axonal injury; detects intracranial abnormalities in ~27% of CT-negative mild TBI patients and has prognostic value Advanced/multimodal MRI (functional MRI, cerebral blood flow, diffusion) - increasing sensitivity for subtle injury Blood-based biomarkers GFAP and UCHL1 - point-of-care detection and prognostication across the TBI spectrum GCS scoring before sedation/paralysis or intubation Validated symptom inventories (e.g., Rivermead Post-Concussion Symptom Questionnaire) to quantify and track recovery Intracranial pressure monitoring (ventricular catheter or fiberoptic device) in severe TBI to guide therapy (note: has not been shown to improve outcome)

Spinal cord compression — Intradural extramedullary tumours (meningioma, neurofibroma/schwannoma) - usually slow-growing and benign; long symptom duration favours an intradural origin (p.3606) Intramedullary lesions (ependymoma, haemangioblastoma, low-grade astrocytoma, rarely metastasis) - present with poorly localised burning pain and SACRAL SPARING rather than radicular pain (p.3604, 3606) Cervical spondylotic / degenerative cervical myelopathy - osteophytes, ossified posterior longitudinal ligament/ligamentum flavum, disk degeneration; insidious, stepwise; early signs are subtle (paraesthesia, loss of hand dexterity, 'clumsiness') (p.173) Acute spondylytic myelopathy from hyperextension injury on a pre-existing stenotic canal, sometimes producing a central cord syndrome (p.3606) Conus medullaris syndrome - saddle anaesthesia (S3-S5), early prominent bladder/bowel dysfunction with lax anal tone, preserved leg strength (p.3604) Spinal epidural abscess - midline spinal/neck pain, fever and progressive limb weakness; mostly Staphylococcus aureus (consider MRSA), with gram-negative bacilli, streptococci, anaerobes and fungi less commonly; risk factors include diabetes, IV drug use, alcoholism, renal failure, malignancy, HIV and recent spinal surgery/anaesthesia/trauma (pp.3606-3607) Vertebral osteomyelitis / diskitis - neurological deficit in about a third of cases, mostly mediated by epidural abscess; fever may be absent, especially in cervical disease (pp.131, 1105)

Pathogenesis is now viewed as multifactorial rather than simply low-fiber diet: gut dysbiosis, chronic low-grade inflammation driving neuronal degeneration with resulting dysmotility and high intraluminal pressure, and abnormal collagen cross-linking causing loss of compliance all contribute. Diabetic ketoacidosis — Alcoholic ketoacidosis — high-anion-gap acidosis (predominantly beta-hydroxybutyrate) without hyperglycaemia, usually with preserved renal function, in chronic alcohol use with vomiting and poor intake (p.413). Starvation ketoacidosis — ketoacidosis with normal or low glucose (p.413). Other high-anion-gap acidoses: lactic acidosis, toxic ingestions (e.g. salicylates), and renal failure/uraemia (p.413). Plasma beta-hydroxybutyrate measured directly (more reliable than urine nitroprusside ketones) (p.413). Anion gap calculation, including assessment for a mixed non-anion-gap / high-anion-gap acidosis when the change in bicarbonate exceeds the change in anion gap (p.413). Acute pancreatitis can mimic DKA (and vice versa), with overlapping abdominal pain; DKA may itself be accompanied by amylase elevation, complicating the distinction (p.2788). DKA results from increased fatty acid metabolism with accumulation of the ketoacids acetoacetate and beta-hydroxybutyrate, producing hyperglycaemia, ketonaemia and a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis. It typically occurs in insulin-dependent diabetes when insulin is stopped or when an intercurrent illness (e.g. infection, gastroenteritis, pancreatitis, myocardial infarction) acutely raises insulin requirements. In euglycaemic DKA caused by SGLT2 inhibitors, glycosuria drives an osmotic diuresis and volume depletion while plasma glucose stays in the normal range despite the ketoacidosis (p.413).

Donovanosis — Primary syphilitic chancre (Harrison 22e p.1357) Secondary syphilis with condylomata lata (Harrison 22e p.1357) Chancroid (Harrison 22e p.1357) Lymphogranuloma venereum (Harrison 22e p.1357) Genital herpes (Harrison 22e p.1357) Genital neoplasm / carcinoma (Harrison 22e p.1357) Amebiasis (Harrison 22e p.1357) Rhinoscleroma on histology (Harrison 22e p.1357) Leishmaniasis on histology (Harrison 22e p.1357) Histoplasmosis on histology (Harrison 22e p.1357) Tissue smear for Donovan bodies stained with rapid Giemsa or Wright stain (Harrison 22e p.1357) Crush preparation of granulation tissue spread between two slides (Harrison 22e p.1357) Histologic biopsy showing chronic inflammation, microabscesses, and rete ridge elongation (Harrison 22e p.1357) phoE gene PCR with colorimetric detection to differentiate K. granulomatis from related Klebsiella species (Harrison 22e p.1357) Multiplex genital-ulcer PCR including K. granulomatis (Harrison 22e p.1357) Cervical carcinoma (cervical lesions may mimic it) (Harrison 22e p.1357) Genital neoplasm (Harrison 22e p.1357) Donovanosis is a chronic granulomatous infection caused by the intracellular gram-negative organism Klebsiella granulomatis (formerly Calymmatobacterium granulomatis). The lesion begins as a papule or subcutaneous nodule that ulcerates, often after trauma. The organism resides within macrophages and the stratum malpighii as intracytoplasmic Donovan bodies inside large mononuclear (Pund) cells; these cysts rupture and release infective organisms. Histology shows chronic inflammation with infiltration by plasma cells and neutrophils, and epithelial changes including ulceration, microabscesses, and elongation of the rete ridges. Drug intoxication / poisoning — Characterise overall physiologic state and toxidrome from vital signs and neuromuscular exam (p.3704) Anion gap (raised AGMA in methanol, ethylene glycol, salicylate, or any poisoning causing organ failure, seizures or shock; low anion gap with bromide, calcium, iodine, lithium, magnesium) (p.3705) Osmolal gap (>10 mmol/L suggests a low-molecular-weight solute such as an alcohol or glycol) (p.3705) Serum lactate (low relative to anion gap in alcohol/glycol intoxication, high and near the anion gap in hypoperfusion) (p.3705) Glucose, electrolytes, ketones (hypo-/hyperglycaemia and hypo-/hyperkalaemia patterns can implicate specific agents) (p.3705) ECG (bradycardia/AV block, QRS and QT prolongation, ventricular tachyarrhythmias suggest specific agent classes) (p.3706) Abdominal/chest radiograph (radiopaque densities suggest heavy metals, drug packets, iron, enteric-coated or salicylate tablets; CXR for pulmonary edema/aspiration) (p.3706) Quantitative serum levels (acetaminophen, alcohols incl. ethylene glycol/methanol, anticonvulsants, barbiturates, digoxin, iron, lithium, salicylate, theophylline, carboxyhemoglobin, methemoglobin) guide management (p.3706) Coagulation (PT/INR) for warfarin/rodenticide risk stratification, though unreliable for direct oral anticoagulant overdose (p.3705) Psychogenic illness / anxiety reaction (mass hysteria, fear of poisoning) producing symptoms inconsistent with the exposure history (p.3705)

Deep vein thrombosis — Ruptured Baker's cyst (sudden severe calf discomfort) (Harrison 22e p.2159) Muscle strain or injury (Harrison 22e p.2159) Acute postthrombotic syndrome / chronic venous insufficiency (Harrison 22e p.2159) May-Thurner syndrome (iliac vein compression) presenting as recurrent leg edema (Harrison 22e p.2159) Cellulitis - fever and chills more often herald cellulitis than DVT (Harrison 22e p.2159) Loss of vein compressibility is the primary ultrasound criterion for DVT; a normal vein collapses (a 'wink') under gentle transducer pressure, whereas an acutely thrombosed vein stays distended and may show central, homogeneous, low-echogenicity thrombus (Harrison 22e p.2160). Doppler interrogation adds flow data: calf compression normally augments flow, and loss of respiratory variation suggests an obstructing DVT or a pelvic obstructive process (Harrison 22e p.2160). Contrast (gadolinium) MR venography is an excellent option when pelvic or leg ultrasound is equivocal or technically nondiagnostic (Harrison 22e p.2160-2161). Contrast phlebography is now reserved mainly for when an interventional procedure is planned (Harrison 22e p.2161). An age-adjusted d-dimer cutoff (age x 10 ng/mL in patients >50 years) is endorsed for ruling out PE but does NOT apply to suspected acute DVT (Harrison 22e p.2159-2160). d-Dimer rarely helps in hospitalized patients because levels are frequently elevated by systemic illness (MI, pneumonia, sepsis, cancer, postoperative state, pregnancy) (Harrison 22e p.2159).

Dyslipidemia — Fasting lipid profile: total cholesterol, LDL, HDL, and triglycerides (Harrison 22e p.2046). Lipoprotein(a) measurement, given its role as an independent cardiovascular risk predictor (Harrison 22e p.2017, p.2046). Apolipoprotein B as a marker of atherogenic particle burden (Harrison 22e p.3237). Screening for secondary contributors: glucose/HbA1c and urinalysis for diabetes and renal disease, and thyroid function testing when indicated (Harrison 22e p.2046). High-sensitivity C-reactive protein may be considered as an independent cardiovascular risk marker informing therapeutic decisions (Harrison 22e p.2046). Atherogenic lipoproteins, principally LDL, deposit cholesterol within the arterial wall and disturb normal endothelial functions (control of vascular tone, maintenance of an antithrombotic surface, and regulation of inflammatory cell adhesion and diapedesis), promoting atherosclerosis; LDL, cigarette smoking, hypertension, and diabetes mellitus vary in their relative impact on these endothelial functions. Lipoprotein(a) is thought to add risk through increased cellular lipid accumulation, endothelial dysfunction, and effects on coagulation. Severe hypertriglyceridemia (chylomicron/VLDL accumulation) can precipitate acute pancreatitis (Harrison 22e p.2017, p.2046). Elevated plasma LDL cholesterol is a major modifiable driver of atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease; globally high LDL is estimated to contribute to ~41% of ischemic heart disease deaths and ~9% of stroke deaths (Harrison 22e p.2017).

Substrates vary: in the setting of acute myocardial ischemia/infarction, surviving Purkinje cells within infarcted myocardium can show triggered automaticity, generating recurrent polymorphic VT/VF. Enterovirus, Parechovirus, and Reovirus Infections — Bacterial sepsis (especially in neonatal generalized enteroviral disease) Partially treated bacterial meningitis (can be hard to exclude from enteroviral meningitis) Mumps meningitis (distinguished by low CSF glucose, vs normal in enterovirus) Rubella (enteroviral rubelliform rash lacks lymphadenopathy and occurs in summer) Measles (enteroviral enanthems may mimic Koplik's spots) Herpetic stomatitis (vs herpangina, which lacks gingivitis) Adenoviral or Chlamydia trachomatis conjunctivitis (vs acute hemorrhagic conjunctivitis) Bacterial sepsis of the newborn Bacterial (including partially treated) meningitis Mumps virus meningitis Herpes simplex stomatitis / encephalitis Adenovirus and Chlamydia trachomatis ocular infection Other respiratory viruses causing cold/pneumonia PCR is now the primary diagnostic method; pan-enterovirus reverse-transcription PCR detects all human enteroviruses (CSF PCR ~70-100% sensitive, over 80% specific, faster than culture) but does NOT detect parechoviruses. CSF PCR is less likely positive if presentation is 3 or more days after meningitis onset or with EV71; in those cases throat or rectal swab PCR (less specific) should be considered. Serum PCR is highly sensitive/specific for disseminated disease and useful for diagnosis/monitoring in immunodeficient patients on immunoglobulin whose cultures may be negative; antigen detection is less sensitive than PCR.

It is a highly heterogeneous condition strongly influenced by underlying genetic variation, with environmental factors ubiquitous in developed and developing countries; in some individuals it is attributable entirely to genetic causes. Insulin resistance is one of the earliest complications: muscle (glucose disposal) and liver (glucose production) become less responsive to insulin, prompting compensatory hyperinsulinemia. Helicobacter pylori Infection — Urea breath test (noninvasive) for active infection and for confirming eradication. Stool (fecal) antigen test (noninvasive) for active infection and eradication confirmation. Endoscopic biopsy with histopathology, including for gastric lymphoma staging. PCR or FISH for the t(11;18) translocation in gastric MALT lymphoma to predict responsiveness to eradication therapy (p.649). H. pylori is a flagellated gastric bacterium whose colonization triggers chronic mucosal inflammation. The flagellum lets the organism access the gastric epithelium and is essential for virulence; H. pylori evades innate immunity by producing a flagellin epitope that does not bind TLR5 and tetra-acylated LPS that does not activate TLR4 (p.1009-1010). Adhesion and gastric tropism are mediated by bacterial outer-membrane proteins BabA and SabA interacting with epithelial GM1 ganglioside (p.1009). Chronic H. pylori inflammation, partly via generation of carcinogenic nitrites from dietary nitrates, drives the gastritis-to-cancer sequence and is a recognized cause of peptic ulcer disease, gastric adenocarcinoma (intestinal subtype), and gastric MALT lymphoma; certain higher-virulence strains carry greater cancer risk (p.646). H. pylori has a proven etiologic role in peptic ulcer disease; together with NSAID use it is one of the two most common causes of gastroduodenal ulcers (p.302). In dyspeptic patients under 60 with no alarm features, test-and-treat is the recommended initial strategy: assess H. pylori status by fecal (stool) antigen or urea breath testing, and treat those who are positive (p.303).

Hematopoietic Stem Cells — Deep/next-generation sequencing to detect somatic mutations and clonal hematopoiesis (e.g., DNMT3a, TET2, ASXL1 variant allele fractions) Surface immunophenotyping of stem/progenitor markers (CD34, CD90/Thy-1, CD117/c-Kit, CD133, CD164, CD110/c-Mpl) as described in murine-based studies Hematopoiesis originates from a small self-renewing HSC pool. During development, blood production shifts sequentially from the yolk sac (embryonic-hemoglobin red cells and tissue-resident macrophages) to the placenta and intraembryonic sites near the aorta-gonad-mesonephros region, then to fetal liver, and in the second trimester to bone marrow and spleen; HSCs reach marrow via bloodborne transit from fetal liver after long-bone calcification, and proliferation falls sharply soon after birth. HSCs reside in a specialized perivascular/endosteal marrow niche where mesenchymal, endothelial, neural, and other cells provide regulatory signals (kit ligand, CXCL12) governing survival, expansion, and constraint. Trafficking depends on selectins binding CD162/CD44, integrin-mediated firm adhesion (VCAM-1/VLA-4), and CXCL12-CXCR4 plus calcium-sensing receptor signaling. Most HSCs are deeply quiescent and cytokine-resistant, dividing on the order of months to years; quiescence is enforced by high cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors (e.g., p57/CDKN1c blocking the G1-S transition) and niche signals such as angiogenin, IL-18, and angiopoietin 1. Self-renewal preserves any acquired mutation in the durable stem pool, whereas progenitor mutations are largely lost through terminal differentiation; epigenetic regulators (DNMT3a, TET2, ASXL1) are critical for pool homeostasis and for restraining outgrowth of potentially pathogenic clones.

High plasma/liver iron normally raises hepcidin via the BMP-SMAD pathway, with HFE, transferrin receptor 2, and hemojuvelin contributing to hepcidin upregulation. Mutations in these genes (most commonly HFE) lead to inappropriately low hepcidin, increased iron absorption, and rising transferrin saturation. Because no regulated route of iron excretion exists, iron accumulates progressively. When

Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state — Diabetic ketoacidosis (and the DKA/HHS overlap presentation) (p.3216). Other causes of an altered/hyperosmolar sensorium - the differential for hyperosmolar coma includes uremia, nonketotic hyperosmolar states and other metabolic derangements (p.3216, general). Plasma glucose - typically markedly elevated, may be >55.5 mmol/L (1000 mg/dL) (p.3219). Serum osmolality - characteristically >300 mOsm/L (p.3219). Corrected serum sodium - measured Na may be normal or low, but corrected Na (add ~1.6 meq/L for each 5.6 mmol/L [100 mg/dL] rise in glucose) is usually elevated (p.3219). Renal function (BUN/creatinine) - prerenal azotaemia from volume depletion; creatinine typically moderately raised (p.3219). Ketones/beta-hydroxybutyrate - absent or only mild; serum beta-hydroxybutyrate <1.0 mmol/L; any moderate ketonuria is usually due to starvation (p.3219). Acid-base status - acidosis absent or mild; a small anion-gap metabolic acidosis may reflect raised lactic acid (p.3219). HHS arises from RELATIVE insulin deficiency combined with inadequate fluid intake. Insulin deficiency drives hepatic glucose overproduction (glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis) and impairs glucose uptake by skeletal muscle. The resulting hyperglycaemia causes an osmotic diuresis with intravascular volume depletion that is worsened by inadequate fluid replacement. The reason ketosis is absent is not fully understood; the insulin deficiency is presumed to be only relative and less severe than in DKA, and some studies show lower counterregulatory hormone and free-fatty-acid levels in HHS than in DKA, with possibly reduced hepatic ketone synthesis or an insulin/glucagon ratio that does not favour ketogenesis. Inflammatory markers (cytokines, C-reactive protein) are elevated

Keratinized cells are not viable hosts for replication, so the virus targets viable epithelium at cutaneous and mucosal surfaces. More than 100 HPV types exist; certain oncogenic types (notably 16 and 18) integrate into host epithelium and drive intraepithelial neoplasia and squamous cell carcinoma of the cervix, anus, vulva, and penis, and persistent oral HPV-16 promotes oropharyngeal carcinoma. Histology of affected sites may show changes of typical warts and/or features of intraepidermal carcinoma (Bowen's disease). The oncogenic potential is markedly amplified in immunosuppressed hosts (Harrison 22e p.1525, p.1601).

Symptomatic hyponatraemia / SIADH — Hypovolaemic: GI losses (vomiting, diarrhoea, tube drainage) and insensible loss (sweating, burns) with inadequate replacement — urine Na+ typically <20 mM (p.390). Hyperglycaemia-related ('true') hyponatraemia — plasma Na+ falls ~1.6-2.4 mM per 100 mg/dL rise in glucose; resolves after correcting hyperglycaemia (p.393). Hypovolaemic renal: thiazide diuretics, mineralocorticoid/aldosterone deficiency (primary adrenal insufficiency, hypoaldosteronism), salt-losing nephropathies (reflux nephropathy, interstitial nephropathies, post-obstructive uropathy, medullary cystic disease, recovery phase of ATN) — urine Na+ typically >20 mM (p.390-391). Osmotic/solute-driven hypovolaemic: glycosuria, ketonuria (starvation, diabetic or alcoholic ketoacidosis), bicarbonaturia (RTA, metabolic alkalosis) (p.391). Cerebral salt wasting (subarachnoid haemorrhage, traumatic brain injury, craniotomy, encephalitis, meningitis) (p.391). Hypervolaemic: congestive heart failure, cirrhosis, nephrotic syndrome, and acute or chronic renal failure (the latter uniquely with raised urine Na+) (p.391). Euvolaemic: SIAD, moderate-to-severe hypothyroidism, secondary adrenal insufficiency from pituitary disease (glucocorticoid deficiency) (p.391). Low solute intake: beer potomania (alcoholics whose sole nutrient is beer) and nutrient-restricted/extreme vegetarian diets — urine osmolality <100-200 mOsm/kg, urine Na+ <10-20 mM (p.391-392).

Hypothyroidism — Hyperthyroidism / thyrotoxicosis (opposite end of thyroid dysfunction; thyroiditis can pass through both phases) Sick euthyroid (nonthyroidal illness) syndrome Secondary (central) hypothyroidism from hypopituitarism or hypothalamic disease Multinodular goiter or thyroid carcinoma (asymmetric Hashimoto goiter may mimic these) Primary thyroid lymphoma (rare, strongly associated with pre-existing autoimmune thyroiditis) Depression and dementia (overlapping fatigue, poor concentration, slowing) Serum TSH as the primary screening test (most sensitive for primary disease) Free/unbound T4 to confirm clinical hypothyroidism when TSH is elevated (T3 measurement is not indicated) TPO and thyroglobulin antibodies to establish autoimmune etiology Lipid panel (cholesterol, triglycerides), creatine phosphokinase, and full blood count for associated abnormalities Anterior pituitary function testing when central hypothyroidism is suspected (after excluding drug effect and sick euthyroid syndrome) Thyroid ultrasound to distinguish heterogeneous Hashimoto echotexture from true nodules warranting FNA Depression Dementia Nephrotic syndrome (edema, hyperlipidemia) Chronic fatigue states Anemia of other cause Hypothyroidism is deficient thyroid hormone action, most often from primary thyroid failure. In autoimmune (Hashimoto's) disease, T cell-mediated lymphocytic infiltration with germinal-center formation, follicular atrophy, oxyphil metaplasia, and fibrosis progressively destroy the gland; atrophic thyroiditis represents its fibrotic end stage. As function declines there is a compensated phase in which a rising TSH maintains hormone levels (subclinical hypothyroidism); later free T4 falls and TSH rises further, producing overt disease. Susceptibility reflects genetic fact

IgG4-Related Disease — Pancreatic adenocarcinoma (mimicked by type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis) Primary sclerosing cholangitis and cholangiocarcinoma (mimicked by IgG4-related sclerosing cholangitis) Sjogren's syndrome (Mikulicz's disease presentation) Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (when destructive sinus/middle-ear/nasopharyngeal lesions occur) Lymphoma and other causes of lymphadenopathy or pseudotumor Riedel's thyroiditis and fibrosing variant of Hashimoto's thyroiditis Idiopathic retroperitoneal fibrosis Idiopathic membranous glomerulonephropathy Orbital pseudotumor / orbital myositis from other causes Serum IgG4 concentration (commonly elevated, but normal in ~30% of histologically proven cases; usually measured by nephelometry). Idiopathic intracranial hypertension — Optic disc drusen, which produce pseudopapilloedema and can be mistaken for true papilloedema (p.229). Obstructive sleep apnoea and poorly controlled hypertension, which also cause morning or nocturnal headache (p.117). MRI as the initial study, including MR venography, to look for a mass and to search for dural venous sinus thrombosis or an AV shunt (p.117, p.229). Lumbar puncture performed while the patient is symptomatic, measuring opening pressure in the lateral decubitus position; both the pressure and the symptomatic response to removing 20-30 mL of CSF can be assessed (p.117, p.229). Formal visual field testing, performed even when there is no overt ophthalmic involvement (p.117). B-mode ocular ultrasound to detect buried optic disc drusen (hyperechoic due to calcium) when pseudopapilloedema is suspected (p.229). Space-occupying intracranial lesion causing raised CSF pressure headache (p.117). Dural venous sinus thrombosis (p.229). Arteriovenous (dural) shunt (p.229). Raised CSF pressure without a space-occupying lesion, occurring in the setting of obesity, female sex, and occasionally pregnancy; partial obstruction of the cerebral venous sinuses is found in a small number of cases (p.117). Stenosis at the transverse-sigmoid sinus junction is commonly present, providing the rationale for venous sinus stenting (p.229). Vitamin A excess is a recognised cause of pseudotumor cerebri (p.3379).

Infections Due to Mixed Anaerobic Organisms — Aerobic abscess (e.g., Staphylococcus aureus), which can also produce deep abscesses and lung abscess without an anaerobic component Chemical pneumonitis / Mendelson syndrome (acid aspiration) versus bacterial aspiration pneumonia Foreign-body aspiration with obstruction and atelectasis versus bacterial aspiration pneumonia Simple parapneumonic effusion (e.g., pneumococcal) versus anaerobic empyema Necrotizing pneumonia, bronchopleural fistula with purulent effusion, and pneumatocele in the lung-abscess differential Group A streptococcal necrotizing fasciitis versus mixed aerobic-anaerobic (polymicrobial) necrotizing fasciitis Malignancy or granulomatous disease mimicked by cervicofacial actinomycosis ('lumpy jaw') Staphylococcus aureus abscess or lung abscess (no anaerobic component) Group A streptococcal necrotizing fasciitis (more rapid, 1-3 day progression) Pneumococcal pneumonia with parapneumonic effusion Gram stain of pus/sputum showing a mixed bacterial population, especially when routine culture is negative or grows only streptococci or a single aerobe such as E. coli Anaerobic culture from normally sterile sites (blood, pleural/peritoneal fluid, CSF, sterile-site aspirates or biopsies); samples from mouth, nose, vagina, or feces are unacceptable due to commensal contamination Air-free syringe collection capped and placed in anaerobic transport media with rapid transport; liquid/tissue specimens preferred over swabs

Infections Due to the HACEK Group and Miscellaneous Gram-Negative Bacteria — Viridans group streptococcal endocarditis (also subacute, culture-positive, common in dental-source disease) Enterococcal endocarditis Culture-negative endocarditis (Bartonella, Coxiella burnetii, Tropheryma whipplei) when blood cultures are sterile Staphylococcus aureus endocarditis when the course is more acute Septic arthritis/osteomyelitis from Staphylococcus aureus in children (where K. kingae may have surpassed S. aureus as a leading cause) Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection when ecthyma gangrenosum-like skin lesions are present (Aeromonas) Neisseria meningitidis sepsis (K. kingae bacteremia can produce a similar petechial rash) Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection (Aeromonas can cause indistinguishable ecthyma gangrenosum) Other gram-negative bacteremic pneumonias (Achromobacter xylosoxidans bacteremia, similar high mortality) Other causes of culture-negative or slow-growing endocarditis Blood cultures with notification of the laboratory that a HACEK organism is suspected; modern automated systems (e.g., BACTEC) usually yield growth within the first week 16S rRNA gene amplification (PCR) of blood or cardiac valve specimens for culture-negative or fastidious cases MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry performed directly on colonies for rapid, accurate species identification Echocardiography to detect valvular vegetations (seen in up to 85% of HACEK endocarditis) Real-time PCR of blood or joint fluid for Kingella kingae; inoculation of synovial fluid into aerobic blood culture bottles to improve recovery

Infections of the Skin, Muscles, and Soft Tissues — Vesicular: varicella, herpes zoster, HSV-1/HSV-2, hand-foot-mouth disease (coxsackievirus A16), orf, molluscum contagiosum, rickettsialpox, blistering distal dactylitis, smallpox/mpox Bullous: staphylococcal scalded-skin syndrome, necrotizing fasciitis, gas gangrene, halophilic Vibrio (V. vulnificus) Crusted: impetigo contagiosa/bullous impetigo, ringworm (dermatophytes), sporotrichosis, blastomycosis, disseminated coccidioidomycosis, cutaneous TB, M. chelonae nodules in HIV Papulonodular: M. marinum, cat-scratch disease/bacillary angiomatosis (Bartonella henselae), cutaneous larva migrans, dracunculiasis, onchocerciasis, verruga peruana (B. bacilliformis), cysticercosis, lepromatous leprosy, secondary/tertiary syphilis, HPV warts Ulcers/eschars: cutaneous anthrax, ulceroglandular tularemia, bubonic plague, Buruli ulcer (M. ulcerans), leprosy, cutaneous TB, chancroid, primary syphilis Sebaceous cysts blocked at the follicular duct can resemble or become secondarily infected like staphylococcal abscesses Hidradenitis suppurativa (sweat-gland inflammation, especially axillary) can mimic hair-follicle infection Crusted primary infections with Blastomyces dermatitidis or Sporothrix schenckii can initially resemble ringworm Gram stain and culture of drainage, open wound, or obvious portal of entry give a definitive cellulitis diagnosis when present Needle aspiration of the leading edge or punch biopsy (positive in only ~20% of cellulitis and ~80% negative in deep infections)

Infectious Arthritis — Crystal-induced arthritis (gout, pseudogout) - can clinically mimic and may coexist with septic arthritis Cellulitis Bursitis Acute osteomyelitis Hemarthrosis or fracture Monoarticular flare of rheumatoid arthritis Reactive/postinfectious arthritis Acute rheumatic fever Osteoarthritis Gonococcal disseminated infection presenting as arthritis-dermatitis (versus true septic monoarthritis) Meningococcemia with dermatitis-arthritis or purulent monoarthritis Poncet's disease (reactive polyarthritis of disseminated tuberculosis, with no organisms in the joint) Viral arthritides (parvovirus B19, rubella, hepatitis B, arboviruses) Postinfectious/reactive arthritis following enteric or chlamydial infection Arthrocentesis with synovial fluid cell count, differential, Gram stain, and culture (obtain before antibiotics) Synovial fluid examination for crystals to exclude/identify coexistent gout or pseudogout Blood cultures (positive in up to 50-70% of S. aureus infections) Inoculation of synovial fluid into blood-culture bottles to improve yield for fastidious organisms Nucleic acid amplification tests (NAAT) and MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry for partially treated or culture-negative cases Sonication of explanted prosthetic material to disrupt biofilm and improve culture yield Plain radiographs; ultrasound for hip effusion; CT/MRI for sacroiliac, sternoclavicular, and spinal joint infection Mucosal cultures (endocervical/urethral, rectal, oropharyngeal) and urine NAAT when gonococcal arthritis is suspected

Infectious Complications of Bites — Rat-bite fever versus Rocky Mountain spotted fever, Lyme disease, leptospirosis, and secondary syphilis (p.1143) Localized bite-wound cellulitis versus tissue damage from snake envenomation, which can mimic infection (p.1145) Cat-scratch disease (Bartonella henselae) as a late consequence of cat bites/scratches (p.1143) Inflammatory tissue necrosis from venomous snake envenomation, which can be difficult to distinguish from secondary infection (p.1145) Gram's stain and aerobic culture of all infected wounds; anaerobic cultures when abscess, devitalized tissue, or foul-smelling exudate is present (p.1144) Notify the microbiology laboratory when fastidious organisms such as Eikenella corrodens are suspected in human bites (p.1144) White blood cell count, and blood cultures if systemic infection is suspected (p.1144) Radiographs of penetrating wounds to assess fracture or retained foreign body such as a tooth fragment (p.1144) Hand-surgery consultation for hand injuries to evaluate tendon, nerve, and muscular involvement (p.1144) For suspected Capnocytophaga sepsis, prolonged blood-culture incubation (up to 14 days); organisms may be seen within polymorphonuclear leukocytes on Wright-stained peripheral smears (p.1143) Traumatic soft-tissue injury, crush injury, and laceration without infection Local envenomation reaction Bite injuries inoculate the victim's tissues with the biting animal's oral flora plus environmental and cutaneous organisms, producing a typically polymicrobial mix of aerobes and anaerobes. Deep puncture wounds (cat canines, clenched-fist injuries) drive organisms into joints, tendons, and bone, predisposing to septic arthritis and osteomyelitis. Local spread produces cellulitis with purulent discharge, while seeding ca

Infectious Mononucleosis (EBV) — CMV infection (the most common cause of heterophile-negative mononucleosis; older age, longer fever, exudative pharyngitis uncommon) (Harrison 22e p.1511) Acute HIV infection (diffuse rash, oral/genital ulcers, aseptic meningitis) (Harrison 22e p.1511) Toxoplasmosis (less splenomegaly; exposure to cats or raw meat) (Harrison 22e p.1511) HHV-6 infection (older age at presentation) (Harrison 22e p.1511) Streptococcal pharyngitis (no splenomegaly, less fatigue) (Harrison 22e p.1511) Viral hepatitis (higher aminotransferase levels) (Harrison 22e p.1511) Rubella (maculopapular rash, no splenomegaly) (Harrison 22e p.1511) Lymphoma (fixed, nontender lymph nodes) (Harrison 22e p.1511) Drug reaction, most often to phenytoin, carbamazepine, sulfonamides, or minocycline (can occur at any age) (Harrison 22e p.1511) CMV mononucleosis (heterophile-negative) (Harrison 22e p.1511) Acute (primary) HIV infection (Harrison 22e p.1511) Toxoplasmosis (Harrison 22e p.1511) HHV-6 infection (Harrison 22e p.1511) Streptococcal pharyngitis (Harrison 22e p.1511) Viral hepatitis (Harrison 22e p.1511) Rubella (Harrison 22e p.1511) Heterophile antibody test (titer >=40 diagnostic with compatible symptoms and atypical lymphocytes), or the more sensitive commercial Monospot test (~75% sensitive, ~90% specific vs EBV-specific serology) (Harrison 22e p.1511) EBV-specific serology: IgM and IgG anti-VCA, anti-EBNA, and (less useful for routine diagnosis) anti-early antigen (EA-D, EA-R) (Harrison 22e p.1511)

Infertility and Contraception — Polycystic ovary syndrome (most common cause of anovulatory infertility) Diminished ovarian reserve / premature ovarian insufficiency Hypothalamic amenorrhea (low body weight, excessive exercise) Hyperprolactinemia and thyroid dysfunction causing anovulation Endometriosis (present in ~25-50% of infertile women) Tubal factor disease and hydrosalpinx Uterine fibroids/polyps/intrauterine adhesions distorting the cavity Male obstructive vs nonobstructive azoospermia Hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (e.g., Kallmann syndrome) Tubal factor infertility secondary to sexually transmitted infection-related salpingitis (the infection causes structural damage; chronic infertility itself is non-infective) Mumps orchitis as a historical cause of testicular damage and male infertility Transvaginal and abdominal pelvic ultrasound for uterine/adnexal pathology and antral follicle count (ovarian reserve) Ovulation assessment: urinary LH detection kits or serum progesterone ~7 days after ovulation Hysterosalpingogram (HSG) or saline infusion sonogram to assess tubal patency and intrauterine pathology Ovarian reserve testing: day 2-3 serum FSH and estradiol plus anti-mullerian hormone (AMH) and antral follicle counts Endocrine tests in irregular menses: serum TSH, prolactin, total and free testosterone Semen analysis after 2-7 days abstinence (count, motility, morphology, volume, pH); WHO oligoasthenozoospermia thresholds: sperm count <15 million/mL, motility <40%, normal morphology <4%

Inflammatory Bowel Disease — Indeterminate colitis (overlapping UC/CD features in up to 15% of cases) Celiac disease (especially in lymphocytic colitis, which should prompt exclusion) Eosinophilic gastroenteritis, Behcet's syndrome, graft-versus-host disease, neutropenic colitis Diverticulitis / diverticular-associated colitis (mimics Crohn's colitis) Ischemic colitis (segmental like CD or diffuse like UC) Radiation colitis/enteritis Collagenous and lymphocytic (microscopic) colitis Diversion colitis Solitary rectal ulcer syndrome Immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-related colitis NSAID-associated colitis Campylobacter colitis (can mimic severe UC and trigger UC relapse) Other parasites: Isospora belli, Trichuris trichiura, hookworm, Strongyloides Fungal: histoplasmosis, Candida, Aspergillus (mainly in immunocompromised) Salmonella, Shigella enterocolitis Yersinia enterocolitica (terminal ileal ulceration mimicking Crohn's ileitis) Clostridioides difficile colitis Toxigenic / enteroinvasive / enteroadherent E. coli Gonorrhoea, Chlamydia trachomatis and syphilis proctitis Intestinal tuberculosis and Mycobacterium avium (ileocecal involvement) Cytomegalovirus and herpes simplex colitis/proctitis (may occur even in immunocompetent hosts) Entamoeba histolytica (amebiasis) - must be excluded before treating presumed IBD Acute-phase reactants (CRP, ESR), platelet count, haemoglobin and serum albumin to gauge activity

Inflammatory Myopathies — Inclusion body myositis (IBM) - must exclude in every suspected PM case Polymyalgia rheumatica (older patient, raised ESR/CRP, normal CK and EMG) Fibromyalgia (normal laboratory workup) Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy (can be mimicked by anti-HMGCR myopathy or anti-SRP/seronegative IMNM) Muscular dystrophies and metabolic myopathies (may show inflammatory infiltrate on biopsy) Sporadic late-onset nemaline myopathy (SLONM) Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis / neurogenic process (atrophy with fasciculations) Myasthenia gravis / neuromuscular junction defect (fatigable weakness) Spinal cord disorder or polyneuropathy (concomitant sensory symptoms) Infection-associated myositis (listed by Harrison among other inflammatory myopathies caused by infection) Serum creatine kinase (most sensitive marker of muscle destruction); serum aldolase if CK normal (raised in ~10% of normal-CK DM) Malignancy workup (especially adult DM, anti-TIF1-gamma, anti-NXP-2, anti-SAE, anti-HMGCR myopathy) Myositis-specific and myositis-associated autoantibody panel (anti-Mi-2, anti-TIF1-gamma, anti-MDA5, anti-NXP-2, anti-SAE; anti-HMGCR, anti-SRP; antisynthetase incl. anti-Jo-1; anti-cN-1A) Antinuclear antibody (can be positive but nonspecific) Electromyography and nerve conduction studies (localize to muscle; guide biopsy site) Skeletal muscle MRI (STIR) for edema/inflammation, atrophy, fatty replacement, fasciitis and subtype-specific patterns

Influenza — COVID-19 (SARS-CoV-2) respiratory illness Respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) infection Human metapneumovirus infection Parainfluenza virus infection Rhinovirus / common cold Adenovirus infection Acute bronchitis SARS-CoV-2 (COVID-19) Respiratory syncytial virus Human metapneumovirus Parainfluenza virus Adenovirus Rhinovirus Community-acquired bacterial pneumonia (e.g., S. pneumoniae) RT-PCR molecular testing of respiratory secretions (most sensitive and specific; multiplex respiratory panels available) Rapid antigen-based diagnostic test for influenza viral protein in nasopharyngeal secretions Viral isolation by cell culture in a reference laboratory (gold standard but insensitive/slow) Direct or indirect fluorescent antibody detection of virus-infected cells in nasal secretions Chest radiograph for all patients with suspected pneumonia Acute exacerbation of COPD Acute exacerbation of chronic bronchitis Decompensated cardiovascular disease presenting with fever and dyspnea Influenza is a single-stranded, segmented, negative-sense RNA genome virus of the family Orthomyxoviridae, with four (sero)types: A, B, C, and D. Influenza A and C infect multiple species; B infects humans almost exclusively; D primarily infects cattle and is not known to infect humans. Influenza A is subdivided into 18 hemagglutinin (H) and 11 neuraminidase (N) surface-protein subtypes. Two distinct mechanisms drive antigenic variation: antigenic drift (accumulation of point mutations in the HA and NA molecules) produces the gradual divergence underlying annual epidemics and requires new vaccines each year; antigenic shift, enabled by the segmented genome allowing reassortment between two viruses co-infecting one host, can produce a major novel virus and a pandemic.
