Inherited Defects of Membrane Transport — Other causes of urolithiasis (calcium, uric acid, struvite stones) versus cystine stones Classic urea cycle defects versus the hyperammonemia of lysinuric protein intolerance and citrin deficiency Dietary niacin deficiency versus Hartnup disease as a cause of pellagra Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis versus the fatty liver seen in citrullinemia type 2 Other inherited causes of renal Fanconi syndrome versus nephropathic cystinosis Quantitative urinary amino acid analysis (selective overexcretion of cystine, lysine, arginine, ornithine in cystinuria; distinguishes heterozygotes from homozygotes) Urinary nitroprusside test and microscopy for hexagonal cystine crystals in acidified, concentrated, chilled urine Plasma and urine amino acids (low plasma lysine/arginine/ornithine with increased urinary excretion and orotic acid in lysinuric protein intolerance) Genetic sequencing: SLC3A1/SLC7A9 (cystinuria), SLC7A7 (lysinuric protein intolerance), SLC25A13 (citrin deficiency, on hyperammonemia panels), SLC6A19 or CTLRN/collectrin (Hartnup disease), CTNS including deletion analysis (cystinosis) During acute citrin deficiency attacks: ammonia, citrulline, arginine, glutamine, and red-cell galactose-1-phosphate Slit-lamp corneal examination and white-blood-cell cystine content for cystinosis Dietary niacin deficiency producing pellagra (mimics Hartnup disease but lacks neutral aminoaciduria) Nonalcoholic steatohepatitis on liver histology (mimics citrin deficiency)

Inherited Disorders of Amino Acid Metabolism in Adults — Phenylketonuria versus the cofactor (tetrahydrobiopterin-related) hyperphenylalaninemias such as DHPR, PTPS, and GTP cyclohydrolase 1 deficiencies Classic cystathionine beta-synthase homocystinuria versus remethylation defects (methionine synthase / cblE, cblG) and combined methylmalonic acidemia-homocystinuria (cblC, D, F, J) Urea cycle defects distinguished among each other by plasma citrulline, arginine, and urine orotic acid patterns Ochronotic arthritis of alkaptonuria versus rheumatoid arthritis (small joints typically spared in ochronosis) Nonspecific hepatitis can be misdiagnosed in urea cycle defects presenting with hepatic dysfunction Quantitative plasma amino acid analysis (ion-exchange or LC/tandem MS) Urine organic acid analysis by GC/MS Plasma acylcarnitine profile by tandem mass spectrometry Plasma ammonia and plasma glutamine measurement in suspected urea cycle defects Urine orotic acid to differentiate OTC from CPS-1 and NAGS deficiency Total plasma homocysteine and methionine for the homocystinurias Urine organic acid analysis to identify homogentisic acid in alkaptonuria Enzyme assay on cells/tissues or confirmatory DNA testing Newborn screening (blood phenylalanine, methionine) with confirmatory metabolic testing for positive screens Gastrointestinal disorders, food allergies, and behavioral problems are common misdiagnoses in milder urea cycle defects with protein aversion and recurrent vomiting

Intestinal Nematode (Roundworm) Infections — Strongyloides midepigastric pain resembles peptic ulcer disease, except it is aggravated by food ingestion (p.1816) Heavy trichuriasis with bloody/mucoid diarrhea may resemble inflammatory bowel disease (p.1818) Intestinal/biliary ascariasis may present as a surgical acute abdomen mimicking acute appendicitis in endemic areas (p.1815) Strongyloides hyperinfection-associated gram-negative sepsis, pneumonia, or meningitis can dominate or be mistaken for primary bacterial infection (p.1817) Hookworm rhabditiform larvae in non-fresh stool must be differentiated from Strongyloides larvae (p.1816) Stool microscopy for characteristic ova and parasites: Ascaris eggs (~65 x 45 um), hookworm eggs (~40 x 60 um, species indistinguishable by light microscopy), Trichuris lemon-shaped eggs (~50 x 20 um) (p.1815-1818) Strongyloides: rhabditiform larvae (~250 um, short buccal cavity) on stool microscopy; single stool detects only ~one-third of uncomplicated cases, so serial examinations and agar plate method improve sensitivity; duodenojejunal aspirate/biopsy; ELISA serum antibody serology (sensitive for uncomplicated infection); in dissemination, filariform larvae in stool, sputum, bronchoalveolar lavage, or surgical drainage fluid (p.1817) Enterobius: eggs are NOT found in stool - diagnose with morning cellulose acetate tape applied to the perianal region (eggs oval, ~55 x 25 um, flattened on one side) (p.1818)

Intraabdominal Infections and Abscesses — Primary versus secondary peritonitis (single organism without source versus mixed flora with an identifiable viscus source) Pancreatitis versus its infectious complications (infected pseudocyst, pancreatic abscess, infected pancreatic necrosis) - fever, leukocytosis, and abdominal pain alone do not distinguish them Diverticular abscess versus simple diverticulitis Tuboovarian abscess and other female genital tract infection extending into the pelvis Perinephric/renal abscess versus uncomplicated pyelonephritis when fever persists beyond 4-5 days of therapy Hemoperitoneum (especially in trauma) mimicking infective peritonitis Tuberculous peritonitis (cross-reference Chap. 183) Amebic liver abscess (cross-reference Chap. 230) - positive amebic serology in over 95% of cases Candidal liver or renal abscess following fungemia, often unmasked when PMNs recover after neutropenia Diagnostic paracentesis of any cirrhotic with ascites and fever, with PMN count (>250/uL diagnostic of PBP) and culture of fluid in blood-culture bottles plus simultaneous blood cultures Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT to exclude or identify a primary intraabdominal source (highest yield for abscess localization) Chest and abdominal radiography to exclude free air signaling perforation (pneumoperitoneum) and to suggest liver abscess via raised right hemidiaphragm, basilar infiltrate, or pleural effusion Ultrasonography (particularly useful for right upper quadrant, kidneys, and pelvis) and MRI for abscess characterization

Iron Deficiency Anemia — Anemia of inflammation (anemia of chronic disease) - the second most common anemia worldwide, due to functional iron deficiency; a diagnosis of exclusion usually occurring with an inflammatory disorder such as cancer or infection (Harrison 22e p.765, p.450). Thalassemia trait - microcytosis with normal-to-high ferritin and serum iron; red cells are more homogeneous in volume with a low/normal RDW (Harrison 22e p.450, p.767). Mixed forms (combined absolute and functional iron deficiency) (Harrison 22e p.767). Other nutritional anemias - vitamin B12 and folate deficiency (megaloblastic, macrocytic); may coexist with and mask iron deficiency in malabsorption (Harrison 22e p.765). Sideroblastic anemia (rare) as a cause of microcytic hypochromic red cells (Harrison 22e p.~). Serum ferritin (mainstay; <30 µg/L diagnostic, sensitivity 92% / specificity 98%); note ferritin is an acute-phase reactant and may rise severalfold in inflammation (Harrison 22e p.765, p.450). Transferrin saturation (serum iron/TIBC); iron-restricted erythropoiesis at <15-20% (Harrison 22e p.765). Serum iron (reduced, but diurnal fluctuation prevents use as a single test) (Harrison 22e p.765). MCV and RDW from the CBC (MCV <80 fL when established; RDW often elevated reflecting anisocytosis) (Harrison 22e p.765). Soluble transferrin receptor (sTfR) - increased in iron deficiency; sTfR/log ferritin ratio >2 favors iron deficiency (Harrison 22e p.766, p.767).

Ischemic Heart Disease — Aortic stenosis with severe LVH causing subendocardial ischemia and angina without coronary atherosclerosis (Harrison 22e p.2091) Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (Harrison 22e p.2093) Aortic regurgitation and pulmonary hypertension as causes of angina-like chest discomfort (Harrison 22e p.2093) Microvascular angina / abnormal cardiac nociception in patients with ischemic-type chest pain but no flow-limiting epicardial obstruction, more common in women (Harrison 22e p.2093) Vasospastic (variant) angina due to coronary spasm (Harrison 22e p.2091, 2093) Pericarditis (suggested by discomfort radiating to the trapezius) (Harrison 22e p.2092) Esophageal/gastrointestinal disease and musculoskeletal chest wall pain (Harrison 22e p.2093-2094) Fasting lipid panel (total, LDL, HDL cholesterol, triglycerides, lipoprotein(a)) (Harrison 22e p.2094) Coronary CT angiography for intermediate pretest probability and plaque assessment (Harrison 22e p.2097) Invasive coronary arteriography (with FFR/iwFR) per ISCHEMIA-informed indications (Harrison 22e p.2097-2098) Glucose / hemoglobin A1c, creatinine, hematocrit; urinalysis including microalbuminuria; thyroid function if indicated (Harrison 22e p.2094) High-sensitivity C-reactive protein (1-3 mg/L is an independent risk marker, most useful for reclassifying intermediate-risk patients) (Harrison 22e p.2094) Resting 12-lead ECG (Harrison 22e p.2094) Chest x-ray for cardiac enlargement, ventricular aneurysm, or heart failure signs (Harrison 22e p.2094)

Acute ischemic stroke — Intracerebral hemorrhage (must be excluded by CT before reperfusion) Transient ischemic attack (deficit fully resolving within 24 h with no infarction on imaging) Cerebral venous sinus thrombosis (headache, focal signs, seizures; CT often normal) Hypoxic-ischemic encephalopathy from global hypoperfusion (e.g., cardiac arrest) Brain tumour presenting acutely via hemorrhage, seizure, or hydrocephalus Functional/non-organic deficit Stroke recrudescence: fever or sepsis unmasking a prior deficit, mimicking new hemiparesis, which clears as the infection is treated Infective endocarditis with septic emboli (multifocal deficits; may evolve to abscess or hemorrhagic infarct) Brain abscess CNS infection-related vasculitis (syphilis, tuberculosis, fungal, bacterial, zoster meningitis) Finger-stick blood glucose - one of only two tests (with brain imaging) truly required before IV thrombolysis ECG and continuous cardiac telemetry to detect atrial fibrillation or recent MI; ambulatory monitoring if AF not captured inpatient Echocardiography (transthoracic/transoesophageal); bubble-contrast study to detect right-to-left shunt / PFO Carotid duplex ultrasound and transcranial Doppler (can also detect microemboli) CT/MR perfusion imaging to define the penumbra and select late-window candidates MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging - most sensitive for acute infarction, especially in the posterior fossa, and detects new infarction after TIA

Immune thrombocytopenia (ITP) — Drug-induced thrombocytopenia (e.g., quinine, sulfonamides, vancomycin; classic drug-dependent antibodies react with platelet antigens only when drug is present) (p.922-923) Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT) - associated with thrombosis rather than bleeding, nadir rarely <20,000/uL; use 4T scoring (p.923) Congenital/inherited thrombocytopenia (e.g., autosomal dominant macrothrombocytopenia) (p.922, p.965 algorithm) Pseudothrombocytopenia from platelet clumping (EDTA-dependent) - redraw in sodium citrate or heparin (p.922, p.965 algorithm) Evans syndrome - combined autoimmune hemolytic anemia with ITP (perform direct antiglobulin/Coombs test if anemia present) (p.924) HIV infection - can cause immune thrombocytopenia early; late HIV causes pancytopenia with decreased/dysplastic platelet production (p.922) Hepatitis C virus infection - recognized cause of secondary ITP (p.924) Infectious mononucleosis - immune-mediated thrombocytopenia (p.922) Systemic infection with gram-negative bacteria or COVID-19 - thrombocytopenia that may be associated with DIC (p.922) Helicobacter pylori - association with ITP is unclear but appears to have a geographic distribution (p.924) CBC with peripheral blood smear review to confirm isolated thrombocytopenia and exclude clumping/schistocytes (p.922, p.924) HIV and hepatitis C testing to evaluate for secondary ITP (p.924) Serologic testing for SLE (p.924)

Legionellosis (Legionnaires' Disease) — Other atypical-pneumonia pathogens, notably Mycoplasma pneumoniae and Chlamydia pneumoniae (Harrison 22e p.1272) In immunocompromised patients, Legionella can present as pulmonary nodules with or without cavitation that mimic fungal infection, or as lung abscesses (Harrison 22e p.1273) Lower-respiratory culture (sputum, BAL fluid, lung tissue, or extrapulmonary sites) on cysteine-supplemented buffered charcoal yeast extract (BCYE) agar is the gold standard and is essential for epidemiologic typing; growth is slow (typically 3-5 days, longer for non-pneumophila species) (Harrison 22e p.1273-1274) Polymerase chain reaction / nucleic acid amplification (including LAMP and multiplex respiratory panels) on lower-tract specimens is more sensitive than culture and remains useful during antibiotic therapy, but does not provide serotype information and most assays target only L. pneumophila (Harrison 22e p.1274-1275) Bronchoscopy when urinary antigen is negative and the patient cannot produce adequate sputum, or in severe disease requiring ICU care (Harrison 22e p.1273) Serology (paired acute/convalescent titers; fourfold rise to L. pneumophila serogroup 1 confirms) has limited acute sensitivity but aids outbreak investigation (Harrison 22e p.1274) Direct fluorescent antibody testing of sputum has low and variable sensitivity (~20-70%) and is not recommended for low-risk screening due to false positives (Harrison 22e p.1274)

Leishmaniasis — Malaria (VL is easily mistaken for it) For CL: cutaneous tuberculosis, fungal infections, leprosy, sarcoidosis, and malignant ulcers Typhoid (enteric) fever Tuberculosis Brucellosis Schistosomiasis Histoplasmosis Splenomegaly from portal hypertension Chronic myeloid leukemia Tropical splenomegaly syndrome (hyperreactive malarial splenomegaly) Malaria Typhoid fever Tuberculosis Brucellosis Schistosomiasis Histoplasmosis Splenic aspirate smear (highest sensitivity >95%, but invasive and potentially dangerous) Bone marrow aspirate smear (sensitivity 60-85%) Lymph node aspirate smear (sensitivity ~50%) Culture of tissue aspirates (increases sensitivity) rK39 rapid immunochromatographic antibody test (fingerprick blood/serum, result in ~15 min) ELISA and indirect immunofluorescent antibody test (IFAT) Qualitative and quantitative (real-time) PCR for leishmanial nucleic acid (allows species identification) Loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) of nucleic acids (point-of-care for VL and PKDL) Slit skin smears, lesion aspirates/biopsies for CL; tissue biopsy plus PCR for ML Splenomegaly from portal hypertension Chronic myeloid leukemia Tropical splenomegaly syndrome Malignant ulcers (for cutaneous disease) Sarcoidosis (for cutaneous disease) Sandflies inoculate flagellate promastigotes into the skin; neutrophils first take up the organisms, then macrophages and dendritic cells engulf them, and parasites multiply as nonflagellate amastigotes within macrophages, rupturing cells and invading new macrophages. Acquired resistance depends on a T helper 1 (TH1) response driven by IL-12, IFN-gamma, and TNF-alpha; most infected individuals control infection and never develop symptomatic disease. In active VL there is markedly elevated IL-10, which conditions macr

Leprosy (Hansen's Disease) — Hypopigmented macules: pityriasis alba, vitiligo, progressive macular hypomelanosis, pityriasis versicolor, pityriasis rosea, postinflammatory hypopigmentation, sarcoidosis, post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis, morphea (p.1410) Plaque/nodular lesions: granuloma annulare, cutaneous sarcoidosis, cutaneous leishmaniasis, lupus miliaris disseminatus faciei, nodular histiocytosis, lupus erythematosus, cutaneous T-cell lymphomas (especially mycosis fungoides), secondary syphilis (p.1410) ENL (type 2 reaction) lesions: erythema nodosum of other etiologies, nodular vasculitis, cutaneous polyarteritis nodosa (p.1410) Mononeuropathy: diabetes, amyloidosis, myxedema (p.1410) Acute-onset polyneuropathy: Guillain-Barre syndrome, toxic polyneuropathy (p.1410) Cutaneous leishmaniasis (p.1410) Post-kala-azar dermal leishmaniasis (p.1410) Secondary syphilis (p.1410) Pityriasis versicolor (p.1410) Slit-skin smear from standard sites (right earlobe, forehead, chin, and left buttock/upper thigh), Ziehl-Neelsen stained, graded by bacteriologic index (0-6) and microbiologic index (p.1410) Skin biopsy to confirm diagnosis, classify disease, support diagnosis of reactions, and assess cure; immunochemical staining for M. leprae antigens aids detection of early lesions (p.1410) PCR / gene amplification (conventional, RT-PCR, multiplex targeting RLEP, 16S rRNA, SodA, antigen genes) - useful in bacteriologic-index-negative cases and for subclinical infection in contacts (p.1410)

Less Common Lymphoid and Myeloid Malignancies — Chronic lymphocytic leukemia (distinguished from splenic marginal zone lymphoma by CD5 positivity) Mantle cell lymphoma (overlaps with B-cell prolymphocytic leukemia via CD5 and t(11;14)) Nodular sclerosing Hodgkin's disease (versus mediastinal large B-cell lymphoma; the latter is CD45 positive, lacks lacunar Reed-Sternberg variants) Anaplastic large T-cell lymphoma with t(2;5) (versus primary cutaneous CD30+ T-cell lymphoma, which lacks t(2;5)) Chronic myeloid leukemia, BCR::ABL1 positive (versus atypical CML and chronic neutrophilic leukemia) Reactive neutrophilia from infection or inflammation (mimics chronic neutrophilic leukemia) Reactive monocytosis from tuberculosis, fungal infection, subacute bacterial endocarditis, viral or protozoal infection (mimics chronic myelomonocytic leukemia) Hypereosinophilia from tissue-invasive helminths and other parasitic infection (mimics primary/clonal eosinophilic disorders) Peripheral blood smear and bone marrow morphology with immunophenotyping/flow cytometry for lineage markers Cytogenetics and molecular testing: CSF3R (CNL), KIT D816V (mastocytosis), GATA1 (transient myeloproliferative disorder), SETBP1, RAS-pathway mutations (JMML) FISH or RT-PCR screening for PDGFRA and PDGFRB rearrangements in hypereosinophilia Serum tryptase (mast cell disease; elevation also prompts FIP1L1-PDGFRA testing) and soluble CD25 as a hairy cell leukemia activity marker

Listeriosis — Other causes of community-acquired bacterial meningitis (S. pneumoniae, N. meningitidis, H. influenzae, group B streptococcus) (p.1228, Chap.143) Fungal or tuberculous meningitis (low CSF glucose with mononuclear pleocytosis can mimic Listeria) (p.1228, Chap.143) Brain abscess or other space-occupying CNS infection (Listeria abscess) (p.1228) Other bacteraemic/septic illnesses presenting with fever without a focus (p.1228) Blood cultures (note positive only ~half the time in pregnancy) (p.1229) CSF culture and Gram stain (may show gram-positive rods, but often no organisms or misleading gram-positive cocci/diplococci/diphtheroids) (p.1228-1229) Culture of normally sterile sites: amniotic fluid, placental tissue, fetal tissue (p.1229) Multiplex PCR panel on CSF (includes L. monocytogenes as a target) (p.1229) MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry for rapid isolate identification (p.1229) MRI brain (superior to CT for neurolisteriosis and rhombencephalitis) (p.1228) Selective enrichment medium (PALCAM Listeria Selective Agar or Oxford Agar) for non-sterile specimens / outbreak work-up (p.1229) Whole-genome sequencing for outbreak investigation (p.1229) Primary or metastatic CNS malignancy (Listeria brain abscess may be misdiagnosed as tumour) (p.1228) Neoplasia / haematologic malignancy presenting with fever (also a risk factor and prognostic comorbidity) (p.1228) L. monocytogenes is a ubiquitous, nonsporulating, facultatively anaerobic gram-positive rod (showing small zones of beta-haemolysis and characteristic tumbling motility) that lives in soil and decaying vegetation and can grow at refrigerator temperatures as low as 4 C and tolerate low-pH/high-salt environments. Infection follows ingestion of contaminated food; the infectious dose is likely very low in the se

Liver Transplantation — Posttransplant graft dysfunction: rejection vs biliary obstruction vs primary graft nonfunction vs vascular compromise (portal vein or hepatic artery thrombosis) vs drug hepatotoxicity vs recurrent primary disease vs viral hepatitis/CMV — these are clinically and biochemically difficult to distinguish, often requiring biliary imaging and percutaneous liver biopsy. Recurrent primary biliary cholangitis vs chronic rejection (histologically nearly indistinguishable; a florid inflammatory bile duct lesion favors recurrent PBC but is not specific). Recurrent autoimmune hepatitis or sclerosing cholangitis vs rejection or posttransplant bile duct injury. MELD/MELD-Na/MELD-3.0 score calculation (bilirubin, albumin, sodium, creatinine, INR) for allocation and prognosis; PELD for children under 12. Serum bilirubin and aminotransferases — most reliable, though nonspecific, indicators of allograft rejection. Percutaneous liver biopsy and radiographic visualization of the biliary tree to differentiate causes of graft dysfunction. Donor screening: hemodynamic stability, oxygenation, absence of infection/abdominal trauma/hepatic dysfunction; serologic testing for HBV, HCV, HIV (infected organs now used selectively with matching and informed consent). Recipient cardiopulmonary evaluation (especially age >70) to exclude ischemic cardiac disease; assessment of pulmonary artery pressure and intrapulmonary shunting.

Lung cancer — Pulmonary metastases from non-lung primaries and other neoplasms metastatic to the lung, which constitutional symptoms cannot reliably distinguish from primary lung cancer (p.619) Endobronchial metastases from carcinoid, breast, colon, kidney and other tumours presenting with haemoptysis (referenced p.591/Ch.80) Mesothelioma, which can be hard to separate from adenocarcinoma and is identified by CK5/6, calretinin and WT-1 positivity (p.616) Pulmonary carcinoid tumour, a neuroendocrine tumour that can also secrete ectopic ACTH (p.619, p.662 area) Post-obstructive pneumonia or a persistent pneumonia that does not resolve after repeated antibiotic courses can mask an underlying obstructing tumour (p.618) Lung abscess physiology from tumour cavitation can mimic infective abscess (p.618) Granulomatous infection such as tuberculosis can cause false-positive PET uptake and simulate malignancy on imaging (p.620) Core biopsy (preferred over FNA) for adequate tissue, obtained by bronchoscopic/transbronchial biopsy, image-guided percutaneous biopsy, or EBUS/EUS-guided sampling depending on location (p.620) Next-generation sequencing for driver oncogenes (EGFR, ALK, ROS1, BRAF, KRAS, MET, RET, NTRK, HER2) plus PD-L1 immunohistochemistry reported as tumour proportion score, recommended for all advanced NSCLC (p.620) Circulating tumour DNA 'liquid biopsy' as a non-invasive adjunct when tissue is limited or inaccessible (p.620)

Lyme Disease (Lyme Borreliosis) — Uninfected tick bite (red papule that expands little) versus EM Cellulitis (e.g., streptococcal) or allergic reaction to tick saliva when a lesion expands rapidly Erythema multiforme in patients with secondary annular lesions (but mucosal blistering and palm/sole involvement are NOT features of B. burgdorferi infection) Southern tick-associated rash illness (STARI) from Amblyomma americanum bites, an EM-like lesion whose cause is not yet identified Peripheral spondyloarthropathy or pauciarticular juvenile idiopathic arthritis versus oligoarticular Lyme arthritis Bell's palsy (herpes simplex virus type 1) and Ramsay Hunt syndrome (varicella-zoster virus) versus Lyme facial palsy Chronic fatigue syndrome and fibromyalgia versus late-stage Lyme disease or PTLDS Babesiosis (Babesia microti), co-transmitted by I. scapularis, causing an influenza-like illness with thrombocytopenia and hemolytic anemia Human granulocytotropic anaplasmosis (Anaplasma phagocytophilum), which may cause leukopenia/thrombocytopenia and can elicit a false-positive IgM response to B. burgdorferi Borrelia miyamotoi relapsing fever, co-transmitted by I. scapularis Borrelia mayonii and Ehrlichia muris-like agent infections in the upper midwestern United States Powassan virus (deer tick virus) infection, which may be fatal Ehrlichia chaffeensis transmitted by Amblyomma americanum in the same regions as STARI Two-tier serology: conventional approach with ELISA followed by Western blot for equivocal/positive results, or a modified two-test approach using two enzyme immunoassays (e.g., whole-sonicate ELISA followed by VlsE C6 peptide IgG ELISA) that dispenses with the Western blot

Lysosomal Storage Diseases — Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy (mimicked by late-onset Pompe disease) Idiopathic hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (about 1-3% have Fabry disease) Idiopathic stroke at 35-50 years (about 2-5% carry GLA mutations) Idiopathic renal failure in males (about 5% have GLA mutations) Cryptogenic cirrhosis / nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (childhood/adult-onset LALD) Familial hyperlipidemia (LALD) Parkinson disease (associated with GBA1 carriage) Acute appendicitis or renal colic (Fabry abdominal pain can mimic these) Enzyme assay in nucleated cells, serum/plasma, or leukocytes specific to the suspected disorder Molecular/genetic testing: whole GBA1 sequencing is the standard for Gaucher (enzyme testing has poor sensitivity for heterozygote detection) Slit-lamp examination for corneal and lenticular lesions to support a Fabry diagnosis Decreased acid beta-glucosidase activity (0-20% of normal) in nucleated cells establishes Gaucher disease; the enzyme is normally absent from bodily fluids Markedly reduced acid sphingomyelinase activity (1-10% of normal) in nucleated cells confirms Niemann-Pick A/B Confirmation of specific enzyme deficiency in Morquio (GALNS vs acid beta-galactosidase) before therapy Gene sequencing to confirm CLN2 given overlap among the neuronal ceroid lipofuscinoses Newborn screening (now includes MPS I and, in many states, Pompe disease) Bone imaging / nuclear scan in Gaucher bone crises (localized absent uptake of pyrophosphate agents indicates acute bone infarction)

Malignancy (B-symptoms) — Hodgkin lymphoma (classical) - nontender cervical/supraclavicular/axillary nodes, frequent mediastinal involvement (Harrison 22e p.869) Non-Hodgkin lymphoma - nodal and extranodal disease; B symptoms part of staging (Harrison 22e p.860) Acute or chronic lymphocytic leukaemia (can produce generalised adenopathy and constitutional symptoms) (Harrison 22e p.476) Richter transformation of CLL - rapidly progressive focal adenopathy with night sweats, fever, weight loss and high LDH (Harrison 22e p.897) Metastatic carcinoma to nodes (head/neck, lung, breast, thyroid, GI primaries) (Harrison 22e p.477) Germ-cell tumour (retroperitoneal nodes in young men) (Harrison 22e p.477) Occult solid tumours presenting with involuntary weight loss - GI/hepatobiliary, lung, breast, genitourinary, ovarian, prostate (Harrison 22e p.317) Infectious mononucleosis (EBV or CMV) - generalised adenopathy with constitutional symptoms (Harrison 22e p.476) Tuberculosis - can cause unilateral mediastinal adenopathy and mesenteric lymphadenitis mimicking lymphoma, with night sweats and weight loss (Harrison 22e p.477) Histoplasmosis - unilateral paratracheal node involvement that can mimic lymphoma in endemic regions (Harrison 22e p.477) Toxoplasmosis - generalised reactive adenopathy (Harrison 22e p.476) HIV / AIDS - generalised lymphadenopathy and a recognised lymphoma risk factor (Harrison 22e p.476, p.903)

Malnutrition and Nutritional Assessment — Sarcopenia (progressive generalized loss of skeletal muscle mass and strength; screened with SARC-F) Sarcopenic obesity Cachexia of chronic disease (malignancy, organ failure) Frailty syndrome Dehydration / fluid shifts mimicking weight change Micronutrient deficiency states Validated risk-screening tools: Malnutrition Screening Tool, Malnutrition Universal Screening Tool (MUST), Nutritional Risk Screening 2002, Mini Nutritional Assessment, Subjective Global Assessment Anthropometrics: serial body weight (without shoes/heavy garments), BMI, calf circumference, mid-upper arm circumference; height estimated by arm span or knee-height caliper when needed Body composition: bioelectrical impedance analysis (BIA, portable), dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry (DXA), air displacement plethysmography, and opportunistic CT/MRI muscle measurement Laboratory: complete blood count with differential (screen for iron, B12, folate, vitamin C deficiencies), C-reactive protein for inflammation, specific micronutrient levels Indirect calorimetry for resting energy expenditure; 24-h urine urea nitrogen and nitrogen balance to gauge catabolism and protein adequacy (normal renal/hepatic function required) Functional tests: handgrip strength, Sit-to-Stand test, 6-Meter Walk Test, Clinical Frailty Scale, SARC-F Nutrition-focused physical examination for edema, subcutaneous fat and muscle loss; diet history including oral supplements, enteral and parenteral intake

Mastocytosis — Carcinoid syndrome (exclude with 24-h urine 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid) Pheochromocytoma (exclude with 24-h urine/plasma metanephrines) Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia (autosomal dominant extra copies of the alpha-tryptase gene at TPSAB1; elevated baseline serum tryptase with multisystem mast cell activation symptoms) Recurrent IgE-mediated or idiopathic anaphylaxis (usually presents with urticaria, angioedema and/or bronchospasm, which are not typical manifestations of anaphylaxis in SM) Basal (baseline) serum tryptase as a noninvasive screen before bone marrow biopsy Bone marrow biopsy with mast cell morphology, immunophenotype (CD25, CD2, CD30), and KIT D816V mutation testing for systemic disease Skin biopsy to confirm diffuse cutaneous and bullous mastocytosis subvariants 24-h urine 5-hydroxyindoleacetic acid (carcinoid) and metanephrines (pheochromocytoma) to exclude mimics Bone densitometry, bone scan, or skeletal survey (osteoporosis is increased and may cause pathologic fractures) CT scan or endoscopy and neuropsychiatric evaluation as directed by presentation Carcinoid syndrome (flushing, diarrhea) Pheochromocytoma (flushing, tachycardia, vascular collapse) Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia Idiopathic or IgE-mediated anaphylaxis Mastocytosis is a clonal mast cell disorder driven by somatic gain-of-function mutations in the KIT (stem cell factor receptor) gene, with KIT D816V present in >90% of patients. The mutation produces ligand-independent KIT activation and clonal mast cell proliferation/accumulation in skin, bone marrow, liver, spleen, and gut. KIT mutations occur across all forms of SM and in lesional skin of some children with cutaneous disease; additional mutations (TET2, SRSF2, ASXL1, RUNX1) seen in other hematologic neoplasms can appear in adv

Measles (Rubeola) — Rubella (German measles) - milder, no cough, with posterior auricular/suboccipital lymphadenopathy Kawasaki disease Infectious mononucleosis (atypical lymphocytosis, in contrast to the leukopenia common in measles) Roseola (exanthem subitum) - rash appears after fever subsides Scarlet fever Rocky Mountain spotted fever Enterovirus or adenovirus infection Drug sensitivity/eruption Rubella Infectious mononucleosis (Epstein-Barr virus) Roseola/exanthem subitum (HHV-6/HHV-7) Scarlet fever Rocky Mountain spotted fever Enterovirus (echovirus, coxsackievirus) infection Adenovirus infection Early meningococcemia or rickettsial infection (morbilliform before petechiae/purpura) Detection of measles virus-specific IgM in a single serum or oral fluid specimen is diagnostic of acute infection Fourfold or greater rise in measles virus-specific IgG between acute- and convalescent-phase sera Note timing pitfall: IgM may not be detectable until 4-5 days after rash onset (false-negatives if drawn too early) and usually falls to undetectable within 4-8 weeks Reverse-transcription PCR for measles virus RNA (sensitive/specific; can genotype and distinguish wild-type from vaccine strain) Virus isolation in cell culture from respiratory secretions, nasopharyngeal/conjunctival swabs, blood, or urine Direct detection of giant cells in respiratory secretions, urine, or biopsy tissue Neutralization tests (highly correlated with protective immunity but expensive and laborious)

Megaloblastic Anemias — Megaloblastic anemia from antifolate/antimetabolite drugs (methotrexate, pyrimethamine, trimethoprim; hydroxyurea, cytarabine, mercaptopurine, thioguanine, AZT) (Harrison 22e p.780, p.790) Orotic aciduria (responds to uridine) (Harrison 22e p.780, p.790) Thiamine-responsive megaloblastic anemia (SLC19A2 transporter defect; may have diabetes, deafness, ringed sideroblasts) (Harrison 22e p.780, p.790) Megaloblastic changes in acute myeloid leukemia and myelodysplasia (refractory to folate/cobalamin) (Harrison 22e p.780, p.790) Macrocytosis without true megaloblastic change: alcohol, liver disease, hypothyroidism, pregnancy, myelodysplasia, myeloma/paraproteinemia, aplastic anemia, smoking (Harrison 22e p.790) Serum cobalamin (ELISA or competitive-binding luminescence assay); note IF antibodies can cause falsely normal results in up to 50% of pernicious anemia cases (Harrison 22e p.788) Serum methylmalonic acid (raised in cobalamin deficiency sufficient for anemia/neuropathy; fluctuates in renal failure) (Harrison 22e p.788, p.789) Serum homocysteine (raised in early cobalamin and folate deficiency but nonspecific) (Harrison 22e p.789) Serum folate and red cell folate (red cell folate reflects body stores; false-normal after transfusion or with high reticulocytes) (Harrison 22e p.789) Serum gastrin (raised in pernicious anemia) and pepsinogen I (low) (Harrison 22e p.785, p.789) Intrinsic factor and parietal cell antibodies; gastric endoscopy/biopsy (Harrison 22e p.786, p.789)

Meningococcal Disease — Other causes of bacterial meningitis (presentation of meningococcal meningitis is indistinguishable unless an associated petechial/purpuric rash or gram-negative diplococci are present) (p.1248-1249) Differential of chronic meningococcemia: bacterial endocarditis, acute rheumatic fever, Henoch-Schonlein purpura, infectious mononucleosis, disseminated gonococcal infection, immune-mediated vasculitis (p.1248-1249) Viral infections (enteroviruses, influenza and other respiratory viruses, measles, Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, parvovirus) - most patients presenting with a petechial/purpuric rash have a viral infection (p.1248) Pneumococcal, streptococcal, staphylococcal, or other gram-negative bacterial sepsis (p.1248) Blood culture for confirmation and public health investigation (positive in up to ~75% of cases); avoid media containing sodium polyanethol sulfonate, which may inhibit meningococcal growth, and avoid delay in transport (p.1249) Real-time PCR of whole blood increases diagnostic yield by more than 40% and may remain positive for several days after antibiotics (p.1249) Lumbar puncture for CSF in suspected meningitis (unless contraindicated); CSF Gram stain is up to ~80% sensitive, CSF culture sensitivity ~90%, plus PCR where available; CSF latex agglutination antigen testing is insensitive and should be replaced by molecular diagnosis (p.1249) Inflammatory markers (WBC count, C-reactive protein, procalcitonin, ESR) may support the diagnosis but can be normal or low in rapidly progressive disease and do not exclude it (p.1249)

Menopause and Postmenopausal Hormone Therapy — Pregnancy as a cause of amenorrhea in perimenopausal women (unintentional pregnancy rate in the forties rivals that of adolescents) Premature ovarian insufficiency / primary ovarian insufficiency when ovarian failure occurs well before the usual age Thyroid dysfunction or other endocrine causes of menstrual irregularity and vasomotor-like symptoms Uterine structural lesions (leiomyomata, endometrial polyps, hyperplasia or carcinoma) presenting as abnormal/heavy bleeding Other age-related conditions causing midlife mood, sleep, cognitive, or sexual complaints not attributable to ovarian senescence Menstrual cycle history as the principal STRAW+10 criterion for staging reproductive aging, with biomarkers as supportive criteria FSH measurement: random level >25 IU/L is characteristic of the late menopausal transition; day-3 levels <20, 20 to <30, and >=30 IU/L indicate good, fair, and poor pregnancy likelihood respectively Estradiol levels, recognizing that FSH and estradiol are imperfect diagnostic indicators in still-menstruating perimenopausal women due to marked intraindividual variability Anti-mullerian hormone and inhibin B as additional markers of reproductive aging Transvaginal ultrasound (with saline enhancement) to detect leiomyomata or polyps when bleeding is abnormal Endometrial aspiration/biopsy to identify hyperplastic or premalignant changes when menorrhagia or abnormal bleeding occurs

Menstrual Disorders and Pelvic Pain — Pregnancy (must be excluded first in amenorrhea and in any reproductive-age woman with pelvic pain or bleeding) Polycystic ovary syndrome Rarer causes of hypergonadotropic hypogonadism: FSH/LH receptor mutations, aromatase deficiency, 17-alpha-hydroxylase deficiency Pelvic pain mimics outside the reproductive tract: appendicitis, diverticulitis, inflammatory bowel disease, urinary tract disorders, musculoskeletal/neuromuscular and psychosomatic causes Outflow-tract obstruction: transverse vaginal septum, imperforate hymen Mullerian agenesis (Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome; WNT4 mutations) Androgen insensitivity syndrome (about 10% of primary amenorrhea; 46,XY karyotype, female external genitalia, absent pubic/axillary hair, male-range testosterone) 5-alpha reductase type 2 deficiency Asherman's syndrome (intrauterine adhesions, usually post-curettage; genital tuberculosis in endemic areas) Hypothalamic/pituitary tumors and infiltrative disease, hyperprolactinemia, Sheehan's syndrome, lymphocytic hypophysitis, prior cranial irradiation Isolated hypogonadotropic hypogonadism / Kallmann syndrome Primary ovarian insufficiency (idiopathic, Turner syndrome, autoimmune polyglandular failure, fragile X premutation, post-chemo/radiotherapy) Pelvic inflammatory disease (upper genital tract infection, often Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae) Tubo-ovarian abscess Endometritis (post-instrumentation, postpartum, or STI-associated)

Acute mesenteric ischemia — Chronic mesenteric ischaemia / intestinal angina (postprandial pain, weight loss, fear of eating) Ischaemic colitis (notably after elective or emergent aortic repair) Gastrointestinal malignancy (must be excluded in chronic presentations) Superior mesenteric artery syndrome (duodenal compression after weight loss/immobilisation) Median arcuate ligament syndrome (celiac artery compression) Thin-cut (1 mm or thinner) CT angiography is the gold standard for detecting mesenteric arterial occlusive (embolic/thrombotic) disease and for assessing bowel; venous-phase imaging detects mesenteric venous thrombosis with diffuse bowel-wall thickening and splanchnic thrombus (p.2588-2589). Mesenteric duplex ultrasound is a sensitive/specific screening tool; a high SMA peak flow velocity carries ~80% positive predictive value, and a negative duplex virtually excludes mesenteric ischaemia (test must be done fasting) (p.2588). Leukocytosis, metabolic acidosis and lactic acidosis support advanced ischaemia but may be absent in reversible ischaemia and cannot reliably distinguish reversible ischaemia from frank necrosis (p.2589). ECG and echocardiogram may help identify an embolic cardiac source but must not delay surgical therapy (p.2588). Hypercoagulability workup in suspected mesenteric venous thrombosis (e.g. factor V Leiden, prothrombin mutation, protein C/S or antithrombin deficiency, antiphospholipid syndrome) (p.2587, 2589).

Mesenteric Vascular Insufficiency — Gastrointestinal malignancy (must be excluded in CMI before intervention) Peptic ulcer disease and other causes of epigastric/postprandial pain Biliary colic / biliary tract disease Acute pancreatitis Inflammatory bowel disease (ischemic colitis is commonly confused with IBD) Acute intestinal obstruction (especially strangulated obstruction with vascular insufficiency) Infectious colitis Infectious gastroenteritis CT angiography with thin (1-mm or finer) cuts, including venous phase for venous thrombosis (gold standard) Fasting mesenteric duplex ultrasound (screening; SMA peak velocity) Esophagogastroduodenoscopy and colonoscopy (to exclude malignancy in CMI and assess colonic mucosa in ischemic colitis) Abdominal CT and abdominal ultrasound Electrocardiogram and echocardiogram (to identify embolic source such as atrial fibrillation; should not delay surgery) Laboratory markers: leukocytosis, metabolic acidosis, lactic acidosis (support advanced ischemia but do not reliably distinguish reversible ischemia from necrosis) Hypercoagulability workup in mesenteric venous thrombosis Inflammatory bowel disease Diverticular disease / diverticulitis Colonic neoplasm Peptic ulcer disease Biliary tract disease The intestine is perfused by the celiac artery, superior mesenteric artery (SMA), and inferior mesenteric artery (IMA), with extensive collateralization through the mesenteric arcades; small-bowel collaterals converge at the duodenum and pancreatic bed, while colonic collaterals meet at the splenic flexure (Griffiths' point) and the descending/sigmoid colon (Sudeck's point), the watershed zones most prone to colonic ischemia. The splanchnic bed can receive up to ~30% of cardiac output, and protective mechanisms include abundant collaterals

Metabolic encephalopathy — Dementia and pre-existing cognitive impairment - the major predisposing condition; at least two-thirds of delirium occurs in patients with underlying dementia, and the two coexist and overlap (p.183). Dementia with Lewy bodies - fluctuating course, prominent visual hallucinations and parkinsonism can closely mimic hyperactive delirium (p.183). Nonconvulsive status epilepticus and recurrent seizures with prolonged postictal confusion (p.185). Focal stroke or haemorrhage in nondominant (right) parietal lobe or medial dorsal thalamus - rare structural cause of an acute confusional state (p.184-185). Hypertensive encephalopathy / posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES) and eclampsia (p.184, p.190). Diffuse neoplastic disease - multiple brain metastases, diffuse glioma, CNS lymphoma, carcinomatous meningitis (p.184). Postoperative encephalopathy from a shower of microemboli, particularly after cardiac/cardiopulmonary bypass surgery (p.2348). Acute primary psychiatric disturbance, depression and catatonia - must be distinguished, particularly from the quiet hypoactive subtype (p.184). Systemic infections - urinary tract infection, pneumonia and other respiratory infections, skin/soft tissue infection and frank sepsis; a UTI precipitating acute confusion in an elderly patient with baseline dementia is a classic scenario (p.184). CNS infections - bacterial meningitis, encephalitis (including herpes simplex) and brain abscess; less common causes but high morbidity/mortality if missed (p.184).

Migraine — Tension-type headache - the main differential; distinguished by being completely featureless (no nausea/vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia, osmophobia, throbbing or aggravation with movement), whereas migraine has one or more of these (p.3471). Cluster headache and other trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias (p.3462). Acephalgic migraine / typical aura without headache - recurrent neurologic symptoms with little or no headache (p.3464). Vestibular migraine - common, underdiagnosed cause of episodic vertigo lasting minutes to hours, sometimes without headache (p.3464). Migraine with brainstem aura (formerly basilar/basilar-type migraine) (p.3464). Medication-overuse headache complicating an underlying migraine tendency (p.115-116). Bacterial/viral meningitis - acute severe headache with stiff neck and fever; can be mistaken for migraine because pounding headache, photophobia, nausea and vomiting are shared cardinal features, and there is often striking accentuation of pain on eye movement; lumbar puncture is mandatory (p.113-114). Migraine is a clinical diagnosis in patients with a normal examination and no other reasonable cause for headache (Table 441-3, p.3466). A headache diary aids diagnosis and quantifies disability and attack frequency (p.3462). The Migraine Disability Assessment Score (MIDAS) is a validated tool to grade disability (p.3465). CT or MRI of the brain (equally sensitive as initial screen for intracranial pathology) is indicated for an abnormal neurologic examination or recent-onset headache; lumbar puncture may additionally be required when a benign cause cannot otherwise be established (p.113).

Mitral Regurgitation — Aortic stenosis (basally-radiating MR murmur from posterior leaflet prolapse/flail can be confused with AS) (p.2054) Mitral stenosis (a brief early-diastolic LA-LV gradient with rapid filling sound and mid-diastolic rumble in pure severe MR can masquerade as MS) (p.2053-2054) Ventricular septal defect and other causes of a holosystolic murmur Transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) with Doppler to define mechanism and severity (jet width/area, regurgitant volume, regurgitant fraction, effective regurgitant orifice area, LV volumes/EF, LA/LV size, chordal integrity, annular calcification) (p.2053) Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) for greater anatomic detail (p.2053-2054) Estimation of pulmonary artery systolic pressure from the tricuspid regurgitation jet velocity (p.2053) Exercise (stress) echocardiography to assess exercise capacity and dynamic change in MR severity, PA pressures, and biventricular function when clinical and resting findings disagree (p.2053) Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) for quantitative regurgitant measures when TTE is discordant or insufficient (noted as not widely available) (p.2052-2053) ECG (LA enlargement, possible RA enlargement with pulmonary hypertension, AF, eccentric LVH) (p.2053) Chest X-ray (LA/LV enlargement, pulmonary venous congestion, Kerley B lines, mitral/annular calcification; asymmetric pulmonary edema possible in acute MR) (p.2053-2054)

Mitral Stenosis — Mitral regurgitation (may have an apical diastolic flow murmur, but it begins slightly later, S1 is soft or absent, and there is no opening snap; LV enlargement is common) (p.2049) Severe aortic regurgitation with an Austin Flint murmur (apical mid-diastolic murmur not intensified in presystole and softened by amyl nitrite/arterial vasodilators) (p.2049) Tricuspid stenosis (rare without MS; its diastolic murmur increases with inspiration and the jugular venous y descent is delayed) (p.2049-2050) Atrial septal defect (RV enlargement and increased pulmonary vascularity, but no LA enlargement or Kerley B lines, with fixed splitting of S2) (p.2050) Left atrial myxoma (obstructs LA emptying causing a positional diastolic murmur; often with systemic features such as weight loss, fever, anemia, emboli, elevated IgG/IL-6) (p.2050) Infective endocarditis with large vegetations is itself a recognized (uncommon) cause of left ventricular inflow obstruction mimicking MS (p.2048) Transthoracic echocardiography with color flow and spectral Doppler for mitral inflow velocities, peak/mean gradients, mitral orifice area, leaflet calcification and restriction, and suitability for percutaneous mitral balloon commissurotomy (p.2049) Transesophageal echocardiography when TTE is inadequate, and specifically to exclude left atrial thrombus before commissurotomy (p.2049) Exercise (stress) echocardiography to assess mean mitral diastolic gradient, PA pressures, and RV function when clinical and resting hemodynamic findings are discrepant (p.2049)

Mitral Valve Prolapse — Other causes of primary mitral regurgitation Rheumatic mitral valve disease (chordae thickened but not fused in MVP, unlike rheumatic disease) Innocent or functional systolic murmurs Angina pectoris (when atypical chest pain is present) ECG (often normal; may show biphasic or inverted T waves in leads II, III, aVF and supraventricular or ventricular premature beats) Transthoracic echocardiography to identify abnormal leaflet position and prolapse and define the >=2 mm displacement criterion Color flow and continuous-wave Doppler to assess associated MR and estimate severity Three-dimensional echocardiography and cardiac MRI for more precise LV volumes and detection of papillary muscle fibrosis/late gadolinium enhancement Transesophageal echocardiography when detailed anatomy is needed and for intraoperative or transcatheter procedural guidance Exercise testing (often with rest and immediate poststress TTE) to assess functional capacity, LV/RV function, dynamic MR, and pulmonary pressures Left ventriculography during catheterization (rarely necessary) MVP results from myxomatous degeneration of the mitral valve apparatus with excessive or redundant leaflet tissue and markedly increased glycosaminoglycan content. In many cases the cause is unknown, but some forms are genetically determined; reduced type III collagen production has been implicated, and electron microscopy shows fragmentation of collagen fibrils. Genome-wide association work has identified multiple genetic loci (candidate genes include LMCD1, SPTBN1, LTBP2, TGFB2, NMB, and ALPK3), and associations with LMNA, FLNC, and FLNA that are often expressed as cardiomyopathies. The posterior leaflet is typically more affected, the annulus is often dilated, and elongated, redundant, or ruptured

Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia (MEN) — Germline RET mutation testing in all patients with medullary thyroid carcinoma, with cascade screening of relatives (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.397). MEN1 (menin) gene testing in patients with the parathyroid/pancreatic-islet/pituitary tumor pattern or relevant family history (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.392/ch.376). Biochemical screening for pheochromocytoma and hyperparathyroidism in RET-mutation carriers identified as at risk for MEN2 (Harrison 22e p.3079). Other familial pituitary tumor / endocrine neoplasia syndromes: MEN 4 (CDKN1B mutation; hyperparathyroidism and pituitary adenomas), Carney complex (PRKAR1A; spotty skin pigmentation, myxomas, endocrine tumors), McCune-Albright syndrome, and familial isolated pituitary adenomas (AIP) (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.392). Other inherited predispositions to pheochromocytoma that overlap with MEN2: von Hippel-Lindau disease, neurofibromatosis, and hereditary paraganglioma syndromes (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.247). MEN1 follows the two-hit tumor-suppressor paradigm: the affected individual inherits a mutant copy of the MEN1 gene (menin, chromosome 11q13), and tumorigenesis follows a somatic 'second hit' (deletion or point mutation) that inactivates the remaining normal allele. In contrast, MEN2 is caused by activating point mutations in a single allele of the RET protooncogene, encoding a receptor tyrosine kinase; constitutive RET activity leads to thyroid C-cell hyperplasia in childhood that precedes the development of medullary thyroid carcinoma (Harrison 22e p.3079, ch.388/ch.397).

Myxoedema coma — Sick euthyroid syndrome confounding thyroid function tests in a critically ill or hypothermic patient (p.3769). Adrenal insufficiency / hypopituitarism, which independently increase susceptibility to hypothermia and may coexist (p.3768). Hashimoto's encephalopathy - a steroid-responsive syndrome with TPO antibodies, myoclonus and EEG slow-wave activity (relationship to hypothyroidism not established) (p.3030). Sepsis should be actively suspected as a precipitant; hypothermia obscures fever and leukocytosis, and infectious rigors may be mistaken for shivering (p.3032, p.3769). Pneumonia as a respiration-impairing precipitant (p.3032). Arterial blood gas to detect hypoxia and hypercapnia from hypoventilation (p.3032). Glucose to detect contributing hypoglycemia (p.3032). Septic screen / cultures, since infection is a common precipitant and is masked by hypothermia (p.3032, p.3769). Core temperature measurement (may be very low, down to ~23 degrees C) (p.3032). Environmental / accidental hypothermia from cold exposure, drugs (ethanol, sedatives, antipsychotics, antidepressants), or malnutrition (p.3768). Hypoglycemia from insulin or oral hypoglycemic agents, which itself causes hypothermia via neuroglycopenic hypothalamic effects (p.3768). Long-standing thyroid hormone deficiency depresses the metabolic rate and thermogenesis, producing hypothermia, bradycardia, and reduced myocardial contractility. Dermal accumulation of glycosaminoglycans traps water, giving nonpitting myxedematous swelling. In myxedema coma, hypoventilation is central to pathogenesis: it leads to hypoxia and hypercapnia (CO2 retention). Dilutional hyponatremia (reduced renal perfusion with inappropriate vasopressin) and hypoglycemia further contribute. There is impaired adrenal reserve

Nicotine Addiction — Other substance use disorders (alcohol use disorder, stimulant use) Caffeine use/dependence Primary mood or anxiety disorders presenting with cravings or restlessness Cannabis use via vaping devices (refillable pods may aerosolize marijuana oils) Structured history of total daily frequency of all nicotine products used (cigarettes, cigars, roll-your-own, vaping, oral pouches/snuff) Duration of regular use, prior quit experiences, and current interest in quitting Markers of addiction intensity: episodes per day, spacing through the day, and use within 30 minutes of waking Biomarkers of smoke-toxicant exposure (markedly lower in exclusive e-cigarette users than in cigarette smokers) Withdrawal-related irritability and restlessness mimicking primary anxiety or depressive disorders Chronic cough from smoking-related mucous hyperplasia mimicking other causes of chronic productive cough Nicotine reaching the brain reversibly binds nicotinic acetylcholine receptors that are highly active in networks mediating mood, reward, joy, and excitement. With sustained high exposure, nicotinic receptors are upregulated on brain cells, so that for most people daily use is required to maintain the addicted state. As blood nicotine falls between doses, nicotine detaches from receptors and addicted individuals no longer feel 'normal,' producing a compulsive drive for the next dose. The strength and speed of addiction depend on dosing frequency and on the arterial nicotine concentration reaching the brain, which varies by product. Unprotonated (freebase) nicotine, favored at alkaline pH, is absorbed readily across mucosa but is airway-irritating at high concentration; addictive products use mildly acidic aerosols in the mouth to limit irritation and permit deep inhalation

Nocardiosis — Lymphocutaneous (sporotrichoid) presentation overlaps with Sporothrix schenckii and Mycobacterium marinum infection (p.1360). Mycetoma differential: actinomycetoma (filamentous bacteria, e.g., Nocardia), eumycetoma (fungal), and botryomycosis (cocci/bacilli, often Staphylococcus aureus) are difficult to separate clinically and require granule microscopy, culture, or biopsy (p.1361). Ocular nocardiosis (keratitis, scleritis, endophthalmitis) cannot be distinguished from other ocular infections by signs and symptoms alone (p.1360). Sporothrix schenckii (sporotrichosis) for lymphocutaneous disease Mycobacterium marinum for lymphocutaneous disease Eumycetoma (fungal mycetoma) for actinomycetoma Botryomycosis (often Staphylococcus aureus) for actinomycetoma Other causes of pulmonary nodules/cavitation and ring-enhancing brain lesions in immunocompromised hosts (e.g., fungi, mycobacteria, toxoplasmosis as discussed in brain abscess context) Sputum or pus microscopy for branching beaded Gram-positive filaments plus modified (weak-acid) acid-fast staining; organisms may also take up silver stains (p.1360-1361). Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid or lung biopsy when sputum smears are negative, as they frequently are in pulmonary nocardiosis (p.1361). Selective media (colistin-nalidixic acid agar, modified Thayer-Martin agar, or buffered charcoal-yeast extract agar) for mixed-flora specimens; avoid mycobacterial decontamination procedures, which can kill nocardiae; alert the laboratory to incubate cultures for prolonged periods (up to 2-4 weeks) (p.1361).

Opioid overdose — Cholinergic (muscarinic/nicotinic) poisoning — also causes miosis plus a depressed physiologic state (p.3748) Sedative-hypnotic / GABAergic poisoning (alcohols, barbiturates, benzodiazepines, GHB) — depressed state, distinguished as naloxone-unresponsive (p.3748) Sympatholytic poisoning (alpha-2 agonists e.g. clonidine, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, cardiac glycosides) (p.3747) Other causes of coma including hypoglycemia (reversed by dextrose) (p.3748) Blood/urine toxicology can confirm a suspected diagnosis but must not delay clinical management (p.3690) ECG to detect QT prolongation (e.g. methadone), which can cause sudden death (p.3733) Chest imaging for noncardiogenic pulmonary edema / ARDS, a recognized complication of opioid poisoning (p.3749) In IV users, screen for blood-borne infection (hepatitis B, HIV) and bacterial complications (meningitis, osteomyelitis, abscesses, endocarditis) (p.3733) Hypoglycemia (responds to dextrose, mimics opioid coma) (p.3748) Benzodiazepine intoxication (responds to flumazenil) (p.3748) Opioids act mainly through the mu receptor (also kappa, delta, nociceptin/orphanin), all G protein-coupled, inhibiting the cAMP system and opening GIRK potassium channels to hyperpolarize and silence neurons. Life-threatening respiratory depression results from opioid-induced insensitivity of brainstem (medullary) respiratory neurons to rising carbon dioxide; analgesia and respiratory depression are mediated by receptors in the periaqueductal grey and medulla oblongata. Untreated, progression goes to respiratory and then cardiovascular collapse and death (p.3733, p.3690).

Osteoarthritis — Inflammatory arthritis (suggested by prolonged morning stiffness and involvement of many joints) Bursitis (anserine bursitis medial/distal to the knee; trochanteric bursitis lateral to the hip) Iliotibial band syndrome Internal derangement of the knee (anterior cruciate ligament or meniscal tear), especially after acute injury Septic arthritis (consider when synovial fluid white count is elevated/inflammatory) No blood tests are routinely indicated unless symptoms or signs suggest inflammatory arthritis (Harrison 22e p.2953). Synovial fluid examination is often more helpful diagnostically than x-ray; a white count >1000/uL suggests inflammatory arthritis, gout, or pseudogout, the latter two confirmed by crystals (Harrison 22e p.2953). Radiographs are not routinely indicated; order only when pain and findings are atypical of OA or when pain persists after effective treatment. Imaging findings correlate poorly with pain, and x-rays may be normal in early disease (insensitive to cartilage loss) (Harrison 22e p.2953). MRI is not indicated in the diagnostic workup; meniscal tears and cartilage/bone lesions are common both in OA and in older persons without joint pain, and MRI findings rarely warrant a change in therapy (Harrison 22e p.2953). Gout and pseudogout (crystal arthritis; suggested by synovial fluid white count >1000/uL with identifiable crystals) Rheumatoid arthritis and other inflammatory arthritides

Parvovirus Infections — Other viral exanthems (B19V rash is difficult to distinguish clinically; laboratory confirmation is advised when a definite diagnosis is needed, such as in pregnancy) Rheumatoid arthritis (B19V polyarthropathy can mimic it, and rheumatoid factor may be present) Other causes of nonimmune hydrops fetalis Other causes of transient aplastic crisis or red cell aplasia Other respiratory viral infections (for HBoV1, which presents like other viral RTIs with fever, cough, wheezing) Co-infection with Plasmodium has been suggested to contribute to severe anemia in young children with malaria B19V IgM by indirect enzyme immunoassay - detectable at the time of rash in erythema infectiosum and by the third day of TAC; may persist about 3 months or longer B19V IgG - detectable by the seventh day of illness and persists for life, marking immunity; seroconversion or a fourfold or greater rise on paired sera taken 2 weeks apart is diagnostic of acute infection IgG avidity testing and epitope-type-specific (ETS) EIA to distinguish acute from past infection B19V DNA by PCR in serum (or amniotic fluid), with quantitative PCR preferred because low-level DNA can persist for months to years even in healthy people Bone marrow examination showing giant pronormoblasts and absent/scant erythroid precursors in TAC or PRCA In suspected fetal infection: maternal serology in exposed seronegative mothers, with regular monitoring if positive, and PCR of amniotic fluid or tissue

Pathobiology of Neurologic Diseases — Alzheimer's disease and other amyloid/tau dementias Parkinson's disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, and multiple-system atrophy (alpha-synucleinopathies) Frontotemporal degeneration (tau, TDP-43, FUS; GRN and C9orf72) Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (SOD1, TDP-43, FUS, C9orf72) Huntington's disease and other polyglutamine cerebellar degenerations Multiple sclerosis and autoimmune/neuroinflammatory demyelination Prion diseases (CJD, kuru, GSS, fatal insomnia) Neurodevelopmental disorders (primary microcephaly, lissencephaly/Miller-Dieker, fragile X, Rett, Timothy syndrome) Slow-virus paradigm historically invoked for kuru, CJD, and scrapie, later supplanted by the nucleic-acid-free prion hypothesis Congenital Zika virus syndrome producing microcephaly via direct infection of neural progenitor cells Microbiome/bacterial-protein seeding hypotheses (e.g., E. coli Curli templating alpha-synuclein) blurring infective versus degenerative boundaries Genetic testing for disease-causing/modifying mutations (APP, MAPT, SNCA, LRRK2, parkin, PINK1, DJ-1, GBA, SOD1, TDP-43, FUS, C9orf72, GRN, PRNP, VPS35, FMR1, MECP2, CACNA1C) Neuropathologic/immunostaining characterization of aggregates (Abeta plaques, neurofibrillary tau tangles, Lewy bodies, glial cytoplasmic inclusions, ubiquitinated TDP-43 inclusions) Patient-derived iPSC lines and cerebral organoids for disease modeling and high-throughput compound screening

Pathogenesis, Diagnosis, and Treatment of Fungal Infections — Distinguishing true invasive fungal infection from colonization or laboratory contamination when fungi are recovered from culture (Harrison 22e p.1690) Chronic cavitary pulmonary mycosis versus cavitary tuberculosis (Harrison 22e p.1690) Allergic bronchopulmonary aspergillosis versus invasive pulmonary aspergillosis in differing host settings (Harrison 22e p.1688) Mycobacterial infection (notably tuberculosis), which shares granulomatous histology and intramacrophagic survival with endemic dimorphic fungi (Harrison 22e p.1689) Salmonellosis and other intramacrophagic pathogens that exploit the same IL-12/IFN-gamma defects as intramacrophagic fungi (Harrison 22e p.1689) Histopathology with PAS and GMS stains, plus H&E to assess granuloma, angioinvasion, and necrosis (Harrison 22e p.1690) Calcofluor white staining with fluorescence microscopy for fungi in fluid specimens (Harrison 22e p.1690) Lysis-centrifugation blood culture to increase sensitivity for Candida and less common fungi such as Histoplasma (Harrison 22e p.1690) MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry for detection and speciation of cultured fungi (Harrison 22e pp.1690-1691) Antigen and serologic assays: cryptococcal polysaccharide antigen, Histoplasma antigen, Coccidioides antibody, galactomannan (BAL preferred), and serum beta-D-glucan (Harrison 22e p.1691) T2 magnetic resonance assay for Candida in whole blood (Harrison 22e p.1691)

Pulmonary embolism — Congestive heart failure Pericarditis Pleurisy / costochondritis / musculoskeletal chest discomfort Anxiety Vasovagal syncope Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH) for persistent exertional breathlessness Pneumonia Cellulitis (mimics DVT; fever and chills favor cellulitis over DVT) Sepsis (elevates D-dimer and can confound) Age-adjusted D-dimer (age x 10 ng/mL upper limit) for patients >50 years with low/intermediate clinical probability of PE; does not apply to suspected acute DVT (p.2159-2160) RV-to-LV diameter ratio >1 on chest CT as a marker of RV enlargement (p.2161) Wells point-score clinical decision rule to stratify pretest probability (validated in ambulatory, not hospitalized, patients); low/low-to-moderate probability with normal D-dimer can avoid imaging (p.2159) BNP / NT-proBNP as markers of RV myocardial stretch (p.2160) ECG looking for S1Q3T3 (specific but insensitive) and T-wave inversion in V1-V4 from RV strain (p.2160) Chest x-ray signs: focal oligemia (Westermark's sign), peripheral pleural-based density (Hampton's hump, from infarction), enlarged right descending pulmonary artery (Palla's sign); often normal (p.2160) Echocardiography to assess RV dysfunction and to detect mimics (MI, tamponade, aortic dissection); usually normal in PE so not a reliable rule-out (p.2161) Compression venous ultrasonography for DVT (loss of vein compressibility) (p.2160)

Peptic ulcer disease / upper GI bleed — Functional (non-ulcer/essential) dyspepsia - the commonest cause of upper abdominal discomfort, subdivided into postprandial distress syndrome and epigastric pain syndrome; up to ~80% of patients evaluated for dyspepsia have a negative work-up (p.2523). Proximal gastrointestinal tumours (p.2523). Gastro-oesophageal reflux disease (p.2523). Pancreaticobiliary disease - biliary colic, chronic pancreatitis (p.2523). Gastroduodenal Crohn's disease (p.2523). Vascular (mesenteric/ischaemic) disease presenting as upper abdominal pain (p.2523). Cytomegalovirus-related ulceration (a non-Hp, non-NSAID ulcer cause) (p.2523). Herpes simplex virus-related ulceration (p.2523). Helicobacter heilmannii infection (p.2523). Endoscopy is the most sensitive and specific test, allowing direct visualisation, biopsy to exclude malignancy (GU) and to test for H. pylori, and identification of a bleeding source (p.2523). Barium studies of the upper GI tract can document an ulcer but are now rarely used as a first test (p.2523). Biopsy urease tests (e.g. CLOtest, PyloriTek, Hpfast, Pronto Dry) with sensitivity/specificity >90-95% for H. pylori (p.2523). Non-invasive H. pylori tests - serology, 13C-urea breath test, and monoclonal stool antigen test; the urea breath test or monoclonal stool antigen test is preferred to document eradication, performed off antisecretory drugs for at least 7 days (serology is not useful for confirming eradication) (pp.2523, 2531).

Peptic Ulcer Disease and Related Disorders — Functional (non-ulcer/essential) dyspepsia, including postprandial distress syndrome and epigastric pain syndrome (commonest cause of upper abdominal discomfort) Gastroesophageal reflux disease Proximal gastrointestinal tumors / gastric malignancy Pancreaticobiliary disease (biliary colic, chronic pancreatitis) Gastroduodenal Crohn's disease Mesenteric vascular disease Zollinger-Ellison syndrome (gastrinoma) Cytomegalovirus gastritis/ulceration (immunocompromised hosts) Herpes simplex virus gastritis/ulceration Helicobacter heilmannii infection Phlegmonous (bacterial) gastritis Infectious causes of large gastric folds mimicking Menetrier's disease (CMV, histoplasmosis, syphilis, tuberculosis) Upper endoscopy with biopsy (most sensitive/specific; biopsy gastric ulcers to exclude malignancy) H. pylori testing: rapid urease biopsy test, histology, culture (allows susceptibility testing) Noninvasive H. pylori tests: 13C-urea breath test and stool monoclonal antigen test (both >95% sensitivity/specificity); serology cannot distinguish active from prior infection Fasting serum gastrin (two occasions) when ZES is suspected Secretin stimulation test (rise >=120 pg/mL at 15 min) and gastric pH/acid analysis for gastrinoma Serum calcium, parathyroid hormone, prolactin, and pancreatic polypeptide to screen for MEN 1 in gastrinoma patients Tumor localization imaging and somatostatin-receptor-based studies for gastrinoma

Periarticular Disorders of the Extremities — Glenohumeral osteoarthritis Rheumatoid arthritis Gout and crystal arthropathy Spondyloarthritis Cervical radiculopathy referring to the shoulder Acromioclavicular joint pathology Intraarticular knee pathology (osteoarthritis, meniscal injury) versus periarticular knee pain Septic bursitis (e.g., olecranon or prepatellar) Infectious tenosynovitis Septic arthritis presenting as periarticular pain and swelling History and directed physical examination (often sufficient for diagnosis) Provocative maneuvers (painful abduction arc, drop-arm test, Finkelstein test, Yergason's test) Bursal aspiration with Gram stain, culture, and crystal analysis when infection or gout is suspected Ultrasound (for bursitis, tendinitis, rotator cuff tears, calcific deposits, plantar fascia thickening, and guided injection) Plain radiographs (may show tendon calcification or incidental heel spurs) MRI (sensitive for rotator cuff tears, tendon integrity, and plantar fasciitis when diagnosis is unclear) Gouty bursitis/tendinitis (urate deposition) Calcium pyrophosphate or apatite crystal deposition Rheumatoid or inflammatory arthritis involving periarticular structures Referred pain from intraarticular degenerative joint disease These are disorders of the soft tissues surrounding joints rather than the synovial joint itself. Bursitis is synovial inflammation of a bursa from frictional overuse, trauma, systemic inflammatory/crystal disease, or infection. Tendinopathies (rotator cuff, bicipital, patellar, epicondylar, De Quervain's) result from mechanical impingement and repetitive resisted loading producing microtears, inflammation, and degeneration at tendon insertions; the supraspinatus is uniquely vulnerable to impingement beneath the acromion. Pericardial Disease — Acute myocardial infarction (common confusion with acute pericarditis; in pericarditis ST elevations are upwardly concave, biomarker elevations are modest, and pain may precede or coincide with fever) (Harrison 22e p.2079, p.2083) Restrictive cardiomyopathy (shares restriction of ventricular filling; must be distinguished from constrictive pericarditis because the latter is surgically correctable) (Harrison 22e p.2084) Right ventricular infarction (may mimic tamponade with hypotension, elevated JVP, slow y descent, occasional paradoxical pulse) (Harrison 22e p.2082) Cor pulmonale (systemic venous hypertension and paradoxical pulse, but Kussmaul's sign is negative and advanced parenchymal lung disease is apparent) (Harrison 22e p.2084) Tricuspid stenosis (congestive hepatomegaly, splenomegaly, ascites, venous distention, but characteristic murmur present) (Harrison 22e p.2084) Hepatic cirrhosis (constrictive pericarditis with hepatomegaly, jaundice, and intractable ascites may be mistaken for cirrhosis; inspection of distended neck veins avoids the error) (Harrison 22e p.2084) Viral pericarditis (coxsackievirus A and B, echovirus, influenza, mumps, herpes simplex, varicella-zoster, adenovirus, cytomegalovirus, HIV, post-acute COVID, mpox) (Harrison 22e p.2079, p.2082) Tuberculous pericarditis (effusion, constriction, or effusive-constrictive disease; suggested by high adenosine deaminase or M. tuberculosis DNA by PCR, often requiring pericardial tissue) (Harrison 22e p.2082, p.2084)

Acute pericarditis — Acute myocardial ischaemia / STEMI Acute aortic syndrome (dissection) Pulmonary embolism Pleuritis / pneumonia Musculoskeletal chest wall pain (e.g. costochondritis) Gastro-oesophageal reflux / oesophageal disease Herpes zoster Acute myocarditis (often viral; chest discomfort and ST/T-wave changes can overlap) Pneumonia / pleuritis 12-lead ECG looking for diffuse ST-segment elevation with PR-segment depression (p.149) Chest radiograph (pericardial calcification suggests chronic pericarditis; usually unremarkable in acute disease) (p.150) Echocardiography to detect effusion (may be normal in 34-50% of acute cases) (p.90) Measurement of pulsus paradoxus when tamponade is suspected (p.312) Acute coronary syndrome / STEMI (diffuse ST elevation of pericarditis can be mistaken for infarction) Takotsubo (stress) cardiomyopathy (ST elevation and biomarker rise mimicking MI) Aortic dissection extending into the pericardium Pulmonary embolism Inflammation of the pericardium from infectious or noninfectious causes. Because the visceral and most of the parietal pericardium are insensitive to pain, the discomfort is attributed mainly to associated pleural inflammation, producing pleuritic, position-dependent pain that, via overlapping phrenic and C3-C5 somatic innervation, may be referred to the shoulder, neck, and trapezius ridge (p.147, p.149). Diagnosis rests on the combination of characteristic chest pain, a pericardial friction rub, and characteristic ECG changes; echocardiography can be normal in roughly a third to half of cases, so a normal echo does not exclude pericarditis (p.90).

Peripheral Neuropathy — Inflammatory demyelinating polyneuropathy - Guillain-Barre syndrome (acute) and CIDP (chronic/relapsing) (Pattern 1) (Harrison 22e p.3595) Cryptogenic/idiopathic sensory polyneuropathy (CSPN) - no etiology found in about half of patients despite extensive evaluation (Harrison 22e p.3595) Diabetes mellitus and other metabolic neuropathies (DSPN, autonomic, radiculoplexus/Bruns-Garland, mononeuropathies) (Harrison 22e p.3604) Hereditary neuropathies - Charcot-Marie-Tooth, HSAN, familial amyloid polyneuropathy, SORD neuropathy (Harrison 22e p.3596) Vasculitic neuropathy presenting as mononeuropathy multiplex (Pattern 3) (Harrison 22e p.3596) Uremic neuropathy in renal failure (~60% of patients) (Harrison 22e p.3605) Nutritional/toxic neuropathies (B12, thiamine, alcohol, drugs, chemotherapy, heavy metals) (Harrison 22e p.3611) Sensory neuronopathy/ganglionopathy - paraneoplastic (anti-Hu), Sjogren's syndrome, CANVAS, cisplatin, vitamin B6 toxicity (Pattern 9) (Harrison 22e p.3596) Connective tissue/autoimmune disease - rheumatoid arthritis, SLE, scleroderma, sarcoidosis (Harrison 22e p.3605) HIV infection - distal symmetric polyneuropathy, AIDP/CIDP, progressive polyradiculopathy, multiple mononeuropathies, sensory ganglionopathy (Harrison 22e p.3606) Leprosy (Mycobacterium leprae) - most common cause of peripheral neuropathy in Southeast Asia, Africa, and South America; mononeuropathies or symmetric sensorimotor polyneuropathy (Harrison 22e p.3606)

Pertussis (Whooping Cough) — Bordetella parapertussis (causes a similar but typically milder illness; does not express pertussis toxin gene) (p.1276). Bordetella holmesii (found in up to 20% of patients with a pertussis-like syndrome using improved PCR) (p.1276). Mycoplasma pneumoniae (p.1280). Chlamydia pneumoniae (p.1280). Adenovirus (p.1280). Influenza virus and other respiratory viruses (p.1280). Respiratory syncytial virus and rhinovirus -- isolated from patients with clinical pertussis but probably represent co-infection, particularly in children under 1 year (p.1280). Bordetella parapertussis infection (p.1280) Bordetella holmesii infection (p.1276) Mycoplasma pneumoniae infection (p.1280) Chlamydia pneumoniae infection (p.1280) Adenovirus, influenza, and other respiratory viral infections (p.1280) Nasopharyngeal culture (Bordet-Gengou or Regan-Lowe medium) -- gold standard owing to 100% specificity; cultures become positive by day 5 of incubation (p.1279). PCR / multitarget real-time PCR -- has replaced culture in most laboratories due to greater sensitivity and faster (hours) results; differentiates B. pertussis, B. parapertussis, and B. holmesii (p.1279). Nasopharyngeal aspiration is the best specimen; B. pertussis is highly sensitive to drying so specimens must be inoculated without delay or placed in transport medium (p.1279). Complete blood count for lymphocytosis (informative in young children, not in adolescents/adults) (p.1279).

Phaeochromocytoma crisis — Cushing's syndrome and other secondary causes of hypertension (more common than pheochromocytoma, so the classic triad is frequently misleading) (p.2140). Thyrotoxicosis / hyperthyroidism (overlapping palpitations, sweating, tremor; an endocrine cause of palpitations) (palpitations chapter). Panic / anxiety disorder and somatization (episodic palpitations, sweating, sense of doom mimicking paroxysms) (palpitations chapter). Stimulant toxicity — cocaine, amphetamines and related catecholaminergic drugs (produce hypertension, tachyarrhythmia, microvascular ischaemia resembling pheochromocytoma) (cardiomyopathy chapter). Systemic mastocytosis / mast-cell activation (flushing, palpitations, hypotensive episodes) (mastocytosis chapter). Blood and 24-hour urinary catecholamine measurement (in addition to plasma/urine metanephrines) (p.2140). Functional/positron emission tomography (PET) imaging in addition to CT/MRI of the abdomen for localisation (p.2140). Nuclear localisation with 131-I-metaiodobenzylguanidine (MIBG) scanning, e.g. for extra-adrenal/cardiac paraganglioma (cardiac-tumour chapter). Genetic evaluation when a hereditary predisposition is suspected (MEN2/RET, von Hippel-Lindau, neurofibromatosis type 1, hereditary paraganglioma syndromes) (p.2140). Systemic mastocytosis — flushing and palpitation attacks; urinary metanephrines help exclude pheochromocytoma when evaluating mast-cell symptoms (mastocytosis chapter).

Pheochromocytoma — Essential hypertension Anxiety/panic attacks (may be mistaken for psychiatric illness) Cocaine or amphetamine use Mastocytosis or carcinoid syndrome (usually without hypertension) Intracranial lesions Clonidine withdrawal Autonomic epilepsy Factitious crises (sympathomimetic amine use) For an asymptomatic adrenal mass: nonfunctioning adrenal adenoma, aldosteronoma, cortisol-producing adenoma (Cushing's syndrome) 24-hour urinary fractionated metanephrines and catecholamines (high sensitivity for initial screening) Plasma free metanephrines (most sensitive, least stress-confounded) Contrast CT or T2-weighted MRI with gadolinium for localization (MRI somewhat better for extra-adrenal disease) Functional imaging: 68Ga-DOTATATE PET/CT and 18F-DOPA PET/CT (very high sensitivity and specificity, >95%) 123I/131I-MIBG scintigraphy and 18F-FDG PET, useful in hereditary and metastatic disease Immunohistochemistry (chromogranin, synaptophysin, S-100, SDHB) on resected tissue Universal germline genetic panel testing Postoperative documentation of catecholamine normalization and ACTH stimulation test after bilateral cortex-sparing surgery Essential hypertension with adrenergic features Panic disorder / anxiety attacks Sympathomimetic drug effect (cocaine, amphetamines) Carcinoid syndrome and systemic mastocytosis Clonidine or other antihypertensive withdrawal PPGLs are well-vascularized neuroendocrine tumors derived from chromaffin cells of the sympathetic and parasympathetic paraganglial system. They synthesize and store catecholamines (norepinephrine, epinephrine, dopamine), and tumoral release drives the clinical syndrome; the name pheochromocytoma reflects the dark staining produced by chromaffin oxidation of catecholamines.
