Physical Examination of the Cardiovascular System — Aortic stenosis (pulsus parvus et tardus, sustained apex, soft A2) Aortic regurgitation (water-hammer pulse, wide pulse pressure, low diastolic pressure) Tricuspid regurgitation (prominent v wave, systolic hepatic pulsations) Constrictive pericarditis (Kussmaul's sign, prominent rapid y descent, pericardial knock) Pericardial tamponade (pulsus paradoxus, blunted y descent) Atrial septal defect (fixed split S2) Hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy (bisferiens pulse, triple apical cadence) Mitral valve prolapse (nonejection click and dynamic murmur) Aortic coarctation / dissection (interarm or arm-leg blood pressure differential, femoral delay) Infective endocarditis presenting with peripheral stigmata (Janeway lesions, Osler's nodes, splinter hemorrhages, splenomegaly, clubbing, Roth-type funduscopic findings) Noninvasive imaging (echocardiography, including hand-held ultrasound) to confirm structural cardiac disease Screening abdominal ultrasound when an abdominal aortic aneurysm is suspected by palpation 24-hour ambulatory blood pressure monitoring to detect white coat and masked hypertension Ankle-brachial index measurement for peripheral arterial disease and cardiovascular risk Funduscopic examination of the microvasculature in atherosclerosis, hypertension, diabetes, suspected endocarditis, and acute visual change Allen's test before radial artery instrumentation Pulse oximetry comparing finger and toe oxygen saturation for lower extremity peripheral arterial disease

Physiologic and Nonphysiologic Sinus Rhythm — Focal atrial tachycardia arising near the sinus node (abrupt onset/offset favors AT) Premature atrial contractions causing rhythm irregularity (varying P-wave morphology) Inappropriate sinus tachycardia versus appropriate physiologic sinus tachycardia Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome Anxiety or panic disorder presenting with sinus tachycardia Fever or systemic infection driving appropriate (physiologic) sinus tachycardia Postviral autonomic dysfunction producing a POTS-like picture, including post-COVID-19 (long COVID) 12-lead ECG to confirm sinus P-wave morphology and axis Ambulatory / outpatient telemetry monitoring to distinguish gradual sinus tachycardia from paroxysmal atrial tachycardia Thyroid function testing to exclude hyperthyroidism as a reversible cause Hemoglobin / evaluation for anemia Orthostatic (supine-to-standing) heart rate and blood pressure assessment when POTS is suspected Invasive electrophysiology study in selected cases where the ECG distinction remains unclear Anemia Hyperthyroidism and other thyroid dysfunction Dehydration / volume depletion Pulmonary embolism Pheochromocytoma Decompensated heart failure or valvular disease Anxiety / panic attack Stimulant or drug effect (caffeine, sympathomimetics, cocaine, amphetamines, beta-blocker withdrawal) Sinus rhythm originates from spontaneous depolarization of pacemaker cells in the sinus node at the right atrium-SVC junction within the crista terminalis. Heart rate is modulated by the autonomic balance between sympathetic input (which accelerates and shifts the activation focus) and parasympathetic (vagal) input (which slows the node). Pituitary Tumor Syndromes — Craniopharyngioma (suprasellar cystic, often calcified, Rathke's pouch origin; BRAF V600E in papillary type) Lymphocytic hypophysitis Langerhans cell histiocytosis / Histiocytosis X Empty sella Arachnoid cyst Macroprolactinemia (biologically inactive aggregated PRL causing falsely high PRL) Meningioma (enhancing, may show bony hyperostosis/calcification) Rathke's cleft cyst Sellar/clival chordoma Hypothalamic hamartoma or gangliocytoma (may secrete GnRH/GHRH/CRH) Hypothalamic and optic gliomas Parasellar germ cell tumors (germinoma, dysgerminoma, teratoma, choriocarcinoma) Pituitary metastases (esp. breast and lung; favor posterior pituitary) Lymphoma, leukemia, plasmacytoma involving the sella Sagittal and coronal T1-weighted MRI before and after gadolinium (adenomas are hypodense on T1, brighter on T2); CT reserved for bony erosion or calcification Immunohistochemistry for hormones and cell-specific transcription factors on resected tissue for histologic confirmation Formal perimetric visual field testing for any chiasm-impinging mass Baseline pituitary hormonal screen: prolactin, IGF-1, 24-h urinary free cortisol and/or overnight 1-mg dexamethasone suppression, alpha-subunit/FSH/LH, and thyroid function tests Acromegaly: IGF-1 (age/sex matched) and oral glucose tolerance test with GH at 0/30/60 min (failure to suppress confirms diagnosis) Hyperprolactinemia: fasting morning PRL with sample dilution when very high (assay 'hook' artifact) and exclusion of macroprolactin

Plague — Acute focal lymphadenopathy of other etiologies (for bubonic plague): streptococcal or staphylococcal infection, tularemia, cat-scratch disease, tick typhus, infectious mononucleosis, lymphatic filariasis (p.1343). Tuberculosis (in differential of fever and hemoptysis in plague-endemic areas, as a small-airborne-particle-transmitted infection) (p.1347). Tonsillitis with peritonsillar abscess (resembles plague pharyngitis) (p.1344). Tularemia (Francisella tularensis) (p.1343) Cat-scratch disease (Bartonella henselae) (p.1343) Tick typhus (rickettsial) (p.1343) Infectious mononucleosis (p.1343) Lymphatic filariasis (p.1343) Streptococcal or staphylococcal lymphadenitis (p.1343) Tuberculosis (fever and hemoptysis differential) (p.1347) Bubo aspirate (bubonic), bronchoalveolar lavage fluid or sputum (pneumonic), and blood (septicemic) are the appropriate specimens; culture of postmortem organ biopsy can also be diagnostic. Transport medium such as Cary-Blair preserves viability (p.1345). Direct microscopy: Gram-negative coccobacilli with characteristic bipolar 'closed safety pin' appearance on Wayson or Wright-Giemsa stain; bipolar bacilli may be visible on direct blood smear in septicemic plague, indicating very high circulating bacterial numbers and a poor prognosis (p.1345). Culture on nutrient-rich media (sheep blood agar, brain-heart infusion broth) and selective agar (MacConkey, EMB, or Yersinia-specific CIN agar); optimal growth at <37 degC (25-29 degC). Y. pestis is oxidase-negative, catalase-positive, urease-negative, indole-negative, lactose-negative, and nonmotile (distinguishing it from other Yersinia species) (p.1345).

Plasma Cell Disorders (MGUS, Waldenström) — Monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance (MGUS) AL (primary) amyloidosis Heavy chain diseases (gamma/Franklin's, alpha/Seligmann's and IPSID, mu) Marginal zone lymphoma and CLL with plasmacytic differentiation Smoldering (asymptomatic) multiple myeloma Symptomatic multiple myeloma (CRAB / myeloma-defining events) Solitary plasmacytoma of bone or soft tissue Nonsecretory myeloma Plasma cell leukemia (>2000 circulating plasma cells/uL) Waldenström's macroglobulinemia IgM myeloma (lytic lesions, CD138+ plasma cells, t(11;14)) POEMS syndrome Serum protein electrophoresis (SPEP) for M-protein quantitation Tissue biopsy with Congo red staining and mass spectrometry-based typing when amyloidosis is suspected (SPEP/UPEP alone are inadequate screens for AL) Serum and urine immunofixation electrophoresis (SIFE/UIFE) to confirm monoclonality and identify heavy/light chain type Urine protein electrophoresis (UPEP) / 24-h urine for Bence Jones (free light chain) protein Serum free light chain assay with kappa/lambda ratio (essential to assess ratio, not just absolute level, since renal insufficiency nonspecifically raises both) Bone marrow biopsy/aspirate for clonal plasma cell percentage and CD138+ / kappa or lambda light chain restriction by flow cytometry, immunohistochemistry, or in situ hybridization MYD88 (L265P) and CXCR4 mutation testing to discriminate WM from MZL, IgM myeloma, and CLL

Platelet Disorders (Thrombocytopenia) — Pseudothrombocytopenia (in vitro EDTA-induced platelet clumping) Inherited thrombocytopenia (e.g., MYH9-related autosomal dominant macrothrombocytopenia: May-Hegglin anomaly, Sebastian, Epstein, Fechtner syndromes) Evans syndrome (combined autoimmune hemolytic anemia with ITP) Decreased production (bone marrow disorders, myelodysplasia, chemotherapy-induced marrow suppression) Splenic sequestration / hypersplenism Drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia (HIT/HITT) Immune thrombocytopenic purpura (ITP) Thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP) Hemolytic-uremic syndrome (HUS) including atypical HUS Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC) Viral and bacterial infections causing thrombocytopenia (most common noniatrogenic cause) Systemic gram-negative bacterial infection with DIC COVID-19-associated thrombocytopenia/DIC Infectious mononucleosis and early HIV (immune-mediated thrombocytopenia) Late HIV with pancytopenia and dysplastic platelet production Hepatitis C and HIV as secondary causes of ITP Escherichia coli O157:H7 (diarrhea-associated HUS) Helicobacter pylori (uncertain, geographically variable association with ITP) Peripheral blood smear review (rule out clumping; assess RBC morphology and platelet size) PT and aPTT (normal in TTP/HUS; elevated in DIC) Direct antiglobulin (Coombs) test if anemia present (rule out Evans syndrome) Secondary ITP workup: HIV, hepatitis C, SLE serology, serum protein electrophoresis, immunoglobulin levels, IgA deficiency / monoclonal gammopathy testing, H. pylori

Pleural effusion — Congestive heart failure (typically bilateral transudative effusions) (Harrison 22e p.314) Cirrhosis / hepatic hydrothorax (often right-sided) (Harrison 22e p.366, p.373) Nephrotic syndrome and other hypoalbuminemic states (Harrison 22e p.422) Parapneumonic effusion / empyema complicating pneumonia (Harrison 22e p.1235) Malignant effusion (e.g., lung cancer, metastatic disease) (Harrison 22e p.662) Tuberculous pleurisy (Harrison 22e p.1430) Pulmonary embolism (Harrison 22e p.314) Tuberculous pleural effusion — straw-colored (sometimes hemorrhagic) lymphocyte-predominant exudate that can mimic a parapneumonic or malignant effusion (Harrison 22e p.1430). Tuberculous empyema, usually from rupture of a cavity into the pleural space, sometimes with a bronchopleural fistula and air in the pleural space (Harrison 22e p.1431). Spontaneous bacterial empyema complicating hepatic hydrothorax in cirrhosis (Harrison 22e p.373). Diagnostic thoracentesis to determine whether the fluid is a transudate or an exudate and to identify the underlying cause (Harrison 22e p.1430). Pleural fluid pH — a value of ≤7.1 in a parapneumonic setting indicates empyema requiring drainage (Harrison 22e p.1235). Pleural fluid protein, glucose, and cell count/differential; in TB the fluid is an exudate with protein >50% of serum (often ~4-6 g/dL), normal-to-low glucose, pH ~7.3 (occasionally <7.2), and 500-6000 WBC/uL, with neutrophils early and lymphocyte predominance later (Harrison 22e p.1430).

Polymyalgia rheumatica — Seronegative rheumatoid arthritis in the elderly, which can be difficult to distinguish from PMR; RA predominantly affects wrists/hands and ankles/feet at onset whereas PMR is girdle-predominant (p.2920). Remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema (RS3PE) — prominent distal limb pitting edema, prompt response to low-dose prednisone (p.2920). Other inflammatory arthropathies / seronegative RA in patients who develop a worsening pattern of peripheral arthritis (p.2945). Fibromyalgia — listed among conditions confused with PMR; PMR appears in the fibromyalgia differential (p.2965). Osteoarthritis and other noninflammatory nonarticular conditions (bursitis, tendinitis) (p.2938-2939). Rheumatoid factor and anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide (anti-CCP) should be negative; positive results point toward seronegative-RA spectrum or other inflammatory arthropathy (p.2946). Serum creatine kinase is NOT elevated in PMR; elevation should prompt consideration of a myopathic process (p.2946). Normochromic or slightly hypochromic anemia and elevated alkaline phosphatase (liver function abnormalities) may accompany the inflammatory state in the GCA/PMR spectrum (p.2945). If GCA is suspected, evaluate temporal arteries (biopsy, or ultrasonography showing a noncompressible 'halo' sign) and consider vascular imaging (MR/CT, PET investigational) for large-vessel disease; therapy should not be delayed pending these studies (p.2945-2946).

Prion Diseases (CJD) — Alzheimer's disease (can occasionally present as rapidly progressive dementia) Corticobasal degeneration (CBD) - rapid degenerative dementia with prominent movement abnormalities, more likely mistaken for CJD Dementia with Lewy bodies (DLB) - rapid degenerative dementia with prominent movement abnormalities, more likely mistaken for CJD Other rapidly progressive dementias Viral encephalitides Bacterial encephalitides Other CNS infections causing rapidly progressive dementia MRI diffusion-weighted imaging - restricted diffusion in cortical ribbon and/or basal ganglia (cortical ribboning); basal ganglia or thalamus hyperintensity on diffusion/FLAIR EEG - periodic complexes (repetitive bursts of diffuse high-amplitude sharp waves) Lumbar puncture/CSF - to exclude CNS infection or inflammation among rapidly progressive dementia mimics MRI/neuroimaging to exclude treatable structural causes (neoplasm, subdural hematoma, NPH) Hashimoto's encephalopathy CNS vasculitis CNS lymphoma Paraneoplastic/autoimmune syndromes (autoimmune encephalitis) Prolonged focal or generalized seizures (can rarely produce a similar imaging appearance) Prion diseases are caused by prions, host-encoded proteins (the prion protein) that adopt an alternative, abnormal conformation (misfolded PrPSc) which undergoes self-propagation. PrPSc imposes its conformation on the normal precursor protein, which in turn becomes self-templating, producing faithful copies; the misfolded protein is enriched for beta-sheet and assembles into amyloid fibrils. The amyloid plaques in kuru and CJD are filled with PrPSc prions assembled into fibrils. CJD is one of the major degenerative dementias characterized by abnormal aggregation of a specific protein (misfolded prion protein, PrPSc). Familial CJ

Pulmonic Valve Disease — Aortic regurgitation (the Graham Steell murmur of PR can mimic the AR murmur) Other causes of a midsystolic murmur such as aortic stenosis, hypertrophic obstructive physiology, or an atrial septal defect with enhanced pulmonic flow Pulmonary hypertension as the dominant clinical problem rather than the valve lesion itself Infective endocarditis of the pulmonic valve (an etiology of both PS from bulky vegetations and PR) ECG: right axis deviation, RV hypertrophy, and right atrial enlargement in severe PS; RVH/RA enlargement may appear in PR depending on etiology and severity Chest x-ray: poststenotic dilation of the main pulmonary artery on the frontal view, retrosternal airspace filling from RV enlargement on the lateral view, and apex lifted off the left hemidiaphragm in some patients Transthoracic echocardiography (Doppler): definitive diagnosis in most cases, with jet velocity, gradient, RV function, pulmonary artery pressures (which should be low in PS), and associated lesions; RV systolic pressure estimated from the tricuspid regurgitant jet Transesophageal echocardiography: better delineation of the RV outflow tract and infundibular hypertrophy when needed Cardiac MR: greater anatomic detail and precise RV volume/function assessment, especially in repaired congenital heart disease Cardiac catheterization: not routinely required; if performed in PS, pressures are taken just below and above the valve with attention to a possible dynamic gradient

Rabies — Herpes simplex encephalitis Arboviral encephalitis (e.g., West Nile) Anti-NMDA receptor and other autoimmune encephalitides Postinfectious (immune-mediated) encephalomyelitis (following influenza, measles, mumps, or neural-tissue rabies vaccine) Guillain-Barre syndrome (mimicked by paralytic rabies) Rabies hysteria / somatic symptom disorder (psychological response to fear of rabies) Misdiagnosis as a primary psychiatric disorder Herpes simplex encephalitis Arboviral (e.g., West Nile) encephalitis Postinfectious encephalomyelitis after influenza, measles, or mumps Rabies virus-specific serum neutralizing antibodies (diagnostic in a previously unimmunized patient; may not develop until late and some patients die without them) Rabies virus-specific neutralizing antibodies in CSF (suggest rabies encephalitis regardless of immunization status) RT-PCR for rabies virus RNA (highly sensitive/specific; saliva, skin biopsy, CSF [less sensitive], brain tissue; genetic sequencing can identify the variant/source) Direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) testing for rabies virus antigen (skin biopsy and brain tissue; in skin, antigen detected in cutaneous nerves at the base of hair follicles) Skin biopsy from hairy skin at the nape of the neck CSF examination (typically mild mononuclear pleocytosis with mildly elevated protein) MRI brain (variable, nonspecific brainstem/gray-matter signal abnormalities); CT usually normal; EEG nonspecific

Most cases are sporadic, but familial forms exist. Clear cell RCC (the predominant subtype) is characterized by loss of chromosome 3p as the earliest event, causing loss of heterozygosity for 3p genes including VHL, PBRM1, BAP1, and SETD2. VHL encodes a tumor-suppressor protein that regulates transcription of VEGF and other effectors via ubiquitination of hypoxia-inducible factors (HIF); VHL inactivation upregulates VEGF signaling, promoting tumor angiogenesis and growth and rendering clear cell RCC susceptible to antiangiogenic therapy. Renal / ureteric colic — Ruptured/impending-rupture abdominal aortic aneurysm — abdominal pain radiating to the flank, sacral region, or genitalia should always raise suspicion of a leaking AAA; pain may precede rupture by days (p.154). Acute mesenteric ischemia (pain out of proportion to exam in a vascular patient) (p.154). Other causes of acute lower abdominal pain such as appendicitis, salpingitis, ectopic pregnancy, inguinal hernia, inflammatory bowel disease, and bowel obstruction (p.18 abdominal pain differential table). Ureteric obstruction due to extrinsic malignancy (pelvic/prostatic/gynecologic tumors, retroperitoneal nodes) or post-radiation ureteric fibrosis, which can mimic stone-related obstruction (p.631). Acute pyelonephritis (flank pain, fever, pyuria) (p.1118). Perinephric or renal abscess — flank/abdominal pain, fever in at least half; suspect when pyelonephritis remains febrile after 4-5 days, when urine culture is polymicrobial, when stones are known, or when fever and pyuria coexist with a sterile urine culture (p.1118). Renal ultrasonography — useful to identify hydronephrosis/ureteric and pelvic dilation, though it may be falsely negative early or when ureteric dilation is prevented (e.g., retroperitoneal fibrosis or tumor encasement) (p.383, p.631). Abdominal CT and renal ultrasound are the most useful modalities when perinephric/renal abscess is suspected (p.1118). Urinalysis showing alkaline urine plus a urease-producing organism (e.g., Proteus) may prompt evaluation for urolithiasis, though Harrison notes clinical support for routine action on this finding is lacking (p.1334).

Renovascular Disease — Essential (primary) hypertension Renal parenchymal disease Primary aldosteronism Pheochromocytoma Hypertensive nephrosclerosis / arteriolonephrosclerosis Atheroembolic renal disease Thromboembolic renal disease / renal infarction Renal infarction from septic emboli (e.g., subacute bacterial endocarditis vegetations) Thrombotic renal occlusion precipitated by systemic infection such as COVID-19 Duplex (Doppler) ultrasonography: peak systolic renal artery velocity >200 cm/s suggests >60% occlusion (some trials use >300 cm/s to reduce false positives); renal resistive index informs kidney viability but is operator-dependent Contrast-enhanced CT angiography: excellent vascular images and assessment of accessory/distal vessels; stents do not cause artifacts; small contrast toxicity risk Magnetic resonance angiography: non-nephrotoxic but gadolinium is avoided when eGFR <30 due to nephrogenic systemic fibrosis risk; cannot visualize stented vessels Captopril renography (99mTc-MAG3): strong negative predictive value when entirely normal; limited utility with advanced atherosclerosis or creatinine >2.0 mg/dL Intraarterial (digital subtraction) angiography: gold standard for large-vessel disease, often performed at time of planned intervention Plasma renin activity is subject to timing, drugs, and sodium intake and does not reliably predict response to revascularization; renal venous renin sampling is now rarely used due to false results

Rhabdomyolysis — Clostridial myositis/myonecrosis — predictably precipitates acute rhabdomyolysis (Harrison 22e p.1096). Streptococcal (group A) myositis — also predictably causes acute rhabdomyolysis (Harrison 22e p.1096). Viral myositis — influenza, echovirus, coxsackievirus and Epstein-Barr virus infections may be associated with rhabdomyolysis (Harrison 22e p.1096). Legionella infection — reported association with rhabdomyolysis (Harrison 22e p.1096). Urine dipstick for blood with microscopy — dipstick blood-positive but RBC-negative supports myoglobinuria rather than true haematuria (Harrison 22e p.343). Urine sediment / microscopy for muddy-brown (pigmented) granular casts and tubular epithelial cells, indicating accompanying acute tubular necrosis (Harrison 22e p.343). Serum phosphate and calcium — hyperphosphataemia and hypocalcaemia accompany acute muscle injury (Harrison 22e p.359, p.363). Fractional excretion of sodium (FENa) — may be <1% in early rhabdomyolysis-associated ATN, limiting its discriminatory value (Harrison 22e p.343). Massive skeletal muscle breakdown releases intracellular contents — including myoglobin, potassium, phosphate and creatine kinase — into the circulation. Filtered myoglobin (a heme protein) is nephrotoxic and contributes to pigment-induced acute tubular necrosis; the released heme pigment also causes a false-positive dipstick reaction for blood. Concurrent volume sequestration into injured muscle produces a prerenal/hypovolaemic insult that compounds the tubular injury (Harrison 22e p.343).

Rheumatoid arthritis — Primary Sjogren's syndrome - polyarthralgia and mild synovitis can mimic RA, and ~50% are RF-positive; distinguished by predominant sicca symptoms, ANA positivity and anti-Ro/SSA in about two-thirds (Harrison 22e p.2847). Spondyloarthropathies (psoriatic arthritis, enteropathy-associated arthritis) - distinguished by sacroiliitis, enthesopathy, and presence of psoriasis or inflammatory bowel disease (Harrison 22e p.2847). Polymyalgia rheumatica in elderly patients - can resemble seronegative RA; PMR centres on neck/shoulder and hip girdle, whereas RA predominantly affects wrists/hands and ankles/feet, especially at onset (Harrison 22e p.2847). Remitting seronegative symmetrical synovitis with pitting edema (RS3PE) - features prominent distal-limb pitting edema (unusual in RA) and responds promptly to low-dose prednisone (Harrison 22e p.2847). Paraneoplastic syndromes - may be confused with early RA (Harrison 22e p.2847). Virus-related polyarthritis syndromes - can mimic RA and cause transient RF production, but usually resolve within 2-3 weeks (Harrison 22e p.2847). Hepatitis C-related arthropathy - often involves small joints of the hands and is RF-positive in about half of cases, but generally anti-CCP negative (Harrison 22e p.2847). Subacute bacterial endocarditis and chronic hepatitis B/C - chronic infections that can produce a positive RF and confound interpretation (Harrison 22e p.2847).

Rickettsial Diseases — Influenza and other viral febrile illnesses Immune thrombocytopenic purpura and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura Kawasaki disease Immune-complex vasculitis Bacterial or viral meningoencephalitis (when CNS involvement predominates) Acute abdomen / enterocolitis (when GI symptoms predominate, has prompted laparotomy) Culture-negative endocarditis (chronic Q fever) Enteroviral infection and infectious mononucleosis Viral hepatitis Leptospirosis Typhoid (enteric) fever Gram-negative or gram-positive bacterial sepsis / toxic shock syndrome Meningococcemia and disseminated gonococcal infection Measles (rubeola), rubella, secondary syphilis Drug hypersensitivity reaction Other rickettsioses within the group (RMSF vs HME, HGA, murine typhus, sylvatic flying-squirrel typhus, rickettsialpox can mimic one another) Epidemic typhus is frequently misdiagnosed as typhoid fever in tropical settings HGA can mimic atypical or severe Lyme disease and patients may develop Lyme antibodies without true co-infection Leptospirosis, dengue, and other tropical febrile illnesses Q fever pneumonia mimics community-acquired pneumonia of other etiologies; Q fever hepatitis mimics other granulomatous hepatitides Indirect immunofluorescence (IFA) serology on paired acute and convalescent sera is the mainstay; for RMSF a titer of >=64 is not detectable until ~7-10 days after onset (IgG sensitivity 89-100%, specificity 99-100%), so it is usually negative at presentation

IgG avidity testing to distinguish primary infection (low-avidity antibodies, recent infection) from reinfection (mature high-avidity IgG indicating infection at least ~2 months earlier); especially useful in pregnant women to assess CRS risk (Harrison 22e p.1644). Salicylate toxicity — Serial quantitative serum salicylate level (guides management) (p.3706) Anion gap and serum lactate (lactate typically lower than the anion gap in salicylate vs near-equal in shock/organ failure) (p.3705) Serum glucose and calcium (risk of hypoglycemia, hypocalcemia) (p.3714) Potassium (hypokalemia) (p.3714) Abdominal x-ray/CT may show radiopaque enteric-coated salicylate tablets or concretions (p.3706) Other high-anion-gap metabolic acidoses: methanol, ethylene glycol, alcoholic/diabetic/starvation ketoacidosis, lactic acidosis, kidney failure (p.412) Other causes of ketosis: acetone, isopropyl alcohol, alcoholic ketoacidosis (p.3705) Other causes of drug-induced respiratory alkalosis: theophylline/aminophylline; also sepsis, hepatic failure, pregnancy/progesterone (p.376) Salicylate increases sensitivity of the CNS respiratory center and directly stimulates the medullary chemoreceptor, driving hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis. It also uncouples oxidative phosphorylation, inhibits Krebs cycle enzymes, and stimulates carbohydrate and lipid metabolism, generating unmeasured endogenous anions (and increased lactate) that produce a high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis (p.376, p.3714). Classic course: early nausea/vomiting and hyperventilation with respiratory alkalosis and alkaline urine, evolving to a mixed respiratory alkalosis plus high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis with paradoxical aciduria; late stages show acidemia with CNS and respiratory depression (p.3714).

Sexually Transmitted Infections: Overview and Clinical Approach — Acute epididymitis must be distinguished from testicular torsion (a surgical emergency with sudden pain, testicular elevation, and absent Doppler flow), testicular tumor, and trauma (Harrison 22e p.1101) Dysuric women: STI-associated urethral syndrome (sterile pyuria, <10^2 conventional uropathogens/mL) versus bacterial cystitis (single uropathogen >=10^2/mL) versus acute pyelonephritis (costovertebral tenderness/fever) (Harrison 22e p.1100-1101) Persistent genital ulcer not resolving with syndrome-based therapy: consider donovanosis, carcinoma, and other nonvenereal dermatoses on biopsy (Harrison 22e p.1108) Pelvic inflammatory disease that is not due to specific STIs (secondary to appendicitis, regional ileitis, diverticulitis, hematogenous tuberculosis or staphylococcal bacteremia, or tropical disease such as schistosomiasis) (Harrison 22e p.1104) Chronic granulomatous epididymal disease such as tuberculosis mimicking sexually acquired epididymitis when symptoms persist after therapy (Harrison 22e p.1101) Risk assessment using a structured sexual-history questionnaire (e.g., the eleven-question STD/HIV risk assessment) to guide screening and presumptive treatment decisions (Harrison 22e p.1098) Urethral Gram's stain to confirm urethritis and detect gram-negative diplococci, recognizing that up to ~30% of gonococcal urethral infections can yield a negative Gram's stain (Harrison 22e p.1099)

Shigellosis — Salmonella infection Campylobacter jejuni infection Clostridium difficile colitis Yersinia enterocolitica infection Entamoeba histolytica (amebic dysentery) Inflammatory bowel disease (first flare of Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis), particularly in industrialized countries Enteroinvasive E. coli (can cause a shigellosis-like dysentery) Salmonellosis Campylobacter jejuni enteritis Clostridium difficile colitis Yersinia enterocolitica enterocolitis Amebic dysentery (Entamoeba histolytica) Enteroinvasive E. coli dysentery Enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) infection (predominant cause of HUS in industrialized countries) Stool culture is the gold standard; sample the bloody/mucopurulent portion directly, or use rectal swabs (highest yield in the acute phase). Because Shigella is fragile and dies during transport, use a holding medium (buffered glycerol saline or Cary-Blair) with prompt inoculation onto isolation media. Use multiple media to raise yield: nonselective (bromocresol-purple lactose), low-selectivity (MacConkey, eosin-methylene blue), and high-selectivity (Hektoen, Salmonella-Shigella, or xylose-lysine-deoxycholate agar). Microscopy of stool smears: bacterial enteroinvasive infection (including shigellosis) shows high PMN counts per field, whereas E. histolytica shows erythrophagocytic trophozoites with very few PMNs. Identify shigellae as non-lactose-fermenting colonies that are glucose-positive (usually no gas), lactose-negative, H2S-negative, and nonmotile; confirm serogroup by slide agglutination.

Sickle Cell Disease — Acute chest syndrome (pneumonia-like illness with chest pain, cough, fever, hypoxia and a pulmonary infiltrate) closely resembles and may coexist with bacterial pneumonia; antibiotics are almost always used even though a causative bacterium is often not cultured (p.775). Multiorgan failure accompanying severe acute chest syndrome is often confused with, and can coexist with, sepsis (p.774, Table 103-3). High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) and hemoglobin electrophoresis to quantify hemoglobin fractions (HbS, HbF, HbA, HbA2, HbC) and distinguish trait, sickle cell anaemia and HbSC disease (Table 103-2, Fig. 103-4, p.772). Peripheral blood film: irreversibly sickled cells, target cells and nucleated red cells in HbSS/HbS-beta0 thalassaemia; HbC crystals, taco-folded cells and contracted microspherocytes in HbSC disease (Fig. 103-4, p.772-774). DNA-based diagnosis for genetic counselling and family planning; antenatal diagnosis by chorionic villus sampling or cell-free DNA (p.772, 776). Transcranial Doppler screening in children (ages 2-16) to identify stroke risk (Table 103-3, p.776). Echocardiographic measurement of tricuspid regurgitant jet velocity (TRV) annually to screen for pulmonary hypertension. Screening for microalbuminuria from age 10 for nephropathy, and annual fluorescein angiography from age 10 for retinopathy. HbS behaves like HbA except that it polymerises when deoxygenated: contacts between beta6 valine residues of deoxy-HbS and beta/alpha-globin residues form hemoglobin fascicles that injure the sickle erythrocyte, after a delay between initiation of polymerisation and accumulation of damaging polymer. Giant cell (temporal) arteritis — Migraine - common in the elderly (more prevalent than GCA) and may improve with prednisone, so a steroid response does not by itself confirm GCA (Harrison 22e p.115). Nonarteritic anterior ischemic optic neuropathy - associated with a crowded 'disc-at-risk' / small optic cup, in which glucocorticoids should NOT be prescribed, contrasting with the arteritic form (Harrison 22e p.227). Isolated polymyalgia rheumatica without arteritis (Harrison 22e p.2903). Other inflammatory causes of secondary headache such as sarcoidosis and Behcet's syndrome (Harrison 22e p.115). Temporal artery biopsy: yield improved by harvesting a long segment (3-5 cm) with serial sectioning because involvement is segmental/patchy; biopsy may still show vasculitis even after about 14 days of glucocorticoids, but prolonged treatment can mask findings (Harrison 22e p.227, p.2903). Temporal artery ultrasonography (alone or with axillary arteries) showing a noncompressible 'halo' sign supports the diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.2903). Large-vessel imaging by MR or CT angiography to confirm large-vessel disease suggested by diminished pulses or bruits; PET is increasingly studied but its diagnostic/monitoring role remains unclear (Harrison 22e p.2903). Note: in patients treated with an IL-6 inhibitor, CRP and ESR normalize and can no longer be used to monitor disease activity or assess for infection (Harrison 22e p.2902).

Tension-type headache — Migraine (the main differential, defined by migrainous accompaniments TTH lacks) (Harrison 22e p.3514) Migraine-TTH overlap / mixed phenotype with intercurrent migraine attacks (Harrison 22e p.3514) TTH is a clinical diagnosis; neuroimaging is not routine but CT or MRI of the brain is indicated when the examination is abnormal or the headache is recent-onset, with CT and MRI being comparably sensitive as initial screens (Harrison 22e p.157). Lumbar puncture may be required when a serious secondary cause is suspected and a benign etiology cannot otherwise be established (Harrison 22e p.157). General evaluation of acute headache may add palpation of cranial arteries, cervical spine assessment, blood pressure and urine for cardiovascular/renal status, and ocular examination including funduscopy and intraocular pressure (Harrison 22e p.157). Chronic migraine within the chronic daily headache spectrum (Harrison 22e p.158, Table 17-3) Medication-overuse headache (refractory daily/near-daily headache from analgesic overuse) (Harrison 22e p.158-159) Other secondary causes of chronic daily headache: post-traumatic, inflammatory (e.g., giant cell arteritis, sarcoidosis, Behcet syndrome), and chronic CNS infection (Harrison 22e p.158, Table 17-3) The mechanism of TTH is incompletely understood. Harrison favors a primary disorder of central nervous system pain modulation alone, contrasting it with migraine, which involves more generalized disturbance of sensory modulation. Despite the name, there is no clear evidence that nervous tension is causative; importantly, muscle contraction does NOT reliably distinguish TTH from migraine, as no difference in contraction is seen between the two headache types. Tetanus — Strychnine poisoning Dystonic reactions to antidopaminergic (antidopaminergic drug) agents Stiff person syndrome Somatic symptom disorder Hypocalcemia (in neonatal tetanus) Meningoencephalitis (in neonatal tetanus) Oropharyngeal, peritonsillar, or submaxillary infection / lymphadenitis and cranial nerve disease (mimics of cephalic tetanus / trismus) Intracranial hemorrhage Peritonitis or acute abdominal emergency (versus continuous abdominal rigidity of tetanus) Oropharyngeal infection Peritonsillar infection Submaxillary lymphadenitis Meningoencephalitis Diagnosis is clinical; confirmatory laboratory testing is limited. Wound culture of C. tetani cannot confirm the diagnosis (a positive culture is non-confirmatory). Serum antitetanus IgG measured before antitoxin/immunoglobulin administration: levels >0.1 IU/mL (standard ELISA) are deemed protective and argue against tetanus. Serum tetanus toxin bioassay may help if antibody is below the protective threshold, but a negative result does not exclude tetanus and the assay is not generally performed. PCR and recombinase polymerase amplification to detect the tetanus neurotoxin gene are promising but emerging techniques. Thyroid storm — Other causes of thyrotoxicosis besides Graves' disease must be considered (e.g. toxic adenoma, toxic multinodular goitre, destructive thyroiditis, ectopic thyroid tissue, factitious thyrotoxicosis); radionuclide scan/uptake or color-flow Doppler ultrasonography helps distinguish hyperthyroidism from destructive thyroiditis (Harrison 22e p.3078). Suppressed TSH with elevated total and unbound (free) T4 and T3 (Harrison 22e p.3078). T3 toxicosis (only T3 raised) in 2-5% of patients, more in areas of borderline iodine intake; T4 toxicosis (raised T4, normal T3) is occasionally seen when hyperthyroidism is iodine-induced (Harrison 22e p.3078). TRAb (TSH receptor antibody) measurement to support a diagnosis of Graves' disease (Harrison 22e p.3078). Watch for confounding biochemistry: elevated bilirubin, liver enzymes and ferritin, plus microcytic anaemia and thrombocytopenia, may accompany thyrotoxicosis (Harrison 22e p.3078). Thyroid storm represents a severe, decompensated form of thyroid hormone excess (thyrotoxicosis), typically arising when an acute stressor is superimposed on partially treated or untreated hyperthyroidism. Excess circulating thyroid hormone drives a hypermetabolic, hyperadrenergic state; high cardiac output produces a bounding pulse, widened pulse pressure and may precipitate or worsen heart failure or angina, particularly in the elderly or those with pre-existing heart disease (Harrison 22e p.3077, p.3080).

Chorioretinitis in an AIDS patient: CMV, syphilis, HSV, VZV, and fungal infection (Harrison 22e p.1801). Urinary Tract Infections: Cystitis, Prostatitis, and Pyelonephritis — Asymptomatic bacteriuria (positive culture without localizing symptoms) Sexually transmitted infections - urethritis/cervicitis from Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, Mycoplasma genitalium Vaginitis (Candida albicans, Trichomonas vaginalis) Herpetic urethritis Interstitial cystitis Chronic pelvic pain syndrome (in men) Noninfectious vulvar/vaginal irritation Cervicitis due to Chlamydia trachomatis or Neisseria gonorrhoeae Vaginitis (Trichomonas vaginalis, Candida albicans) Herpetic urethritis Urethritis from Mycoplasma genitalium Urine dipstick for nitrite and leukocyte esterase (best used to help rule out UTI; only Enterobacterales convert nitrate to nitrite, so non-Enterobacterales and dilute frequently-voided urine can be falsely negative) Microscopic urinalysis for pyuria and hematuria Urine culture with susceptibilities - warranted in pregnancy, suspected resistant organisms, recurrent or complicated UTI, and all male UTI; ASB screening in pregnancy must use culture because dipstick is not sufficiently sensitive Blood cultures when fever or systemic signs suggest infection beyond the bladder Imaging (CT or ultrasound) in men with febrile UTI (even first episode) to evaluate for obstruction or anatomic abnormality; suspect intraparenchymal abscess with persistent fever/bacteremia despite therapy Urologic consultation for unclear diagnosis or recurrent UTI in men

Urinary Tract Obstruction — Benign prostatic hyperplasia (bladder outlet obstruction) Neurogenic bladder / functional obstruction (diabetic neuropathy, spinal cord disease, cauda equina syndrome) Pregnant uterus / uterine leiomyomata Accidental surgical ligation or injury of the ureter during pelvic or colonic surgery Aortic aneurysm (extrinsic ureteric compression) Drug-related urinary retention (anticholinergics, alpha-adrenergic agonists, opiates) Carcinoma of prostate, bladder, cervix, colon, or rectum Retroperitoneal fibrosis Lymphoma (particularly follicular) with retroperitoneal involvement Calculi (ureteric, bladder, urethral) Urethral stricture Ureteropelvic junction (UPJ) narrowing/obstruction Vesicoureteral reflux Posterior urethral valves (boys) Pyelonephritis (urinary stasis from obstruction encourages organism growth; UTO must always be considered with UTIs) Generalized sepsis from an infected obstructed system Bladder catheter insertion and postvoid residual measurement Abdominal scout film/KUB (insensitive; may show nephrocalcinosis or radiopaque stone) Furosemide-augmented imaging to distinguish functional from anatomic obstruction Bedside bladder ultrasound to assess bladder volume Abdominal ultrasonography (~90% sensitive and specific for hydronephrosis) Noncontrast multidetector CT (test of choice for acute flank pain; visualizes retroperitoneum and intrinsic/extrinsic sites of obstruction; characterizes stones by Hounsfield units)

Urticaria, Angioedema & Allergic Rhinitis — Acute vs chronic urticaria/angioedema (cutoff 6 weeks duration) Serum sickness and hypocomplementemic urticarial vasculitis Allergic rhinitis: nonallergic rhinitis with eosinophilia (NARES), vasomotor/perennial nonallergic rhinitis, rhinitis medicamentosa, gustatory rhinitis, hormonal (pregnancy) rhinitis, drug-induced rhinitis, hypothyroidism, anatomic/structural nasal defects, nasal foreign body Inducible (physical) urticarias: dermatographism, cholinergic, cold, solar, pressure, vibratory, heat, aquagenic, contact Urticarial vasculitis (immune-complex disease; small-vessel leukocytoclastic vasculitis) Mastocytosis (cutaneous or systemic; urticaria pigmentosa) Hereditary angioedema (C1INH type 1/2; type 3 with normal C1INH e.g. factor XII mutation) Acquired C1INH deficiency (lymphoproliferative or autoimmune disease) ACE inhibitor-induced (bradykinin-mediated) angioedema CIAS1/NLRP3-associated periodic fever syndromes (familial cold autoinflammatory syndrome, Muckle-Wells syndrome) Schnitzler's syndrome, Gleich's syndrome, hypereosinophilic syndrome Viral infection-associated acute urticaria (a common trigger of new-onset acute urticaria) Bacterial or parasitic infection-associated urticaria (travel history should prompt parasite evaluation) Hepatitis B or C and SARS-CoV-2 infection associated with urticaria/urticarial vasculitis Upper respiratory tract infection mimicking rhinitis; secondary bacterial sinusitis/otitis from mucosal swelling

Variceal bleeding — Peptic ulcer disease — the most common cause of upper GI bleeding (~50% of UGIB hospitalisations) (p.360) Mallory-Weiss tear — ~2-10% of UGIB, classically preceded by vomiting/retching/coughing, usually on the gastric side of the gastro-oesophageal junction; stops spontaneously in ~80-90% (p.360) Bleeding gastric varices, intestinal varices, and portal hypertensive gastropathy/enterocolopathy — other portal-hypertension-related sources distinct from oesophageal varices (p.361, p.2714) Erosive disease — erosive oesophagitis, gastritis, duodenitis (up to ~30% of UGIB), commonly NSAID-related (p.361) Stress-related gastric mucosal injury in the critically ill (p.361) Less common: neoplasm, vascular ectasias (including hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, gastric antral vascular ectasia), Dieulafoy's lesion, aortoenteric fistula, haemobilia/haemosuccus pancreaticus (p.361) Upper endoscopy within 24 h is first-line both to diagnose the bleeding source and to treat acutely; more urgent endoscopy (6-12 h) does not improve outcomes and may worsen them in high-risk patients (p.362, p.2714) Endoscopic surveillance for varices: recommended at diagnosis of compensated cirrhosis, then every 2 years (active liver disease) or every 3 years (inactive); also at the time of hepatic decompensation (p.2714) Liver stiffness by transient elastography — if <20 kPa and no thrombocytopenia, high-risk varices are rare and screening endoscopy may be deferred (p.2714)

Varicella-Zoster Virus Infection — For chickenpox: disseminated HSV infection in patients with atopic dermatitis; disseminated vesiculopapular lesions of coxsackievirus or echovirus infection; atypical measles (these rashes are more often morbilliform/hemorrhagic than vesicular) (p.1506) Rickettsialpox - distinguished by the 'herald spot' (eschar) at the mite-bite site and a more pronounced headache; serology helps differentiate it from varicella (p.1506) Mpox - consider in travelers from endemic areas and in HIV-infected individuals (p.1506) Smallpox - bioterrorism concern; smallpox lesions are larger than chickenpox lesions and all at the same stage of evolution at any given time (p.1506) For herpes zoster: both HSV and coxsackievirus infections can cause dermatomal vesicular lesions (p.1506) Disseminated HSV infection (notably in atopic dermatitis) (p.1506) Coxsackievirus infection (p.1506) Echovirus infection (p.1506) Atypical measles (p.1506) Rickettsialpox (p.1506) Mpox (p.1506) Smallpox (p.1506) HSV and coxsackievirus causing dermatomal vesicular lesions (mimicking zoster) (p.1506) PCR for VZV DNA in vesicular fluid - diagnostic method of choice; also performed on lesions, blood, and saliva (p.1507) Tzanck smear (scraping of lesion base for multinucleated giant cells) - rapid but low sensitivity (~60%) (p.1507) Viral isolation in susceptible tissue-culture cell lines (unequivocal confirmation) (p.1507) Direct immunofluorescent staining of cells from the lesion base or immunoperoxidase detection of viral antigens (p.1507)

Vascular Dementia — Alzheimer's disease (most common dementia; mixed AD-vascular pathology very common) Dementia with Lewy bodies / PDD spectrum Frontotemporal dementia Limbic-predominant age-related TDP-43 encephalopathy (LATE) Normal pressure hydrocephalus Delirium Brain MRI is the mainstay for detection and subtyping of cerebrovascular disease; should include FLAIR, diffusion-weighted, and T2*-weighted sequences to detect large and small chronic infarcts, acute microinfarcts, microbleeds, and white matter hyperintensities (p.3491) Diffusion tensor MRI (e.g., peak width of skeletonized mean diffusivity, PSMD) detects white matter disconnection (largely research use) (p.3490) Vessel imaging (CT or MR angiography) is not required for initial cognitive evaluation but may help determine the cause of identified macroscopic infarcts (p.3491) Screening for atrial fibrillation in individuals with asymptomatic infarcts; prolonged cardiac monitoring for embolic-appearing infarcts (p.3491) Genetic testing for hereditary VCID (CADASIL, hereditary cerebral amyloid angiopathy) when young onset, positive family history, or suggestive imaging—otherwise unnecessary (p.3491) Alzheimer's disease (frequently coexists as mixed dementia—a key pitfall) Normal pressure hydrocephalus (shares gait disturbance) Delirium (prominent attention/executive deficits) Vascular dementia results from the cumulative impact of cerebrovascular disease on age-related cognitive decline. Symptomatic strokes (ischemic or hemorrhagic) produce irreversible injury whose cognitive effect depends on size and location. Systemic vasculitis — Granulomatosis with polyangiitis (GPA) - upper + lower respiratory tract granulomatous vasculitis plus pauci-immune glomerulonephritis; PR3/cANCA in >90% of active disease (Harrison 22e p.2939-2940) Lymphomatoid granulomatosis - EBV-positive angiocentric B-cell proliferation with lung/skin/CNS/kidney involvement that mimics GPA but is not a true vasculitis (Harrison 22e p.2941) Microscopic polyangiitis (MPA) - pauci-immune small-vessel necrotizing vasculitis with frequent glomerulonephritis and pulmonary capillaritis but no granulomas; MPO/pANCA in ~75% (Harrison 22e p.2942) Eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis / Churg-Strauss (EGPA) - asthma, eosinophilia, extravascular granuloma, vasculitis; ANCA (anti-MPO) in ~48% (Harrison 22e p.2943-2944) Polyarteritis nodosa (PAN) - necrotizing vasculitis of small/medium muscular arteries with microaneurysms, sparing lungs and glomeruli; associated with hepatitis B (and C); consider DADA2 in early-onset disease (Harrison 22e p.2944-2945) Giant cell (temporal) arteritis with polymyalgia rheumatica - medium/large-vessel arteritis in patients over 50 (Harrison 22e p.2945-2946) Takayasu arteritis - large-vessel arteritis of the aorta and its branches in young women (Harrison 22e p.2946-2947) IgA vasculitis (Henoch-Schonlein) - small-vessel immune-complex vasculitis with palpable purpura, arthralgia, GI symptoms, glomerulonephritis; IgA/C3 on biopsy (Harrison 22e p.2947-2948)

Vasovagal / orthostatic syncope — Generalized and partial/partial-complex seizures (with secondary generalization, usually preceded by an aura such as an unpleasant smell, fear, anxiety, or abdominal/visceral sensation). Autonomic seizures (autonomic epilepsy), whose cardiovascular, GI, pulmonary, urogenital, pupillary, and cutaneous manifestations mimic syncopal prodrome; accompanying non-autonomic auras help distinguish them. Hypoglycemia, typically in insulin-treated type 1 or type 2 diabetes (tremor, palpitations, anxiety, diaphoresis, hunger, paresthesias; hunger is not a typical syncope prodrome). Cataplexy (abrupt loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion such as laughter or anger; consciousness is preserved, lasts 30 s to 2 min, no prodrome; occurs in 60-75% of narcolepsy). Vertebrobasilar ischemia and hypoxemia as other causes of transient loss of consciousness. Falls due to vestibular dysfunction, cerebellar disease, extrapyramidal/gait disorders, and falls with head trauma (especially difficult in patients with dementia and repeated falls). Psychogenic apparent loss of consciousness from psychiatric disorders (generalized anxiety, panic disorder, major depression, somatization), suggested by frequent fainting without prodrome and rare injury despite numerous falls, with no significant hemodynamic change. 12-lead ECG when arrhythmia or underlying cardiac disease is suspected; look for brady-/tachyarrhythmias, AV block, acute or old myocardial ischemia/infarction, long QT, and bundle branch block.

Viral Gastroenteritis — Bacterial gastroenteritis (e.g., Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter, Vibrio cholerae, enterotoxigenic E. coli) - distinguished by inflammatory/bloody diarrhea, fecal leukocytes, and epidemiologic features Preformed bacterial toxin food poisoning (Staphylococcus aureus, Bacillus cereus) - very short incubation of hours Clostridioides difficile colitis Protozoal/parasitic diarrhea (e.g., Giardia, Cryptosporidium) Bacterial enteritis (Salmonella, Shigella, Campylobacter jejuni, Vibrio, E. coli) Staphylococcus aureus and Bacillus cereus preformed-toxin food poisoning Clostridioides difficile colitis Gastrointestinal symptoms of systemic respiratory viral infections (SARS-CoV, influenza A/H5N1, pandemic influenza A/H1N1) Commercial enzyme immunoassays (EIA) for rotavirus and enteric adenovirus in stool RT-PCR / multiplex molecular panels for norovirus and other enteric pathogens (increasingly used clinically) Electron microscopy and polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE) for viral RNA - largely research/public-health tools Fecal examination for leukocytes and blood to help separate viral (typically negative) from inflammatory bacterial causes Stool culture on special media when bacterial pathogens are suspected Osmotic or secretory diarrhea from other causes Carbohydrate malabsorption states Other causes of acute vomiting without true gastroenteritis Enteric viruses injure the small-intestinal mucosa to produce predominantly watery diarrhea. Viral Hemorrhagic Fever — Falciparum malaria (a most important mimic and a treatable, potentially fatal alternative) Typhoid fever Other treatable travel-associated febrile illnesses: shigellosis, leptospirosis, relapsing fever, rickettsial diseases Other VHFs/high-consequence viral infections, in particular Lassa fever and yellow fever Dengue and other viral hemorrhagic fevers in the bleeding/febrile traveler Falciparum malaria Other high-consequence viral infections (Lassa fever, yellow fever) Typhoid fever Enterohemorrhagic E. coli enteritis Gram-negative septicemia (including shigellosis) Meningococcal septicemia Rickettsial infections Fulminant viral hepatitis Leptospirosis Measles RT-PCR targeting one or more filovirid genes is the diagnostic assay of choice; in-field PCR platforms (e.g., Cepheid GeneXpert) are deployed during outbreaks Acute-phase blood/serum is the preferred specimen as it usually contains high virion titers Antigen-capture ELISA / immunochromatographic rapid diagnostic tests (currently limited; EBOV antigen RDT sensitivity restricts use largely to postmortem samples) IgM- and IgG-capture ELISAs (including multiplex) for antibodies in later disease and in survivors Virus isolation/plaque assays and electron microscopy require maximum-containment laboratories; in-field genome sequencing supports outbreak epidemiology Supportive labs typically show leukopenia (then leukocytosis), thrombocytopenia, raised aminotransferases (AST > ALT) and GGT, raised creatinine/urea with proteinuria, electrolyte derangement, hypoglycemia, hypoalbuminemia, prolonged PT/PTT, elevated CPK, and markedly elevated CRP in severe illness

Vitamin and Trace Mineral Deficiency and Excess — Protein-energy malnutrition Malabsorption syndromes (celiac disease, Crohn's disease, short-bowel syndrome) Chronic alcohol use disorder Post-bariatric-surgery nutrient deficiency Inborn errors of metabolism affecting micronutrient handling (Hartnup disease, biotinidase deficiency, abetalipoproteinemia, Menkes/Wilson disease) Erythrocyte transketolase activity with thiamine pyrophosphate stimulation (>25% / activity coefficient >1.25 abnormal); serum/blood thiamine by HPLC Erythrocyte glutathione reductase activity for riboflavin; urinary 2-pyridone/2-methylnicotinamide for niacin Plasma pyridoxal 5'-phosphate (deficiency <20 nmol/L) for vitamin B6; plasma/leukocyte ascorbate for vitamin C Serum retinol (normal 1.05-3.50 micromol/L; deficient <0.70 micromol/L [20 microg/dL]) interpreted alongside C-reactive protein and alpha1-acid glycoprotein Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (>20 ng/mL adequate for bone health); plasma alpha-tocopherol (deficient <5 microg/mL) for vitamin E Prothrombin time and PIVKA-II (undercarboxylated prothrombin) plus serum phylloquinone (<0.15 microg/L) for vitamin K Serum zinc (<12 micromol/L / <70 microg/dL), serum copper (<65 microg/dL) with ceruloplasmin (<20 mg/dL), interpreted with albumin and acute-phase status Peripheral neuropathy from diabetes or heavy-metal toxicity (mimics thiamine, B6, B12, or vitamin E deficiency) Dermatitis/seborrhea of other cause (mimics niacin, riboflavin, biotin, or zinc deficiency)

Wernicke encephalopathy — Supranuclear gaze disorder mimicking combined abducens and oculomotor nerve palsy (Wernicke can itself cause this pattern) Other metabolic encephalopathies (hepatic, hypercarbic, hyper-/hyponatremic, hyper-/hypoglycemic) Sepsis-associated encephalopathy Osmotic demyelination syndrome (central pontine myelinolysis) Marchiafava-Bignami disease (corpus callosum degeneration in chronic alcoholism) Alcoholic cerebellar degeneration Encephalitis (including herpes simplex encephalitis as a cause of an amnestic state) Whipple's disease (cause of supranuclear gaze palsy) MRI may show changes including abnormal enhancement of the mammillary bodies (coronal T1 postcontrast), typical of acute Wernicke Erythrocyte transketolase activity assay measured before and after adding thiamine pyrophosphate; >25% stimulation (activity coefficient >=1.25) is abnormal Serum/blood thiamine or its phosphorylated esters by high-performance liquid chromatography Serum magnesium (required cofactor for thiamine activation) Autoimmune limbic encephalitis (e.g., AMPAR, LGI1 antibodies) causing amnesia Paraneoplastic encephalitis (e.g., Ma antibodies) Thalamic, medial temporal, or posterior corpus callosum tumor causing amnesia Anterior/posterior cerebral artery territory infarction causing amnesia Stroke (infarct/hemorrhage), multiple sclerosis, vasculitis, or tumor causing supranuclear gaze palsy Wernicke disease results from thiamine (vitamin B1) deficiency. Thiamine is a cofactor for several enzymes including transketolase, pyruvate dehydrogenase, and alpha-ketoglutarate dehydrogenase. Whipple Disease — Seronegative inflammatory arthritis / rheumatoid arthritis (initial arthralgic phase is often confused with rheumatologic disorders; RF and ANA usually negative) (p.1368) Lymphoma (mesenteric/retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy on CT commonly raises this concern) (p.1368) Sarcoidosis or granulomatous vasculitis (noncaseating granulomas from lymphatic/hepatic involvement; ocular disease may also be misdiagnosed as sarcoid) (p.1368) Behcet's disease (in patients with ocular/uveitic disease) (p.1368) Mycobacterial infection (PAS positivity is nonspecific and also occurs with mycobacteria and other microorganisms) (p.1369) Giardia lamblia co-infection, occasionally identified, can cause diagnostic misdirection (p.1368) Other causes of culture-negative endocarditis (T. whipplei causes 2.6-6.3% of culture-negative endocarditis) (p.1368) Postbulbar (more distal) duodenal biopsies with PAS staining for diastase-resistant inclusions in lamina propria macrophages plus PCR for T. whipplei (tissue yield exceeds body-fluid yield) (p.1369) Video-capsule endoscopy to identify more distal small-bowel lesions when initial duodenal biopsy is nondiagnostic (p.1368) Urine PCR as a potential noninvasive test and therapeutic-monitoring tool (positive in ~75% of cases pretreatment in one small study); plasma cell-free DNA next-generation sequencing for endocarditis (p.1369, p.1370) PCR of duodenal biopsy: a cycle threshold of <=30 can help confirm the diagnosis even when PAS staining is negative (p.1369)

Wilson's Disease — Viral hepatitis and cirrhosis (often the initial diagnostic considerations in patients who actually have WD) (p.3338) Autoimmune hepatitis / chronic hepatitis (WD in adolescence may present with chronic-hepatitis features long before neurologic signs or Kayser-Fleischer rings appear) (p.3026-area AIH text, ch.355/427) Parkinson disease and other movement disorders (WD may be mistakenly diagnosed as these) (p.3338, p.3518) Substance abuse (a competing consideration in late-teen/early-twenties patients presenting with psychiatric features) (p.3339) Viral hepatitis (a frequent initial misdiagnosis in patients with the hepatic presentation of WD) (p.3338) Serum ceruloplasmin (initial screening test; characteristically low) and serum copper (low) (p.3339) 24-h urinary copper excretion (elevated, >100 ug/24 h; use acid-washed copper-free containers); penicillamine challenge with serial urine copper as a variation (p.3339) Percutaneous needle liver biopsy for quantitative hepatic copper (gold standard; >200 ug/g dry weight characteristic) by ICP-MS or atomic absorption spectrometry; histochemical copper staining is less reliable (p.3339) Slit-lamp or optical coherence tomography ophthalmologic examination for Kayser-Fleischer rings (required to detect early rings) (p.3339) Radiolabeled 64Cu incorporation into ceruloplasmin (highly specific; WD patients incorporate very little) (p.3339)
